title: Environmental Protection Bill, 2024
text:
ENVIRONMENTAL PROD

MEMORANDUM

The object of the Bill is to amend and consolidate laws relating to
environmental protection; establish the Environmental Protection
Authority to regulate and protect the environment, provide for pesticide
control and regulation; provide for the control, management and disposal
of hazardous waste and electrical and electronic waste; provide for the
co-ordination of climate change responses and for related matters.

The Environmental Protection Agency Act, 1994 (Act 490) was
enacted twenty-nine years ago for the regulation of matters that affect
the environment and to coordinate the activities of bodies concerned with
the practical and technical aspects of the environment. Prior to the
enactment of Act 490, the body was established by the Environmental
Protection Council Decree, 1974 (N.R.C.D 239) as the Environmental
Protection Council. The Council advised government on environmental
matters without any enforcement powers. With the enactment of Act 490
in 1994, the Council transitioned into an Agency with regulatory powers.

Act 490 clothed the Agency with the mandate to advise the Minister,
co-ordinate, regulate, control, collaborate, educate, promote studies and
research on the environment as well as investigate and promote effective
planning in the management of the environment. In exercising this
mandate, the Agency has been confronted with several challenges
particularly with respect to the fragmented environmental management
provisions in other enactments across other sectors and the complex
emerging environmental challenges, among others.

The fragmented environmental provisions in other enactments across
other sectors make it difficult for the Agency to exercise general oversight
responsibility over the environment. Institutions such as the Forestry
Commission, the Petroleum Commission, the Fisheries Commission,
and the Ghana Maritime Authority, among others, have some
environmental provisions in their enabling enactments and exercising
oversight responsibility over these institutions is not clearly provided for

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

In addition, the Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies,
the Forestry Commission and the Minerals Commission predated the
Agency and were already exercising a level of regulatory functions over
some aspects of the environment. Oversight of environmental
compliance by such institutions is very challenging because the provisions
in Act 490 do not make the Agency the lead institution for the
environment of Ghana due to the absence of express provisions to reflect
this status.

Furthermore, emerging issues such as plastic pollution, biodiversity
loss, climate change, air quality, upstream petroleum and illegal mining,
among others, are not adequately addressed in Act 490 and as such pose
serious enforcement challenges. This is in spite of the fact that the Agency
has expanded the scope of operations to include these environmental
issues.

It should be noted that the country like the rest of the world is
currently faced with the triple planetary crises which are interlinked. These
crises are climate change, pollution and biodiversity loss and these have
their own causes and effects. Each issue needs to be well-regulated and
managed to enable us have a viable future on this planet.

Climate change is the most pressing issue facing humanity today
and the long-term changes in temperatures and shifts in weather patterns
if not addressed efficiently would in the long-run completely alter the
ecosystems that support human and animal life. Human activities are
the main drivers of climate change and almost every human activity
releases emissions. Energy use, industry, transport, buildings and
agriculture are the main causes for the release of greenhouse gases into
the atmosphere. The consequences of climate change manifest through
increased intensity and severity of droughts, water scarcity, wildfires,
rising sea levels, flooding, catastrophic storms and declining biodiversity.

The potential disruptive effects of climate change on Ghana are not
markedly different from the rest of Africa. Climate change threatens to
erode the developmental gains of the country and hamper the ability to 

ii

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

omplish the sustainable development aspirations. More than thirty
*rs of climate records show that climatic conditions in the country
•'e severely deteriorated and are more likely to worsen in the future.

As of 2019, the contribution of Ghana to global greenhouse gas
issions was estimated to be sixty million tonnes and is likely to increase
lundred million tonnes by 2030, if action is not taken. On the average,
cost of Ghana’s carbon emissions to the global community is two

ion three hundred million United States Dollars each year, equivalent
hree point nine percent (3.9%) of Ghana’s Gross Domestic Product.

.ana’s Second Biennial Update to the United Nations Convention on
anate Change estimated the total net greenhouse gas emissions at about
y-two million two hundred thousand United States Dollars tCO2eq
2016 (MESTI, 2018). Agriculture, forestry and other land uses were
largest source of emissions, followed by energy.

As part of measures to address the climate crises, Ghana has updated
11 enhanced its nationally determined contribution for ten years from
.0 to 2030 in fulfilment of her obligations under the Paris Agreement

U the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change in
cision One of the Twenty-First Meeting of the Conference of Parties.
ana has also developed a national strategy to build a resilient society
tt can adequately withstand the impacts of climate change and
^tribute to mitigating global emissions.

Ghana aims to reduce its absolute greenhouse gas emissions by sixty-four
:ilion tonnes when the nationally-determined contributions are
wlemented. Article Six of the Paris Agreement on carbon markets
>wides the opportunity to implement the nationally determined
ftributions effectively.

The Bill provides a legislative framework to comprehensively respond
’limate change and its effects, and domesticate the United Nations
tmework Convention on Climate Change and its subsidiary protocols

agreements. The Bill also seeks to ensure a just transition to climate
Uience and low-emission development in future.

iii

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

Climate change is multisectoral and being the focal institution for
climate change, there is the need to bring all the actors together and
co-ordinate the implementation of climate change response at all levels.
The Bill therefore seeks to facilitate mainstreaming of climate change
interventions and harmonise the fragmented and ad-hoc nature of
institutional arrangements for climate change.

Another environmental challenge is biodiversity loss which refers to
the decline or disappearance of biological diversity including animals,
plants and ecosystems. The reasons for biodiversity loss include
overfishing, deforestation, land degradation and climate change.
Biodiversity is the baseline for everything on the planet as in the end we
are all interlinked. Loss of biodiversity impacts food supplies and access
to clean water. Without biodiversity, humans have no future on the planet.

In 2022, eighteen thousand hectares of forest was lost in the country.
This was seven thousand three hundred hectares more as compared to
2021. The total annual cost of overfishing in Ghana is estimated at two
hundred and thirty-three United States Dollars which is, equivalent to
zero point four per cent (0.4%) of the Gross Domestic Product of 2017.
The cost of soil erosion is estimated at about US$0.54 billion, or zero
point nine per cent (0.9%) of the country’s Gross Domestic Product. Land
degradation harms Ghana’s most vulnerable population, the rural poor,
by making them even poorer and as such entrenching them further in
extreme poverty.

The country is also faced with massive environmental degradation
caused by illegal small-scale mining, plastic pollution, air pollution,
excessive noise making, water pollution and deforestation, among others.
In 2021, it was estimated that the country lost an estimated eleven billion
United States Dollars as a result of environmental degradation. The
environmental analysis of the country by the World Bank concluded that
environmental degradation and unsustainable use of natural resource pose
a significant risk to economic growth, and public and ecosystem health.

iv

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

Plastics waste management has become one of the biggest and
complex challenges of this century, and as such requires innovative and
integrated solutions to reduce additional cost to conventional
development. Although plastics are a globally important material with
diverse applications in the food and beverage industry, textiles,
construction, electronic and electrical equipment, medicine and pharmacy,
agriculture, amongst others, there are many environmental concerns
associated with the use of plastics. The hazards posed by plastics are
numerous and multi-dimensional and the impacts transcend national
borders.

Ghana has developed the National Plastic Policy that adopts a
circular economy approach to plastics. The Policy aims at creating
economic opportunities for the re-use of plastics, and encouraging
recycling, recovery and remanufacturing of plastics as well as creating a
system to reduce, recover and eliminate the single use of plastics.

The United Nations Environment Assembly has established an
Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee to develop an international
legally binding instrument on plastic pollution. The global treaty intends
to address plastic pollution and could include both binding and voluntary
approaches based on the full life cycle of plastics, taking into account
among other things, national circumstances and capabilities. According
to the United Nations Environment Assembly resolution, the treaty is to
include a series of technical provisions that would promote substantial
production and consumption of plastics from product design to
environmentally sound waste management, through resource efficiency
and safe and just circular economy approaches that are feasible for all
member States including Ghana. There is a need for Ghana through the
Agency, the focal authority for multilateral environmental agreements,
to place itself in readiness to implement the provisions of this treaty when
ratified and domesticated.

Air pollution is generated by a diverse set of sources including point
sources such as industrial sources, mobile sources such as vehicles, area
sources such as wind-blown dust and sea salt, and man-made sources

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

such as cook-stoves and open burning of waste. Air pollution is Ghana’s
number one environmental risk to public health and is responsible for
about eight per cent of the total annual mortality.

The Agency estimated in 2015 that about two thousand eight hundred
lives were lost in Greater Accra Region alone as a result of air pollution.
This number is projected to increase to approximately four thousand six
hundred by the year 2030 if no action is taken. The economic cost of air
pollution is estimated at two billion, five hundred million United States
Dollars or about four point two per cent (4.2%) of Gross Domestic
Product. The sources of air pollution thus need to be effectively monitored
and regulated.

Act 490 has very minimal provisions on penalties to serve as a
deterrent to offenders. Act 490 does hot deal with the life cycle of plastic
management, offshore petroleum activities, schemes for the payment of
environmental services, registration and certification of environmental
management practitioners and service providers, among others.

The expanded mandate resulting from the emerging issues will
impose additional financial burdens on the Agency and since the Agency
is non-subvented, the Agency cannot offload the additional financial
burdens on Central Government and therefore needs to expand the
revenue generation base or streams of the Agency to finance the expanded
mandate.

Whereas the nomenclature “Agency” is used in our legislation to
refer to an establishment that performs specialised functions or assists in
implementing government policy in a specialised area, the nomenclature
“Authority” is used to refer to statutory bodies which perform among
others regulatory, supervisory or management functions. In view of the
expanded mandate of the Agency, the nomenclature “Authority” best
describes the statutory body to be established.

The Bill therefore seeks to transition the Agency into an Authority,
to address the gaps and the challenges in the implementation of Act 490 

vi

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

and the complexities of current environmental issues. The transition of
the Agency into an Authority also aligns with best practice on the continent
for institutions of this nature such as the National Environment
Management Authority of Kenya, the Rwanda Environment
Management Authority, the National Environment Management
Authority of Uganda and the Ethiopian Environmental Protection
Authority. This also aligns with national institutions such as the Ghana
Standards Authority, the Food and Drugs Authority, the National
Biodiversity Authority and the Nuclear Regulatory Authority, among
others, who are performing regulatory functions within their mandate.

The Bill consists of six parts. Parts One and Two re-enact the
Environmental Protection Agency Act, 1994 (Act 490). Parts Three and
Four re-enact the Hazardous and Electronic Waste Control and
Management Act, 2016 (Act 917). Part Five contains provisions on
climate change which are not in Act 490. Part Six contains general
provisions on enforcement, development of guidelines and standards,
and transitional provisions.

Part One of the Bill covers environmental protection.

Clauses 1 to 3 provide for the Environmental Protection Authority.

Clause 1 establishes the Environmental Protection Authority as a
body corporate.

The object of the Authority as specified in clause 2 is to regulate,
protect, manage and exercise general oversight and co-ordination over
all matters relating to the environment.

The functions of the Authority are set out under clause 3. The
Authority is mandated to advise the Minister on the formulation of
policies on the environment and in particular, make recommendations
for the protection of the environment; have oversight responsibility and
co-ordinate the activities of bodies concerned with the technical or
practical aspects of the environment and serve as a channel of
communication between the bodies and the Ministry; regulate and 

vii

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

co-ordinate the activities of the relevant bodies for the purposes of
controlling the generation, treatment, storage, transportation and disposal
of industrial waste; secure solely or in collaboration with any other person,
the control and prevention of discharge of waste into the environment
and the protection and improvement of the quality of the environment;
collaborate or co-ordinate with foreign and international agencies for
the purposes of the Bill and act as the focal institution to co-ordinate the
implementation of multilateral environmental agreements.

Other functions of the Authority include issuing environmental
permits for undertakings to control the volume, types, constituents and
effects of waste discharges, emissions, deposits, noise or any other source
of pollutants and of substances which are hazardous or potentially
dangerous to the quality of the environment or a segment of the
environment; issuing notices in the form of orders, directives, procedures
or warnings to a person for the purpose of controlling waste, discharges,
emissions, deposits, noise or any other source of pollutants and of
substances which are hazardous or potentially dangerous to the quality
of the environment or a segment of the environment; ensuring the
enforcement of environmental laws and, subject to clause (4) of article 88
of the Constitution, be authorised by the Attorney-General, for the
purposes of the Bill, to initiate and conduct the prosecution of
environment-related offences and ensure the establishment and
operationalisation of the polluter pays principle and extended polluter
responsibility schemes.

The Authority is further mandated to prescribe standards and
guidelines relating to the pollution of air, water, land and any other form
of environmental pollution including the discharge of waste and the
control of toxic substances; ensure compliance with the laid down
environmental assessment procedures in the planning and implementation
of policies, plans, programmes and projects, including compliance in
respect of existing projects; act in liaison and co-operation with Ministries,
Departments and Agencies and any other bodies to control pollution and
generally protect the environment; ensure that the District Assemblies 

viii

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

take responsibility for the improvement and management of the
environment in the district; and conduct investigations into environmental
issues.

Furthermore, the Authority is required to promote and carry out
studies, research, surveys and analyses and disseminate information on
findings for the improvement and protection of the environment; initiate
and pursue formal and non-formal education programmes for the
creation of public awareness on the importance of the environment;
integrate environmental management practices into planning in
collaboration with relevant bodies; develop a comprehensive database
on the environment for environmental protection and management;
publish periodic reports on the state of the environment; establish a
reclamation financial security scheme for the extractive industry; impose
and collect environmental protection levies in accordance with this Act
and the Regulations and institute a scheme for the payment for
environmental services.

Other functions of the Authority are regulating the activities in
respect of the management of industrial and consumer chemicals;
regulating the activities in respect of the management of pesticides; issuing
permits and licences for activities relating to the control and management
of pesticides and industrial and consumer chemicals; registering and
certifying environmental practitioners and service providers; regulating
the activities in respect of the management of hazardous electrical and
electronic wastes and other wastes in order to protect human health and
the environment; promoting the adoption of new environmentally sound
technologies including cleaner production approaches, resource efficiency,
extended producer responsibility and circular economy; establishing a
funding scheme to support environmental emergency situations at the
national, regional and district levels and regulating the removal of urban
tree cover.

The Authority is also responsible for formulating programmes and
plans to enhance the management of natural resources for the benefit of
society and institute measures to reduce threat to biodiversity in
collaboration with relevant stakeholders; collaborating with relevant

ix

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

stakeholders to formulate and implement plans to ensure a dean, healthy
and enhanced biodiverse coastal and marine ecosystem; co-ordinating
activities of the relevant bodies for the purposes of oil pollution
preparedness, response and control; acting as the National Co-ordinator
and designated authority for the preparation, update and implementation
of the National Oil Spill Contingency Plan and related documents for
effective response to oil pollution incidents and performing any other
functions conferred on the Authority under the Bill or any other
enactment.

Clauses 1 to 3 provide for the establishment of the Environmental
Protection Authority. Clause 1 establishes the Authority as abody corporate
with peipertual succession. The object of the authority is provided for in
clause 2. The object of the Authority is to regulate, protect, co-ordinate
and exercise general oversight over all matters relating to climate change
and the environment. Clause 3 provides for the functions of the Authority
which include advising and supporting the Minister on the formulation
of policies on the environment ^nd in particular, make recommendations
for the protection of the environment and ensuring compliance over the
enforcement of provisions on environmental protection in existing
enactments.

Clauses 4 to 16 provide for the governance of the Authority.

Clause 4 provides for a fourteen-member governing body of the
Authority. The members of the Board comprise the chairperson, die Chief
Executive Officer of the Authority, a representative each of the Ministries
responsible for Environment, Local Government, Finance, Health and
Education and a representative each of the Council for Scientific and
Industrial Research, Ghana Standards Authority, Association of Ghana
Industries and three other persons nominated by the President at least
two of whom are women.

Clause 5provides for the functions of the Board. The Board is required
to exercise general oversight responsibility for the strategic direction of
the Authority and ensure that the functions of the Authority are effectively
and efficiently performed.

x

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

Standard provisions on the tenure of office of members of the Board,
meetings of the Board, disclosure of interest, establishment of committees,
allowances and ministerial directives are provided for in clauses 6, 7, 8,
9,10 and 11 respectively.

Clauses 12 and 13 provide for the Coordinating Committee and the
functions of the Coordinating Committee respectively.

Clause 12 provides for the establishment of the Coordinating
Committee with the membership outlined in the clause.

The functions of the Coordinating Committee include deliberating
on the agenda of Conference of Parties including Basel, Rotterdam,
Stockholm, Minamata, and other related conventions and frameworks
on chemicals and waste ahead of their respective Conference of Parties
for purposes of developing relevant national contributions prior to the
conferences; and reviewing action plans of the specific chemical related
multilateral environment agreements and frameworks and identifying
opportunities for synergies and providing guidance for joint­
programming, clause 13. The Coordinating Committee is further required
to ensure timely implementation and reporting of decisions of Conference
of Parties; identify and make recommendations for capacity development
of related national institutions and personnel; provide guidance for the
mainstreaming of the sound management of chemicals into national
development plans; and provide a framework for data collection,
standardisation and harmonisation to inform policy and programmes.

Clauses 14, 15 and 16 provide for the establishment of technical
committees, functions of the technical committees and a Technical Review
Committee respectively.

Clauses 17 to 22 provide for the administration of the Authority.
Under clause 17, the Authority is empowered to create divisions,
directorates and departments of the Authority as determined by the Board
for the efficient performance of the functions of the Authority. The
Authority is further empowered to establish regional and district offices
to perform functions determined by the Authority, clause 18.

xi

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

The appointment and functions of the Chief Executive Officer are
provided for in clauses 19 and 20 respectively. Under clause 19, the President
is to appoint a Chief Executive Officer with the relevant qualifications
and expertise in matters related to the functions of the Authority to hold
office on the terms and conditions specified in the letter of appointment.

The Chief Executive Officer is responsible for the day-to-day
administration of the affairs of the Authority and implementing decisions
of the Board. The Chief Executive Officer is also answerable to the Board
in the performance of functions and is required to perform any other
function determined by the Board, clause 20.

Clause 21 provides for the Secretary to the Board. The Authority is
required to designate the Director of the Legal Department as Secretary
to the Board.The functions of the Secretary to the Board include advising
the Board on the legal implications of decisions of the Board; ensuring
that the business of the Board is arranged; ensuring that the minutes of
the meetings and decisions of the Board are kept in the form required by
the Board and performing any other function that the Board or die Chief
Executive Officer may direct.

Clause 22 provides for the appointment of other staff for the efficient
and effective performance of the functions of the Authority. The Authority
is empowered to engage the services of consultants and experts on the
recommendation of the Board.

Matters related to the finances of the Authority are covered by clauses
23 to 28.

Clause 23 provides for the establishment of an Internal Audit Unit in
accordance with section 83 of the Public Financial Management Act,
2016 (Act 921).

Clause 24 enumerates the funds of the Authority. The funds of the
Authority are moneys payable to the Authority under any other enactment; 

xii

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

administrative penalties payable under the Bill; loans, donations and
grants; moneys accruing to the Authority from investments;
environmental protection levies and any other internally generated funds.

Clauses 25 and 26 provide for the bank account and expenditure of
the Authority respectively.

Standard provisions on accounts and audit and annual report and
other reports are provided for in clauses 27 and 28 respectively.

Clauses 29 to 37 deal with enforcement and control.

Clause 29 deals with environmental assessment. Under the clause,
power is conferred on the Authority to, by notice in writing, require an
entity responsible for an undertaking which in the opinion of the
Authority has, or is likely to have an adverse effect on the environment,
to conduct an environmental assessment.

Clause 30 provides for relocation, displacement and compensation.
Where the environmental assessment report indicates that the land to be
used for the proposed undertaking will have an impact on property and
livelihood of people, result in the relocation of people, result in the
displacement of people or restrict the land use, the proponent is required
to prepare a compensation plan or compensation policy framework in
accordance with guidelines issued by the Authority.

Clauses 31 provides for certification of environmental management
practitioners.

Under clause 32, the Authority is to monitor an undertaking to ensure
that all environmental management systems and strategies are in place
and work efficiently to manage and minimise the impact the undertaking
has on the environment and ensure compliance with relevant enactments,
the standards developed by the Authority and the standards specified in
the First Schedule, commitments in the environmental assessment and
conditions in the environmental permit.

xiii

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

Clause 33 requries the Authority to carry out an environmental
inspection or audit of an undertaking to ensure compliance with the
environmental requirements, compliance with the permit conditions and
commitments, the effectiveness of environmental management systems,
verify data that has been submitted to the Authority and determine any
non-compliance with paragraph (a) that requires immediate remedial
action.

Clause 34 provides for the Authority to establish an environmental
performance and public disclosure system to rate an undertaking in
accordance with guidelines issued by die Authority.

Under clause 35, the Authority is required to issue a notice, directive,
procedure or warning for the purpose of non-compliance with an
environmental permit, a pollution abatement notice, a pesticide registration
and licence or a hazardous chemical and waste permit. Under the clause,
the Authority is required to serve on a person responsible for an
undertaking, an enforcement notice requiring that person to take the steps
stipulated by the Authority to prevent or stop the activity or undertaking
where the Authority considers that the activity or an undertaking poses a
threat to the environment or public health.

Clause 36 gives the Minister the power to take appropriate steps to
ensure compliance with a notice served under clause 35.

Clause 37 covers a request for information by the Chief Executive
Officer or an officer of the Authority authorised by the Chief Executive
Officer which the Chief Executive Officer considers reasonably necessary
for purposes of the Bill.

Clauses 38 to 42 deal with the National Environment Fund.

Clause 38 provides for the establishment of the National Environment
Fund.

Clause 39 specifies the object of the Fund which is to support the
regulation of the environment in all its forms with the view to ensure the 

xiv

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

efficient and effective management and protection of the environment
of the country; that emerging environmental issues are addressed to
achieve sustainable development; human resource development; response
to environmental emergencies and the promotion of research and
awareness creation on environmental issues and any other purpose
determined by the Board in consultation with the Minister.

The sources of money for the Fund are grants and donations; fifteen per
cent of the plastic levy payable under the Customs and Excise (Duties
and Other Taxes) Act, 1996 (Act 512); five per cent of any amount of
money remaining to the credit of the Authority after having made
provision for the expenditure under clause 26 in a financial year; income
from investment of moneys of the National Environment Fund and
moneys approved by Parliament, clause 40.

Clauses 41 and 42 provide for the bank account of the Fund and
management of the Fund respectively.

Under clause 41, moneys for the National Environment Fund are
required to be paid into a bank account opened for that purpose by the
Board with the approval of the Controller and Accountant-General.

The Fund is to be administered by the Board. The Board is required,
for the purposes of administering the Fund to formulate policies to
generate money for the Fund; determine the allocations to be made
towards the objects of the Fund and determine the annual targets of the
Fund, clause 42.

Miscellaneous matters are provided for in clauses 43 and 44. Clause
43 empowers the Minister to make Regulations for the effective
implementation of Part One of the Bill. Clause 44 provides for the
interpretation of words and phrases used in Part One of the Bill.

Part Two of the Bill deals with Pesticides Control and Management.
Clauses 45 and 46 provide for the Pesticides Technical Committee. Clause
45 establishes the Pesticides Technical Committee whilst clause 46 provides
for the functions of the Pesticides Technical Committee.

xv

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

Clauses 47 to 63 provide for the registration of pesticides.

Claused! provides for the requirement for registration of pesticides.
Under the clause, a person is prohibited from manufacturing, formulating,
repackaging, importing, exporting, transporting, storing, distributing,
labelling, advertising, selling or using a pesticide unless the pesticide has
been registered by the Authority in accordance with Part Two of the Bill.

Clause 48 provides for the application for registration of pesticide.
A person who seeks to register a pesticide under clause 47 is required to
apply to the Authority in the requisite form. The application is also
required to be accompanied with samples of the pesticide product;
samples of the technical grade of the active ingredient of the pesticide;
samples of the laboratory standard of the active ingredient of the
pesticide; any other sample or information that may be required by the
Authority and the prescribed fee.

Clause 49 provides for the determination of completeness of an
application for the registration of a pesticide.

Clause 50 specifies the procedure for consideration of an application
for registration of a pesticide by the Authority. Where the Authority
determines that an application is complete, the Authority is required to
evaluate the application and forward the evaluation report to the Pesticides
Technical Committee for consideration. On receipt of the application,
the Pesticides Technical Committee is required to consider the application
and make a recommendation to the Authority on the application within
sixty days after the date of receipt of the evaluation report.

Clause 51 provides for the classification of pesticides. The Authority
is mandated, for the purposes of registration of a pesticide, to classify a
pesticide as being for general use, for restricted or suspended use, a banned
pesticide or for any other use determined by the Authority.

Clause 52 provides for provisional approval. A pesticide that is being
introduced to the market for the first time is required to have a provisional 

xvi

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

approval. The Authority is, however, empowered to consider an
application for the registration of a pesticide referred to in subclause (1) if
the provisional approval expires and the applicant meets all the necessary
requirements for registration.

A provisional approval for a pesticide is valid for one year, clause 53.

Clause 54 provides for the approval of pesticides subject to the
conditions as determined by the Authority and upon the Authority being
satisfied that the pre-conditions spelt out in the clause have been met.

Where a pesticide is registered, the Authority is required to issue a
certificate of registration, clause 55. Under clause 56, the Authority has
the power to refuse to register a pesticide if the pesticide fails to meet the
requirement in clause 47.

Clause 57 provides for the duration and renewal of registration of a
pesticide. The registration of a pesticide remains valid for a period of
three years from the date of registration. The Authority has the power to
renew the registration for a further period of three years at a time where
the Authority is satisfied that a registered pesticide remains safe and
effective for use in the Republic.

Clause 58 relates to the re-registration of a pesticide. The Authority
is required to cause the re-registration of an existing pesticide twelve years
after the initial registration in accordance with the requirements of clauses
47 and 54 and any other requirement that the Authority may determine.

Clause 59 covers the expiration of registration.

Clause 60 deals with non-disclosure of confidential information.

Clause 61 empowers the Authority to amend the classification of a
pesticide, suspend orban a pesticide, cancel the registration of a pesticide
or cancel the provisional approval of a pesticide at any time after the
registration or during the period of a provisional approval.

xvii

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

Under clause 62, the Authority has the power to cause the withdrawal
of a pesticide from the Republic if the registration of the pesticide is
suspended, cancelled or banned or if the continued use of the pesticide
will cause unacceptable risk of harm to human beings, crops, animals or
the environment or if the shell-life of the pesticide has expired.

The Authority is required to maintain a register of pesticides under
clause 63. The contents of the register of pesticides are to be updated
every six months by the Authority.

Clauses 64 to 74 provide for the licensing of pesticide dealers.

Clause 64 prohibits a person from engaging in the manufacture,
formulation, repackaging, importation, exportation, transportation,
storage, advertisement, distribution, sale, commercial application or
disposal of a pesticide without a licence issued under Part Two of the Bill.

Clause 65 spells out the requirements for applying for a licence to
engage in any of the activities mentioned in clause 64. Clause 66 provides
for the grant of a licence. Under the clause, where the application meets
the requirements spelt out under clause 65, the Authority is empowered
to grant a licence to the applicant to manufacture, formulate, repadcage,
import, export, transport, store, advertise, distribute, sell, commercially
apply or dispose of a pesticide.

The circumstances under which the Authority may refuse to issue a
licence are enumerated under clause 67. The Authority has the discretion
to refuse to issue a licence if an applicant fails to meet the requirements
under clause 65 or falsifies any part of the information in the application.

Clause 68 provides for the validity of a licence granted under the Bill.

Clause 69 provides the requirements and procedure for the renewal
of a licence granted by the Authority.

Clause 70 prohibits the transfer of licence granted by the Authority
without the approval of the Authority in writing. The grounds and 

xviii

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

procedure for the suspension or cancellation of a licence granted by the
Authority are outlined in clause 71.

Clauses 72 and 73 provide for export permit and import permit
respectively.

Under clause 74, a person dissatisfied with the decision of the
Authority has the right to appeal to the Minister. Where that person is
dissatisfied with a failure of the Minister to determine the matter within
thirty days or is dissatisfied with the decision of the Minister, the person
has the right of appeal to the High Court.

Clauses 75 to 84 relate to the Pesticides Management Fund.

Clause 75 provides for the establishment of the Pesticides
Management Fund whilst clause 76 specifies the object of the Fund which
is to improve the control and management of pesticides in the country.

The sources of money for the Pesticides Management Fund comprise
a zero point three per cent of the free on board value of all pesticides
imported into the country and paid at the time of application for an
export permit or an import permit; a zero point three per cent of the
value of production per annum of all pesticides manufactured in the
country and paid at the time of placement on the market and donations,
grants and gifts, clause 77.

Clause 78 provides for the management of the Pesticides Management
Fund. The Fund is required to be managed by the Pesticides Management
Fund Committee.

The functions of the Pesticides Management Fund Committee are
provided in clause 79. Clause 80 deals with the tenure of office of members
of the Pesticides Management Fund Committee.

The meetings of the Pesticide Management Fund Committee are
provided for in clause 81 whilst clause 82 provides for allowances of the
Pesticides Management Fund Committee.

xix

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

Clauses 83 and 84 provide for the bank account of the Pesticides
Management Fund and the disbursement from die Fund respectively.

Clauses 85 to 96 are general provisions on pesticides. Clause 85
provides safeguards for a user of pesticides and a worker on premises
where pesticide is manufactured, formulated, packaged or stored,
proscribes the use of a pesticide in a manner that is inconsistent with
Part Two of the Bill or Regulations made under Part Two of the Bill and
imposes an administrative penalty of two hundred penalty units for a
contravention of the clause.

Clause 86 deals with pesticide residue and mandates the Authority to
set a maximum permissible concentration for pesticide residue in food
and animal feed to be known as a Maximum Residue Limit for a pesticide.

Under clause 87, the Authority is mandated to periodically conduct
training programmes in the handling and management of pesticides for
dealers in pesticides and persons in the pesticides industry. The Authority
is to determine the content of the training and issue a certificate of
competence to a participant on completion of the training.

The Authority has the power to restrict or prohibit the use of a
registered pesticide in a designated area during a specified period of time,
clause 88.

Clause 89 prohibits the alteration of a registered pesticide so as to
change the formulation, composition or usage of the pesticide or
alteration of the pesticides in any other manner.

Clause 90 prohibits a person from distributing, selling, formulating,
exporting or importing a counterfeit pesticide into or out of the country.

A person is prohibited from advertising a registered or provisionally
approved pesticide without the vetting and approval of the Authority,
clause 91.

xx

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

Under clause 92, the Authority is to approve a container, a label and
manner of packaging for a pesticide as specified in guidelines issued by
the Authority.

The Authority is mandated to conduct a test of the sample submitted
by the applicant to confirm the information submitted for the registration
of a pesticide, clause 93.

Clause 94 mandates a person who manufactures, formulates,
repackages, imports, exports, transports, stores, distributes, applies, sells
or disposes of a pesticide to make a record of the quantities of pesticides
manufactured, formulated, repackaged, imported, exported, transported,
stored, distributed, applied, sold or disposed of by that person. The record
is required to be maintained for ten years from the time the record is
made and be made available to the Authority at the request of the Authority
at the time and in the manner required by the Authority.

The location for storage, sale and distribution of pesticides is covered
under clause 95. A person is required to construct or rent premises for
storage, sale and distribution of pesticides in accordance with the
Environmental Assessment Regulations, 1999 (L.1.1652) and the Pesticides
Licensing Guidelines developed by the Authority.

Clause 96 mandates the Authority to establish a laboratory to be
known as the Pesticides Quality Control Laboratory to perform functions
related to the quality of pesticides regulated under Part Two of the Bill.

Miscellaneous provisions are dealt with in clauses 97 to 102. Other
offences and their correlative punishments are provided for under clause
97. The penalty for failure or refusal to maintain or submit the contents
of records maintained to the Authority is provided under clause 98.

Under clause 99, it is not a defence for a person charged with the
manufacturing, formulation, importation or sale of a pesticide contrary
to clause 46 to plead that at the time of the sale, there was a reasonable
belief that the pesticide was registered or did not differ in any way from 

xxi

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

the purported contents of the container or the pesticide otherwise did
not fail to meet the requirements of Part Two.

Clause 100 provides for forfeiture to the Republic of equipment, a
pesticide or an appliance used in the commission of an offence and the
suspension or cancellation of a licence of a person in addition to any
other penalty.

Clause 101 provides for the power to make Regulations whilst clause
102 provides for the interpretation of words and phrases used in Part
Two of the Bill.

Part Three of the Bill provides for hazardous wastes and other
wastes.

Clauses 103 to 118 deal with the control and management of
hazardous wastes and other wastes.

Clause 103 prohibits the importation, exportation, transportation,
sale or purchase of hazardous wastes and other wastes specified in the
Sixth Schedule unless the wastes do not possess any of the characteristics
specified in the Eighth Schedule.

Clauses 104 and 105 deal with the importation and exportation of
hazardous wastes or other wastes. Clause 104 stipulates the preconditions
for the issuance of an import permit by the Authority, for the importation
of hazardous wastes or other wastes specified in the Sixth Schedule into
the country. The clause further empowers the Authority to revoke an
import permit if the Authority has reason to believe that the hazardous
wastes or other wastes will not be managed in an environmentally sound
manner.

Clause 105 provides the preconditions for the grant of an export
permit by the Authority for the exportation of hazardous wastes or other
wastes out of the country in accordance with the Basel Convention.

xxii

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

Clause 106 deals with the notification procedure for transboundary
movement of hazardous wastes or other wastes.

Clause 107 prohibits the transit of hazardous wastes or other wastes
through the Republic except with the written consent of the Authority.
The clause further provides for the procedure for obtaining the consent
of the Authority and other requirements for the transit of hazardous
and other wastes through the Republic.

The penalty for contravening clause 107 is the payment of an amount
equivalent to fifteen thousand penalty units and re-exportation of the
hazardous wastes or other wastes to the State of export, clause 108.

Clause 109 prohibits the burning of hazardous wastes or other wastes
in the open.

The Authority is empowered to order the sealing up of an area, site
facility or premises which the Authority has reason to believe that is being
used for the disposal of hazardous wastes or other wastes and publish
the order in the Gazette or in two daily newspapers of nationwide
circulation, clause 110.

Clause 111 provides the offence and related punishment for a person
who, knowing that another person has committed an offence under this
Part, assists that person to avoid an arrest or prosecution.

Under clause 112, a law enforcement officer has the power to search,
seize and arrest in relation to any substance suspected to be hazardous
wastes or other wastes found on a land, premises, facility or vehicle. A
law enforcement officer is further empowered to arrest a person on whose
land, premises or facility or vehicle a substance suspected to be hazardous
wastes or other wastes are found.

A law enforcement officer is to take for testing, a sample of any
substance suspected to be hazardous wastes or other wastes which comes
into the possession of the officer in the course of performance of the 

xxiii

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

functions of that officer to determine the components of the substance
in accordance with the prescribed procedure for sampling, clause 113.

The immunity from prosecution conferred on a person by article 3
of the Diplomatic Immunities Act, 1962 (Act 148) does not extend to a
crime committed by a person under Part Three of the Bill, clause 114.

Clause 115 obliges a person involved in the management of hazardous
wastes and other wastes to obtain an environmental permit in accordance
with the Environmental Assessment Regulations, 1999 (L.I. 1652).

The Authority is to maintain a database of written authorisation
granted by the Authority under Part Three of the Bill, clause 116.

Clause 117 imposes an obligation on a person who generates, collects,
stores, transports or disposes of hazardous wastes or other wastes to
maintain adequate insurance cover in respect of the management of the
hazardous wastes or other wastes.

A holder of a permit issued under Part Three of the Bill is required
to maintain a register to record the quantity, type, quality and origin of
hazardous wastes or other wastes generated, collected, stored,
transported, recovered or disposed of by the holder of the permit and
submit to the Authority each year, information relating to the preceding
year, clause 118.

Clauses 119, 120 and 121 deal with the control and management of
polychlorinated biphenyls.

Clause 119 prohibits the importation of polychlorinated biphenyls
into the country. The provisions on the control and management of
hazardous wastes and other wastes as provided under clauses 103 to 118
apply to polychlorinated biphenyls with the necessary modification.

Provision is made in clauses 120 and 121 for a phase out period for
polychlorinated biphenyls and classification of polychlorinated biphenyls
waste respectively.

xxiv

The power of the Minister to make Regulations under Part Three is
provided for in clause 122.

Clause 123 provides for the interpretation of words and phrases used
in Part Three of the Bill.

Part Four of the Bill deals with electrical and electronic waste.

Clauses 124 to 127 provide for advance electrical and electronic eco
levy.

Clause 124 provides for a person who manufactures electrical or
electronic equipment in the country or imports new or used electrical or
electronic equipment into the country to register with the Authority, obtain
a permit and pay the prescribed advanced eco levy in the Twelfth Schedule
in respect of the items specified in that Schedule.

Clause 125 provides for the importation of waste electrical and
electronic equipment while clause 126 provides for the exportation of waste
electrical and electronic equipment.

Clause 127 prescribes requirements to be met by wholesalers,
distributors and retailers of electrical or electronic equipment
manufactured in the country or imported into the country.

Clauses 128 to 137 provide for matters related to the Electrical and
Electronic Waste Management Fund.

Clauses 128 and 129 provide for the establishment of the Electrical
and Electronic Waste Management Fund and the objects of the Fund
respectively. The objects of the Fund are to provide financial resources
for the management of electrical and electronic waste and reduce the
adverse impact of electrical and electronic waste on human health and
the environment, clause 129.

xxv

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

Clause 130 deals with sources of money for the Fund. The sources of
money for the Fund are moneys approved by Parliament; the advance
eco levy collected in respect of items specified in the Twelfth Schedule;
grants, donations, gifts and other voluntary contributions and any other
moneys that become lawfully payable and vested in the Fund.

Clause 131 provides for the bank account of the Fund. .

Clause 132 provides for the Management Board for the Electrical
and Electronic Waste Management Fund. The Board consists of a
chairperson, one representative from the Ministry responsible for the
Environment not below the rank of a Director nominated by the Minister,
one representative from the Ministry responsible for Sanitation not below
the rank of a Director nominated by the Minister responsible for
Sanitation, one representative of the Authority not below the rank of a
Director nominated by the Chief Executive Officer of the Authority and
the Fund Administrator.

Clauses 133 and 134 deal with the appointment of an Administrator
for the Fund and the functions of the Administrator respectively. Under
clause 133, the Administrator is to be appointed by the President in
accordance with article 195 of the Constitution. The Administrator is
responsible for the management of the Electrical and Electronic Waste
Management Fund under clause 134.

Disbursement from the Fund is provided for under clause 135.

Standard provisions on accounts and audit and annual reports and
other reports of the Fund are provided for in clauses 136 and 137,
respectively.

Clauses 138 to 141 deal with electrical and electronic waste recycling
plants.

Under clause 138, the Minister, on the advice of the Authority, is
empowered to make arrangements for the establishment of electrical and
electronic waste recycling plants and related facilities in the country.

ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION BILL, 2024

A manufacturer, distributor or wholesaler of electrical or electronic
equipment is obliged to take back used or discarded electrical or electronic
equipment manufactured or sold by the manufacturer, distributor or
wholesaler for the purpose of recycling, clause 139.

Clause 140 imposes an obligation on a person responsible for recycling
and disposal of a used or discarded electrical or electronic equipment to
ensure that the disposal is carried out in an environmentally sound
manner.

Under clause 141, the Authority or any other appropriate body
concerned with the management of electrical or electronic waste is required
to serve an enforcement notice on a defaulting person where the Authority
has reasonable grounds to suspect that any of the requirements of Part
Four of the Bill have not been complied with.

Miscellaneous provisions are provided for in clauses 142 and 143.

Clause 142 empowers the Minister, in consultation with the
Authority, to make Regulations while the interpretation of words and
phrases used in Part Four of the Bill are provided for in clause 143.

capacity of human and ecological systems to the impacts of climate

capacity of human and ecological systems to the impacts of climate

change and also mainstream climate change disaster risk reduction into
strategies and institute measures for loss and damage due to climate change
impacts.

The Authority is to collaborate with relevant international, national
and local institutions to support the low-emission development measures
and minimise the impact arising from the implementation of mitigation
policies and programmes in the country or internationally. The Authority
is also to collaborate with institutions to promote local action to reduce
short-lived climate pollutants in the oil and gas, agricultural, refrigeration
and air-conditioning sectors to address climate change and air pollutants,
clause 146.

Implementation of climate change measures is dealt with in clause
147. The Authority is to, in the implementation of climate change
measures, facilitate technical activities of all stakeholders involved in
climate change activities to enhance capacity development through public
awareness, effective participation, behavioural changes and foster national
dialogues on climate actions, identify and promote climate technologies,
green practices and capacity-building needs in all production and
consumption and facilitate approaches and uptakes of technologies that
support climate-resilient and low-emission development, among others.

Under clause 148, the Authority is to serve as the designated national
authority for the international carbon market and non-market approaches,
voluntary carbon market and domestic carbon pricing instruments.

International climate change reporting is provided for in clause 149.
The Authority is enjoined under this clause to co-ordinate the preparation,
review and communication of international climate change reports
required of a Party to the United Nations Framework Convention on
Climate Change and the subsidiary agreements, protocols, accords or
treaties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate
Change.

Clause 150 establishes the Ghana Carbon Registry. The Ghana Carbon
Registry is a digital platform which is to serve as a database for carbon

market project activities in the country and elsewhere and track the transfer
and use of intentionally transferred mitigation outcomes. The Ghana
Carbon Registry is also to facilitate the listing and registration of
mitigation activities and voluntary carbon market projects and host and
provide public access to all internationally transferred mitigation outcome
activities and information on all internationally transferred mitigation
outcomes.

Provisions on the Carbon Market Committee are dealt with in clauses
151 and 152.

The establishment of the Carbon Market Committee is provided for in
clause 151. The Carbon Market Committee consists of nine members
including the chairperson and the Chief Executive Officer of the
Authority.

Clause 152 provides for the functions of the Carbon Market
Committee. The Carbon Market Committee is to approve, among others,
mitigation activities and associated technologies eligible under paragraph
2 of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement; mitigation projects eligible for the
voluntary carbon market; the activities that the country intends to host
under the mechanism specified under paragraph 4 of Article 6 of the
Paris Agreement and the use of an existing approved methodology under
an international crediting standard and the national modalities for the
approval of new baseline and monitoring methodologies.

The Mitigation Fund is dealt with in clauses 153 to 158.

Clause 153 establishes the Mitigation Fund. The objects of the
Mitigation Fund as set out in clause 154 include the provision of financial
support to implement a bilateral cooperative approach for the creation
of authorised internationally transferred mitigation outcomes; the
provision of funds to invest in the generation of additional mitigation
benefits in the country to increase the mitigation outcomes of the country;

and financing the implementation of additional mitigation activities to
raise mitigation ambition in the country.

The source of money for the Mitigation Fund is the Corresponding
Adjustment Fee which is payable to the Authority by a mitigation activity
developer or an acquiring participating Party, clause 155.

Clause 156 provides for the bank account of the Mitigation Fund
into which moneys for the Mitigation Fund are to be paid.

Management of the Mitigation Fund is provided for in clause 157.
The Mitigation Fund is to be managed jointly by the Ministry, the Ministry
responsible for Finance and the Authority through the Mitigation Fund
Committee. The Mitigation.Fund Committee consists of six members
including two representatives of the Authority and one representative of
industry, nominated by the President of the Ghana Association of Bankers
of Ghana. The Board is to appoint the members of the Mitigation Fund
Committee.

The disbursement of moneys from the Mitigation Fund is to be done
in accordance with the purpose specified in the object of the Fund, clause
158.

Miscellaneous matters are provided for in clauses 159 and 160.

Clause 159 empowers the Minister to make Regulations for the
effective implementation of Part Five of the Bill. Clause 160 provides for
the interpretation of words and phrases used in Part Five of the Bill.

Fart Six of the Bill deals with general provisions.

Clauses 161 to 166 provide for enforcement.

For the purpose of ensuring compliance with the Bill, the Authority,
a public officer and any other person is required to be guided by the

principles of common but differentiated responsibility and
intergenerational equity, the precautionary principle, the polluter pays
principle and sustainable development, clause 161.

Under clause 162, the Board is empowered to appoint an environment
protection inspector. An inspector has the discretion to enter any premises
at a reasonable time to ensure compliance with the Bill or any other
enactment that pertains to the protection of the environment. An inspector
is also required to produce the requisite authority when required by the
person in charge of the premises.

Clause 163 provides for the powers of an inspector.

Clause 164 stipulates the consequences for the obstruction of an
inspector in the exercise of a power conferred under Part Six of the Bill
or Regulations made under the Bill and failure to comply with a lawful
enquiry or requirement made by an inspector.

A District Assembly that undertakes an activity that may have an
impact on the environment and human health is required to consult the
Authority, clause 165.

The role of the Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority
in assisting with the enforcement of the Bill and the prevention of the
importation of a chemical, hazardous waste or electrical and electronic
waste where the importation is contrary to the Bill are outlined in clause
166.

Clauses 167 to 172 cover miscellaneous matters.

Clause 167 provides for the establishment of an official bulletin known
as the Environmental Bulletin. The Authority is to keep, maintain and
ensure accessibility of the Environmental Bulletin in an accurate form
determined by the Board and as a secured electronic database. Further,
the Authority is to publish annually in the Environmental Bulletin and on
the website of the Authority, registered pesticides and the classification
of registered pesticides; provisionally authorised pesticides; suspended

or banned pesticides; amendments made to the classification of

undertakings and any other relevant information determined by the
Authority.

Under clause 168, the Authority is mandated to develop guidelines
and standards for the implementation of the Bill.

The Minister has the power to delegate the functions of the Minister
under Parts Three and Four of the Bill to the Authority, clause 169.

are provided for in clause 170.
