title: Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021
text:
GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

MEMORANDUM

The object of the Bill is to establish the Ghana Standards Authority
as the authority responsible for the establishment and promulgation of
standards, enforcement of conformity assessment programmes and
regulation of activities in respect of weights and measures in the country.
The Bill further seeks to revise the law relating to standardisation,
conformity assessment and metrology.

The Ghana Standards Authority formerly Ghana Standards Board
originated from the Institute of Standards and Industrial Research, an
Institute of the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research. The Institute
of Standards and Industrial Research of the Council was established in
1965 as the Industrial Standards Institute of the former Ghana Academy
of Sciences.

In early 1966, the name of the Industrial Standards Institute was
changed to the Institute of Standards and Industrial Research. This was
the situation until the National Liberation Council established the National
Standards Board under the Standards Decree, 1967 (N.L.C.D. 199). This
enactment was subsequently repealed by the Standards Authority Act,
1973 (N. R. C. D. 173). Under N.R.C.D. 173 the name was changed from
the National Standards Board to Ghana Standards Board.

Subsequently, the name of the Ghana Standards Board was changed
to Ghana Standards Authority in line with the dictates of the Laws of
Ghana (Revised Edition) Act, 1998 (Act 562), which sought to distinguish
between the statutory body as a legal entity and the governing body under
the Statute law revision exercise.

Currently, the Ghana Standards Authority is the national standards
body, and a conformity assessment body for all goods and services
manufactured or produced within the country, which are not regulated
by specific entities appointed by law. The Ghana Standards Authority
also administers standards for both imports and exports. In addition to
this, the Authority was appointed the Administrator of Weights and
Measures, Weighing and Measuring Instruments by a Gazette notice under
Gazette No.8 of Friday 2nd February, 1991.

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

As the national standards body, the Authority is responsible for the
development and publication of standards in line with international
standards and in accordance with requirements detailed out in the World
Trade Organisation Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade. In addition
to this, the Authority is also responsible for issuing the respective Ghana
Standards Marks of Conformity for conformity assessment. All these
are intended to enhance the quality infrastructure, protect public health
and ensure the safety of the general public.

The Bill seeks to consolidate the Standards Authority Act, 1973
(N. R. C. D. 173) and the Weights and Measures Act, 1975 (N.R.C.D. 326)
into one enactment for the effective administration of the responsibilities
of the Authority. Furthermore, the Bill re-establishes the Authority as the
Ghana Standards Authority to reflect the nationality of the Authority
and to meet the International Organisation for Standardisation
requirement.

The Bill also strengthens and expands the scope of operations of the
Authority, to face up to the challenges in relation to standards, conformity
assessment and metrology related programmes, due to modernisation
and technological development.

Clauses 1 to 3 provide for the establishment of the Ghana Standards
Authority.

Clause 1 of the Bill establishes the Ghana Standards Authority with
all the incidents of incorporation.

Clause 2 outlines the objects of the Authority which include the
establishment, promulgation and maintenance of standards to ensure
that high quality goods and services are produced or procured in the
country for local consumption or for export, or imported for local
consumption; the promotion of standardisation and metrology in
industry, commerce, health and services; the promotion of conformity
assessment in industry, commerce and services, and the promotion of
industrial efficiency and development. Other objects are the promotion
of standards in public and industrial welfare, health, safety and the 

ii

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

environment and the affiliation with international bodies concerned with
standardisation, metrology, conformity assessment or related matters.

To achieve the objects, the Authority has several functions
enumerated in clause 3. In relation to standardisation, the Authority is
required to prepare, frame, amend or modify, maintain and promulgate
National Standards, establish laboratories and other facilities to promote
research in relation to standardisation; undertake and encourage
educational work in connection with standardisation, collect and
disseminate information concerning standardisation including
publication of reports, pamphlets, booklets, journals and other relevant
publications. Other functions of the Authority in relation to
standardisation are to develop and maintain a collection of library
materials and a museum collection relating to standardisation and allied
matters; to endorse international, regional and national specifications
suitable for use in the country and to collaborate with relevant regulatory
bodies to enact legislation on Technical Regulations or Mandatory
Standards.

In relation to metrology, the functions of the Authority are to realise,
maintain and disseminate the international system of units of
measurement, provide calibration services and inspect and verify weights,
measures, weighing and measuring instruments used in trade, industry,
health, safety and environment. Other functions are to undertake and
encourage academic work in connection with metrology, collect and
disseminate information in relation to metrology and related matters
including the publication of reports, pamphlets, booklets, journals and
other publications. The Authority is further required to develop and
maintain a collection of library materials and a museum collection relating
to metrology and allied matters and to participate in activities of
international bodies concerned with metrology.

Clause 3 further provides for functions of the Authority in relation
to conformity assessment. The functions include establishing and
maintaining facilities for the purpose of carrying out conformity
assessment, to promote research and provide for examination, testing 

iii

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

and certification of goods, services, processes, specimens, systems and
practices and in that regard, establish laboratories and other facilities.

Additional functions include the prohibition of the sale or
manufacture of goods that do not conform to applicable standards, the
prohibition of the import of goods that do not conform to applicable
standards or prescribed Mandatory Standards and similar functions as
regards collection and dissemination of information as in the case of
metrology and standardisation. The Authority is further required to
maintain the required machinery to provide for the issue of a certificate
to the effect that goods prepared and manufactured for local consumption
are of the required standard and goods for export comply with known
requirements of standards in the country to which they are or about to
be consigned before export; to provide for the registration and regulation
of the use of standard marks, to establish, prepare and administer the
procedure and criteria for registration and regulation of conformity
assessment activities, and co-operate with international bodies concerned
to further the functions of the Authority.

For the purpose of exercising the functions of the Authority, the Bill
enumerates in clause 3 powers of the Authority, namely co-operation with
persons outside the country who have similar functions as the Authority;
the request and acceptance of grants, subsidies, donations, gifts,
subscriptions, moneys, land or other property from various persons; the
appointment of agents, the institution of training schemes for the
members of staff of the Authority and the performance of functions under
other enactments.

Clauses 4 to 11 relate to the governance of the Authority.

The composition of the governing body of the Authority is indicated
in clause 4. The Board consists of a chairperson, the Director-General of
the Authority, one representative of the Ministry responsible for Trade 

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

and Industry not below the rank of a Director, a representative each from
the Food and Drugs Authority, National Petroleum Authority,
Environmental Protection Agency, Association of Ghana Industries,
Ghana Shippers Authority and the Centre for Scientific and Industrial
Research, respectively. The representatives should not be below the rank
of a Director or the equivalent of a Director. Other members are two
other persons with knowledge in matters relevant to the functions of the
Authority, one of whom is a representative of a recognised Consumer
Protection Agency and the other who is a woman.

The standard provisions on tenure of office of members of the Board,
meetings of the Board, disclosure of interest, establishment of committees,
Technical Committees and allowances are provided in clauses 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
and 10 respectively. Ministerial directives are provided for in clause 11.

Clauses 12 to 18 provide for the administration of the Authority.

The Bill in clause 12 provides for the appointment of the Director-
General of the Authority. The Director-General is to hold office for a
period of four years and on the terms and conditions specified in the
letter of appointment.

The functions of the Director-General, stated in clause 13, include
the day-to-day administration of the Authority as well as playing the
role of the Custodian of Weights and Measures. The Director-General
may delegate a function to an officer of the Authority but is not to be
relieved of the ultimate responsibility for the performance of the delegated
function.

Clause 14 makes provision for the appointment of Deputy Directors-
General to head each division of the Authority whilst clause 15 establishes
the divisions of the Authority which are the General Services Division,
Conformity Assessment Division and Operations Division. The clause
empowers the Authority to establish new divisions or restructure existing
ones.

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

Clause 16 makes provision for the appointment of the Solicitor
Secretary.

Clause 17 makes provision for the appointment of other staff of the
Authority by the President in accordance with article 195 of the
Constitution. The Authority is also empowered to engage the services of
advisers and consultants on the recommendation of the Board for the
effective performance of the functions of the Authority.

Clause 18 provides for the establishment of regional offices of the
Authority.

Clauses 19 to 24 outline the financial matters of the Authority.

Clause 19 enumerates the sources of funds of the Authority. These
include moneys approved by Parliament and moneys paid to the Authority
by way of subsidies, subscriptions, rent, interest and royalties. Other
sources of funds are moneys derived from the sale of property by or on
behalf of the Authority, the return on investment of funds by the Authority,
donations, gifts and grants and any other internally generated funds.

Clause 20 empowers the Authority to borrow money from the
Government or from a body corporate, local government authority, or
any other person with the approval in writing of the Minister responsible
for Finance. This is however subject to article 181 of the Constitution
and the Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921).

Clause 21 makes provision for opening a bank account by the
Authority with the approval of the Controller and Accountant-General.
An officer or an employee of the Authority who receives money, on behalf
of the Authority is required to pay the money received into the bank
account of the Authority. This is to be done on the next working day
after receipt of the money.

An officer or employee of the Authority is barred from withdrawing
moneys from the bank account of the Authority. Withdrawal transactions
can only be carried out by a cheque signed by an authorised signatory.

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

Accounts and audit are provided for in clause 22. The Board is
required by clause 23 to submit an annual report covering the activities
and the operations of the Authority for the year to which the report relates
to the Minister.

Clause 24 exempts the Authority from the payment of tax.

Clauses 25 to 30 deed with matters concerned with standards and
conformity assessment.

Clause 25 requires the Authority to develop a National Norm for the
development of Ghana Standards approved by the Authority. The clause
provides for the content of the National Norm as well as the procedure
for the development of the National Norm. This clause is a new provision
and seeks to provide legal backing to what already exists in accordance
with international best practice.

Standard specifications and conformity assessment procedures are
provided for in clause 26. The Authority has the power to declare a
specification, including an international, regional or other national
specification, to be a standard specification for the purposes of this Act.
In like manner it may amend or revoke the declaration made. The
Authority is required under this clause to publish the notice of the
declaration, amendment or revocation in the Gazette and by other means
the Authority considers appropriate.

Clause 27 vests the Copyright of the Ghana Standards in the
Authority.

Clause 28 allows for reference to Ghana Standards in other laws and
provides for how such referencing ought to be done. This is to prevent
inappropriate or wrong referencing as well as haphazard referencing of
Ghana Standards in legal documents.

Clause 29 mandates the Minister, on the recommendation of the
Authority to declare a Ghana Standard as mandatory or withdraw a
previous declaration of a Mandatory Standard. This must be based on
public safety, health and environmental protection reasons.

vii

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

Clause 30 requires compliance with Mandatory Standards. A person
who imports, sells or supplies a commodity to which a Mandatory
Standard applies, is required to do so in accordance with the Mandatory
Standards and keep records that the Minister may require.

Clause 31 authorises the Authority to license a person to use a
standard mark in connection with any goods, service, commodity, process,
system or practice. The person may apply to the Authority for the grant
of the licence in the prescribed manner.

Consideration of an application by the Authority is provided for in
clause 32. In this clause, the Authority has to approve that the goods, service,
process, system or practice with respect to which the applicant desires to
use a standard mark conforms to a standard specification, before it grants
the licence or certificate to the applicant to use a standard mark.
Furthermore, a person to whom a licence or certificate is granted under
this clause is required to submit a sample for examination or testing. The
sample may be selected at random by a person authorised by the Authority.

A licence or certificate granted by the Authority under the Bill is
valid for a period determined by the Authority, and may be renewed by
the Authority, clause 33.

Clause 34 provides for the non-transferability of a licence. A licence
issued under the Bill is not transferrable.

Clause 35 empowers the Authority to suspend a licence or certificate
granted under this Bill if the product does not conform to the standards
specified.

Clause 36 empowers the Authority to revoke a licence or certificate
granted under this Bill where the person to whom the licence or certificate
is issued fails to rectify or correct the non-conformity in the product,
scheme or procedure within the time frame specified by the Authority.

viii

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

The Authority is to notify the person in writing within fourteen days
after the decision has been taken to revoke the licence.

Clause 37 outlines a redress mechanism for persons aggrieved by
decisions of the Authority. The process of appeal is set out in clause 37.

The Authority is required under clause 38, to keep and maintain a
Register of licences in which must be recorded the details of each licence.
The register is open for inspection during working hours.

Clause 39 empowers the Director-General to appoint inspectors for
purposes of the Bill.

Clause 40 outlines the duties of an inspector which include to verify
the conformity of goods, processes or services with relevant Mandatory
Standards or other applicable standards and to pursue action on the
payment of fees for the purposes of the Bill.

Clause 41 makes provision for inspectors to enter premises to inspect,
stop a process or practice or seize and detain an article.

Clause 42 provides a cover for employees who disclose information
to inspectors appointed under the Bill.

Under clause 43, the usage of a standard mark in connection with
any goods, service, commodity, process, system or practice or a declaration
that goods, a service, commodity, process, system or practice conforms
to a standard specification is not to give rise to a claim against the
Republic or the Authority. The clause extends the cover of protection to
members of the Board, a committee or employee of the Authority for
acts done or defaults made in the performance of functions under the
Bill.

Clause 44 prohibits the use of a name with any combination of the
words “Ghana Standards Authority” or “Ghana Standards” except with
the written consent of the Minister.

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

Clauses 45 to 51 provide for units and measurements and Physical
Standards.

Clause 45 stipulates the unit of measurement to be used in the country.
The unit is the International System of Units. The International System
of Units comprises the base unit, the supplementary and derived units
and the units which may be used in conjunction with the base,
supplementary and derived units.

The Authority is required, under clause 46, to acquire, procure or
prepare and maintain a National Prototype Standard of mass and
measure of the units of the International System of Units. This is to be
known as the Primary Standards. The Authority is required to calibrate
and certify the Primary Standards in terms of the International Prototype
Standards of mass and measure. The International Prototype is to be
maintained and kept by the International Bureau of Weights and
Measures in the manner that the Authority may determine. Clause 46
stipulates that the Primary Standards are to be the primary standards of
mass and measure by reference to which standards of mass and measure
shall be maintained in the country.

Clause 41 provides for the Secondary Standards of mass and measure,
which are to be procured or prepared and maintained by the Authority.
The Authority is to compare and verify the Secondary Standards from
the Primary Standards.

Clause 48 mandates the Authority to procure or prepare and maintain
copies of Secondary Standards and to verify copies of Secondary
Standards as Tertiary Standards of mass and measure.

The Authority is required, in clause 49, to procure or prepare and
maintain Working Standards of mass and measure in the form
recommended by the Custodian of Weights and Measures.

The Custodian of Weights and Measures is required under this clause
to verify the Working Standards by reference to the Tertiary Standards,
and make an indelible mark on the Working Standards. This is to be 

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

used for the inspection, verification and authentication of the weights
and measures required by the Bill and for other purposes that the Authority
may direct.

Clause 50 places an obligation on the Director-General to calibrate
the Primary Standards at least once in every ten years at the International
Bureau of Weights and Measures or any other accredited laboratory.
While the Primary Standards are being calibrated, the Secondary
Standards which have been verified with the Primary Standards are to be
recognised as the Primary Standards during the period in which the
Primary Standards are out of the country. Calibration of the Secondary,
Tertiary and Working Standards are on the other hand to be done by the
Custodian of Weights and Measures. This is to be done at intervals and
in the manner that the Authority determines.

Clause 51 requires the keeping of the Primary and Secondary
Standards in the custody and under the control of the Custodian of
Weights and Measures. The Authority, on the other hand is required to
keep the Tertiary Standards while the Inspector of Weights and Measures
is to keep the Working Standards in a manner directed by the Authority.

Clauses 52 to 56 deal with matters related to the weights and measures
for trade, industry, health, safety and environment.

Weights and Measures are dealt with in clause 52. The daoseprohibits
a person from using a weight or measure for trade, industry, health, safety
or environment if the unit of measurement of length, area, volume, or
mass or weight is not specified in the First Schedule of the Bill; the linear,
square or cubic measure is not specified in the Bill or a weight, measure
or instrument has not been pattern approved. The requirement of pattern
approved of weights and measures or instruments is to ensure that the
weight or instrument is suitable for trade, health, safety and the
environment and will not facilitate fraud.

xi

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

The requirements of marking of Weights and Measures with
denominations are provided for in clause 53. A weight for use in trade,
industry, health, safety or the environment must have the denomination
of the weight marked on the top or side of the weight in legible figures
and letters.

Stamping, verification and the issue of certificates by an inspector
are provided for in clause 54. The inspector has to verify and stamp a
weight, measure or an instrument for use in trade or industry as specified
in the Third Schedule of the Bill, with a stamp of verification. This is
required to be done with reference to the Working Standards.

Clause 55 prohibits the use of a weight made of lead or pewter or of
a mixture of lead and pewter for trade or in industry. The inspector of
weights and measures, is not to verify, stamp, certify or authenticate a
weight made of lead or pewter or of a mixture of lead and pewter.
However this prohibition does not apply where the weight is wholly and
substantially cased with brass, copper or iron and legibly marked “cased”.

Furthermore, an inspector may refuse to stamp an iron weight or a
weight cased with iron unless it has a plug of softer metal upon which to
impress or affix the stamp.

Clause 56 provides for measures of capacity. The clause specifies the
circumstances under which a measure of capacity may be used to measure
liquid and the measure of capacity a person may use to measure liquid.

Clauses 57 to 62 deal with matters concerned with the administration
of weights and measures.

Clause 57 provides that in accordance with the requirements of the
International Bureau of Weights and Measures, the Authority is the
National Metrology Institute. Under clause 58, the Minister is to publish
a notice in the Gazette notifying the public of the appointment of the
Director-General as the Custodian of Weights and Measures. The notice
is to contain the name of the Custodian and die date of appointment.
Under clauses 59 and 60, the Director-General is empowered to appoint a
Chief Inspector of Weights and Measures and Inspectors of Weights 

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

and Measures respectively. The appointment of inspectors of Weights
and Measures provided for under clause 60, is to ensure the effective
implementation of the Bill. The inspector appointed is issued with a
certificate of appointment by the Authority and is required to produce
the certificate whenever required in the discharge of duties under the Bill.
The Chief Inspector is required to procure the Working Standards and
Instruments for weighing or measuring and to deliver them to inspectors
appointed under clause 60. In addition, the Director-General of the
Authority may give the Chief Inspector directions of a general character
and the Chief Inspector is required to give effect to the directions.

The functions of an inspector appointed under the Bill are stipulated
in clause 61. These include the examination of every weight, measure or
instrument for trade and industry including health, safety and environment
devices which are brought to the Chief Inspector for the purpose of
verification, and the comparison of weight, measures or instruments with
the corresponding Working Standards.

An inspector appointed under the Bill, is empowered in clause 62 at
all reasonable times, to enter premises for the purpose of enforcing the
provisions of the Bill. In the process, the inspector may seize a weight,
measure or instrument for the purpose of comparing it with a Working
Standard, if the inspector finds on an examination of the weight, measure
or instrument that the weight, measure or instrument is made or used in
contravention of a provision of the Bill.

Offences and penalties under the Bill are dealt with in clauses 63 to
73. Clause 63 creates the offences relating to standards mark, specification
and conformity assessment. Amongst others, a person is prohibited from
making a statement or representation, whether in writing or not, or using
a mark, which conveys or is likely to convey the impression that goods, a
process, system or practice complies with a standard specification when
it does not. A contravention of the provision may result in a penalty of
not more than one thousand penalty units.

Furthermore, an inspector who stamps, marks or certifies a product
Or system in contravention of a conformity assessment procedure is liable 

xiii

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

to a penalty of not more than two thousand penalty units or to a term of
imprisonment of not more than four years.

Clause 64 deals with offences in relation to weights, measures and
instruments in trade and industry, health, safety and the environment. It
outlines the weight, measure or instrument that a person in trade or
industry should not use. This includes a weight, measure or an instrument
which is false or unjust, a weight, measure or an instrument which is not
authorised to be used under clause 52, which is not verified, stamped,
certified or authenticated in conformity with the Bill and a weight,
measure or an instrument which has not been issued with a certificate of
verification. Other weights, measures or instruments which cannot be
used are those which have the tag, seal or mark removed without due
authorisation or which have been repaired or installed without required
authorisation.

Furthermore, a person commits an offence if that person sells goods
whether on behaff of that person or on behalf of any other person with a
package or container which does not indicate the relevant gross weight
or measure and the relevant net weight or measure, clause 65.

The Bill also makes it an offence in clause 66 for a person to sell goods
whether personally or on behalf of any other person, by weight or
measure, without weighing the goods, where the goods are sold by weight
or measuring the goods where the goods are sold by measure, in the
presence of the buyer.

Clause 67 of the Bill makes it an offence to trade without the requisite
weight, measure or instrument if the weight, measure or instrument is
considered necessary for the trade.

Clause 68 outlines fraud and forgery offences in relation to a weight,
measure or an instrument. These include a person who knowingly makes,
sells or uses an unjust weight, measure, or instrument or forges or assists
in the forgery or procurement of a stamp or mark used for stamping or
marking a weight, a measure or an instrument amongst others.

Obstruction of an inspector in the performance of functions under
the Bill is categorised as an offence under clause 69.

xiv

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

In the same vein, an inspector who stamps, marks or certifies a
weight, a measure or an instrument without duly verifying it by
comparison with the proper Working Standard, or repairs, alters or adjusts
a weight, measure or an instrument examined by that inspector, commits
an offence under clause 70.

An inspector is empowered by clause 71 to seize a weight, measure
or an instrument if the inspector has reasonable cause to believe that the
weight, measure or instrument, is being used to commit an offence under
the Bill. In cases where the owner of the weight, measure or instrument
cannot be found within thirty days after the seizure, the weight, measure
or instrument shall be forfeited to the State.

Clause 72 stipulates the penalty for corporate bodies.

In the case of a body corporate, other than a partnership, every
director and officer of that body corporate is deemed to have committed
that offence whilst for that of a firm, every partner of that firm is deemed
to have committed that offence.

Clause 73 is a new provision seeking to empower the Authority to
fine offenders without recourse to court proceedings. This is however
only in circumstances where the person found to have committed the
offence admits to the offence in writing.

Clause 74 provides that where a person who carries on a trade or
industry is found in the possession of a weight, measure or an instrument,
that person is deemed to have possession of the weight, measure or
instrument for use in trade, industry, health, safety or the environment
unless the contrary is proved.

Clauses 75 to 83 make provision for miscellaneous matters under the
Bill. Issues relating to confidentiality are provided for in clause 75. This is
to the effect that information obtained by the Authority, the members of
the Board or an officer or an employee of the Authority, or by any other
person in the course of the administration of this Bill in respect of a
formula, process, system or practice is to be treated as confidential.
This however does not apply if the information is obtained in connection
with the administration of the Bill and does not affect a subsequent
application for a patent.

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY BILL, 2021

Clause 76 provides for a permissible margin of error for a weight,
measure or an instrument to be prescribed by Regulations. A weight,
measure or an instrument is not by the clause to have a greater error than
the limits of error prescribed.

The Bill, in clause 77, provides for the conversion of the values of the
units of the International System of Units in terms of the values of other
units of measurement.

Clause 78 extends the application of the Bill by requiring the
construction of a reference to units of measurement contained in an
enactment in force on the coming into force of the Bill as a reference to
the appropriate unit of the International System of Units as specified in
the Fourth Schedule of the Bill.

Clause 79 provides for vessels that are not represented as authorised
measures. The Bill does not prevent the sale, or subject a person to a penalty
for the sale of anything in a vessel, where the vessel is not represented as
containing an amount of a measure authorised under the Bill.
Furthermore, the Bill does not subject a person to a penalty under the
Bill, for the possession of a vessel, where it is shown that the vessel is not
intended for use as a measure.

The Minister is empowered under clause 80 to make Regulations.

The interpretation of words used in the Bill is provided for in clause
81. Clause 82 repeals the existing legislation in respect of the Authority
and clause 83 is on transitional provisions.

BILL
ENTITLED

GHANA STANDARDS AUTHORITY ACT, 2021
AN ACT to establish the Ghana Standards Authority, amend and

consolidate the law relating to standardisation, conformity
assessment and metrology and to provide for related matters.

PASSED by Parliament and assented to by the President:

Establishment of Authority

Establishment of the Ghana Standards Authority
1. (1) There is established by this Act a body corporate with perpetual

succession to be known as the Ghana Standards Authority.
(2) For the performance of the functions of the Authority under

this Act, the Authority may acquire and hold property, dispose of
property and enter into a contract or any other transaction.

(3) Where there is a hindrance to the acquisition of land, the land
may be acquired for the Authority under the Land Act, 2020 (Act 1036)
and the cost shall be borne by the Authority.

6

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

Objects of the Authority
2. The objects of the Authority are to

(a) establish, promulgate and maintain standards to ensure high
quality of goods and services that are

(i) produced or procured in the country for local
consumption or for export, or

(ii) imported for local consumption;
(b) promote standardisation and metrology in industry,

commerce, health and services;
(c) promote conformity assessment in industry, commerce and

services;
(d) promote industrial efficiency and development;
(e) promote standards in public and industrial welfare, health,

safety and environment; and
(f) become a member of or affiliate to an international body

concerned with standardisation, metrology and conformity
assessment or related matters.

Functions of the Authority
3. (1) The Authority shall ensure the achievement of the objects under

section 2.
(2) Without limiting subsection (1), the Authority may, in relation

to
(a) standardisation

(i) prepare, frame, amend or modify, maintain and
promulgate National Standards;

(ii) establish laboratories and other facilities to promote
research in relation to standardisation;

(iii) undertake and encourage educational work in
connection with standardisation;

(iv) collect and disseminate information concerning
standardisation including the publication of reports,
pamphlets, booklets, journals, and any other
publication;

(v) develop and maintain a collection of library
materials and a museum collection relating to
standardisation and allied matters;

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

(vi) endorse an international, regional or any other
national specification suitable for use in the Republic;
and

(vii) collaborate with the relevant regulatory bodies to
enact legislation on Technical Regulations or
applicable Mandatory Standards;

(b) metrology
(i) realise, maintain and disseminate the international

system of units of measurements;
(ii) provide calibration services;
(iii) inspect and verify weights, measures, weighing and

measuring instruments used in trade, industry,
health, safety and environment;

(iv) undertake and encourage academic work in connection
with metrology;

(v) collect and disseminate information in relation to
metrology and related matters, including the
publication of reports, pamphlets, booklets, journals,
and any other publication;

(vi) develop and maintain a collection of library materials
and a museum collection relating to metrology and
allied matters; and

(vii) participate in activities of international bodies

(c) conformity assessment
(i) establish and maintain facilities for the purposes of

(ii) promote research and provide for the examination,

testing and certification of goods, services, processes,
specimens, systems and practices, and in that regard
establish laboratories and other facilities that it
considers fit;

(iii) prohibit, in consultation with the relevant Government
agency and in the national interest, the sale or
manufacture of any kind of goods that does not
conform to the applicable standards;

Development of National Norm

(4) Where the Authority deems it desirable to declare or amend or

(7) A person may, within sixty days of the publication of the

(8) The Authority may, having regard to the objections or

Mandatory Standard under paragraph (b) of subsection (2);
and

(c) in which interested persons are invited to comment on the

enactment that regulates the import, sale or supply of any commodity

Compliance with Mandatory Standards

30. (1) Where the Minister declares a Mandatory Standard, a person
concerned at any stage of the manufacture, production, processing,
treatment or distribution of the commodity in respect of which the
declaration is made, shall ensure compliance with the Mandatory
Standards.

accordance with the Mandatory Standard.

(a) keep or supply to the Authority, records that the Minister

goods, service, commodity, process, system or practice may apply to the
Authority in the prescribed manner.
Consideration of the application

32. (1) The Authority may, if the Authority is satisfied that the goods,
service, commodity, process, system or practice with respect to which the
applicant desires to use a standard mark conforms to a standard specifi­
cation, grant the applicant a licence or certificate to use a standard mark.

section shall, when required by the Authority,

(a) submit a sample for examination or testing;

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

(b) submit itself for audit; or
(c) submit the information required by the Authority.

(3) A sample required under this section for examination or testing
may be selected at random by a person authorised by the Authority.

(4) When a sample is submitted or selected for examination or
testing, the licensee shall pay the prescribed fee.
Validity of licence

33. (1) A licence or certificate granted under this Act
(a) is valid for a period determined by the Authority based on

the applicable standards, and
(b) shall be renewed by the Authority in the prescribed manner.

(2) The Authority may refuse to grant or renew a licence or certificate.
(3) A person aggrieved by the refusal of the Authority to renew a

certificate or licence may appeal to the Appeals Committee established
under section 37.
Non-transferability of licence

34. A licence issued under this Act is not transferrable.
Suspension of licence or certificate

35. (1) The Board may, by notice in writing, suspend a licence or
withdraw a certificate granted under this Act for a product, scheme or
procedure where the product, scheme or procedure, does not conform to
an applicable standard, to enable the person concerned rectify the
non-conformity.

(2) The duration of the suspension shall be as specified in the
applicable standard.
Revocation of licence or certificate

36. (1) The Board may, by notice in writing, revoke a licence or
withdraw a certificate granted under this Act where the person referred to
under subsection (1) of section 35, fails to rectify the non-conformity in
the product, scheme or procedure within the time specified by the
Authority.

(2) The Board shall revoke the licence or withdraw the certificate
granted under this Act where a false declaration has been made in an
application for a licence or certificate granted to the person.

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

(3) The Director-General shall communicate the decision of the
Board to revoke a licence or withdraw a certificate to the person within
fourteen days of the decision to revoke the licence or withdraw the
certificate.

(4) A person who is aggrieved by the revocation or withdrawal
may appeal to the applicable Appeals Committee of the Authority.

Appeals against decisions of the Authority
37. (1) A person dissatisfied with a decision of the Authority may

appeal to the Board against the decision.
(2) The appeal shall be made within twenty-one days after the

appellant has been informed of the decision.
(3) The Board shall, within twenty-eight days after the receipt of

the appeal, set up an Appeals Committee chaired by a member of the
Board to determine the appeal.

(4) The Appeals Committee shall, subject to the rules of natural
justice and any procedures that may be prescribed by the Regulations
determine the procedure of the Appeals Committee.

(5) The Appeals Committee shall determine an appeal within
twenty-one days after the submission of the appeal and may

(a) affirm the decision of the Authority;
(b) vary the decision of the Authority; or
(c) revoke the decision of the Authority.

(6) A person who is dissatisfied with the decision of the Board
may apply to the High Court for review.

Register of licences and certificates
38. (1) The Authority shall keep and maintain a register of licences

and certificates, into which the Authority shall record the details of
licences and certificates granted under this Act.

and an extract from the register may be made by any interested person on

Appointment of inspectors

with subsection (4), the employee shall immediately return the identity
card to the Authority.
Duties of an inspector

40. An inspector shall carry out inspection as the Authority may
direct in compliance with any provision of this Act, to

(a) verify the conformity of goods, processes or services with
the relevant Mandatory Standards or other applicable
standards, and

(b) investigate any fees payable in terms of the administration
of this Act.

Entry of premises and seizure of products
41. (1) An inspector may at all reasonable times and for the purposes

of this Act, enter any premises in which any commodity, process or practice
is or is reasonably suspected of being manufactured, processed, produced,
treated or kept for the purpose of any trade or business.

(2) Pursuant to subsection (1), an inspector may
(a) inspect or take samples of the commodity or of any material

used or suspected to be intended for use in the manufacture,
production, processing or treatment of the commodity;

(b) inspect the process or practice and take notes in relation to
the process or practice;

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

(c) inspect any operation carried out in the premises in connection

relates to the commodity, process or practice; and

(f) require any person to appear before the inspector to answer
any questions in relation to the commodity or process.

(3) Subject to this Act or any other enactment, an inspector may

detaining an article or causing a stop in the process or practice under

(a) direct that the article, process or practice be made to comply

(b) return the article, process or practice seized, detained or
stopped from operating, to the person from whom the article
was taken or the process or practice stopped where the
directive given under paragraph (a) is complied with; or

(c) forfeit the article, surrender the process or practice seized,
detained or stopped, to the Republic where the directive
given under paragraph (a) is not complied with.

(5) The article, process or practice seized, detained or stopped from
operating which is forfeited to the Republic shall be destroyed or
otherwise disposed of in the manner directed by the Director-General.

(6) An inspector or any person authorised under subsection (1)
shall, if required to do so, produce proof of identity in order to exercise
the power under this section.
Disclosure of information by employee

42. (1) Despite anything in an undertaking in respect of disclosure
of information, an employee shall not be liable for any penalty for the

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

disclosure of information to an inspector or an authorised person when

(2) The employer of the employee shall not do anything to

Indemnity

43. (1) The usage of a standard mark in connection with any goods,
service, commodity, process, system or practice or a declaration that goods,

Restriction on use of certain words

(3) Subsection (1) does not apply to a person using a name
described in that subsection prior to the coming into force of this Act.

Units and Measurements
International System of Units

45. (1) The unit of measurement to be used in the Republic is the unit
known as the International System of Units.

(2) The International System of Units comprise
(a) the base units specified in Part One of the First Schedule;
(b) the supplementary and derived units specified in Pent Two

of the First Schedule; and
(c) the units which may be used in conjunction with the base,

supplementary and derived units specified in Part Three of
the First Schedule.

26

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

(3) Multiples and sub-multiples of each of the units of the
International System of Units shall be an integral power often, positive
or negative, as specified in Part Four of the First Schedule.

(4) The base units and supplementary units referred to in subsection
(2) shall have the definitions assigned to them as specified in Part Five of
the First Schedule.

Physical Standards

Primary Standards
46. (1) The Authority may procure or prepare and maintain a

National Prototype Standard of mass and measure of the units of the
International System of Units to be known as the Primary Standards
specified in Part One of the First Schedule.

(2) The Authority shall calibrate and certify the Primary Standards
in terms of the International Prototype Standards of mass and measure
which is maintained and kept by the International Bureau of Weights
and Measures in a manner that the Authority may determine.

(3) The Primary Standards shall be the primary standards of mass
and measure by reference to which standards of mass and measure shall
be maintained in the country.

(4) The Primary Standards shall be in the form and of the material
that the Authority may direct.

(5) The Authority shall maintain the weighing machines and any
other articles that appear to the Authority necessary for giving effect to
this section.

(6) Weighing, measuring instruments and prepackages should have
traceability to the International System of Units through either

(a) the system of national measurement standards and
certified reference material; or

(b) traceability to recognised national measurement standards
or certified reference material of other countries when the
uncertainty level cannot be obtained within the country.

(7) The Ghana Standards Authority as the designated national
measurement institute shall have calibration results, test results and
measurement results established and traceable to the realisation of the 

27

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

International System of Units and presented in compliance with the
recommendation of the General Conference on Weights and Measures
and the International Organisation on Weights and Measures and other
international standards.
Secondary Standards

47. The Authority shall
(a) procure or prepare and maintain secondary standards of

mass and measure consisting of the weights and measures
set out in the Second Schedule; and

(b) cause the secondary standards to be verified from the
primary standards.

Tertiary Standards
48. The Authority shall

(a) procure or prepare and maintain copies of the Secondary
Standards which the Authority may determine, and

(b) verify the copies of the Secondary Standards as Tertiary
Standards of mass and measure.

Working Standards
49. (1) The Authority shall procure or prepare and maintain Working

Standards of mass and measure in the form recommended by the Custodian
of Weights and Measures.

(2) The Custodian shall
(a) verify the Working Standards by reference to the Tertiary

Standards, and
(b) make an indelible mark on the Working Standards.

(3) The Working Standards shall be used for the inspection,
verification and authentication of the weights and measures required by
this Act, and for any other purposes that the Authority may direct.
Calibration of Standards

50. (1) The Director-General shall ensure that the Primary Standards
are calibrated at least once in every ten years at the International Bureau
of Weights and Measures or any other accredited laboratory.

(2) Where the Primary Standards are due for calibration, the
Authority shall deposit with the Custodian, the Secondary Standards 

28

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

which the Authority considers fit, after having provided for them to be
compared and verified with the Primary Standards in the manner
directed by the Authority.

(3) The Secondary Standards which are verified in subsection (2)
shall be the Primary Standards during the time that the Primary Standards
are out of the Republic.

(4) The Custodian shall compare and calibrate the Secondary,
Tertiary and Working Standards at intervals and in the manner that the
Authority may determine.

(5) Where the Custodian is satisfied with the accuracy of the
Secondary, Tertiary or Working Standards, the Custodian shall issue a
certificate of calibration or verification to the person who has custody of
die relevant standard.

(6) A person who has custody of the relevant standards shall
retain the certificate issued under subsection (5).

(7) A Secondary, Tertiary and Working Standard that is duly
verified and certified, shall be considered to be true and accurate and

(8) The Authority
(a) may cancel a Secondary, Tertiary or Working Standard, and
(b) shall by notice published in the Gazette direct that the

cancelled Standard shall not be used for the purposes of
this Act.

Keeping of Standards
51. (1) The Primary and Secondary Standards, in the custody and

under the control of the Custodian, shall be kept in the place determined
by the Authority.

(2) The Custodian shall ensure the security of the Primary and
Secondary Standards in the manner determined by the Authority.

(3) The Authority shall keep the Tertiary Standards in the manner
determined by the Authority.

(4) The Inspector of Weights and Measures shall keep the Working
Standards in the manner directed by the Authority.

Weights and Measures for Trade, Industry, Health, Safety and Environment
Weights and measures

52. (1) A person shall not use for trade, industry, health, safety or
environment or possess for use in trade, industry, health, safety or environment

(a) a unit of measurement of length, area, volume, or mass or
weight, which is not specified in the First Schedule;

(b) linear, square or cubic measure which is not specified in the
Second Schedule or a weight which is not specified in the
Second Schedule; or

(c) a weight, measure or instrument which has not been
Pattern Approved.

(a) a linear measure specified in Part One of the Second Schedule

subdivisions representing a shorter length or lengths; or

shall not be used for trade or industry by means of a
division or subdivision marked on the cubic measure as a
cubic measure of a lesser quantity.

Marking of weights and measures with denomination
53. (1) A manufacturer of, or a person who uses, a weight or measure

for use in trade, industry, health, safety or environment shall ensure that
the weight for use in trade, industry, health, safety or environment specified
in the Third Schedule, has the denomination of the weight marked on
the top or side of the weight in legible figures and letters.

(2) For purposes of subsection (1), where the size of a weight
renders it impracticable to mark that weight, that manufacturer or person

(a) shall supply the certificate in respect of the weight, and
(b) produce the certificate for inspection on the request by an

inspector.
(3) A certificate required to be produced under subsection (2), shall

contain sufficient particulars to enable the identification and denomination
of the weight to be established.

(4) A manufacturer of a measure of capacity, or a person who
uses a measure of capacity in trade, industry, health, safety or environment

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

specified in the Third Schedule shall ensure that the measure of capacity

(5) A weight or measure not in conformity with this section shall

Stamping, verification and issue of certificates
54. (1) Subject to this section, an inspector shall

(a) verify and stamp a weight, a measure or an instrument for
use in trade or industry as specified in the Third Schedule
with a stamp of verification; and

(b) issue a certificate of verification at the time of stamping.
(2) Where the size of the weight, measure or instrument renders it

impracticable for the inspector to verify and stamp it with the stamp of

(3) A certificate of verification issued under this section remains

unless the weight, measure or instrument is unjust.

(4) A person who possesses for use in trade, industry, health, safety
or environment a weight, measure or instrument specified in the Third
Schedule, shall

(a) retain the certificate of verification issued in respect of the
weight, measure or instrument, and

(b) produce the certificate for inspection when required to do
so by an inspector.

(5) An inspector shall authenticate a weight, measure or an
instrument which is stamped and verified under this section within the
prescribed intervals.

(6) The inspection, verification, authentication and stamping
under this section shall be made by reference to the Working Standards.

(7) Where it is impracticable for a weight, measure or an instrument

Measures of capacity

Offences and Penalties
Offences relating to standards mark, specification or conformity
assessment

63. (1) A person who
(a) makes a statement or representation, whether in writing or

not, or uses a mark, which conveys or is likely to convey the
impression that goods, a process, system or practice complies
with a standard specification when the goods, process,
system or practice does not do so;

(b) makes a statement or representation, whether in writing or not,
or uses a mark with reference to goods, a commodity, process,
system or practice, which conveys or is likely to convey the
impression that a person who is not licensed to use a standard
mark with reference to the goods, commodity, process, system
or practice is so licensed to use the standard mark;

35

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

(c) without the authority of the Board, and for the purpose of
gain or profit, whether by means of sale or otherwise, makes
a statement or representation, whether in writing or not,
whereby comparison is made in respect of goods, a
commodity, process, system or practice, with the standard
provided for by a standard specification, unless that person
proves that the act was done without the intent to defraud;

(d) having been licensed to use a standard mark, uses the
standard mark after the revocation of the licence or uses
the standard mark otherwise than in accordance with the
terms and conditions of the licence;

(e) being a person concerned at any stage of the manufacture,

(i) contravenes section 44

commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not

further fine of not more than fifty penalty units for each day that the
contravention continues.

(2) An inspector who stamps, marks or certifies a product or
system in contravention of the conformity assessment procedure, commits
an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not less than

(a) which is false or unjust;

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

Trading without required weights, measures or instruments
67. A person who trades without the requisite weights, measures or

instruments which are necessary for the trade, commits an offence and is
liable on summary conviction to a fine of not less than twenty-five penalty
units and not more than one thousand penalty units.

Fraud and forgery in relation to weights, measures and instruments
68. A person who

(a) knowingly makes, sells or uses, or knowingly causes to be
made, sold or used, an unjust weight, measure, or instrument;

(b) forges or causes to be forged or knowingly assists in forging
or procures a stamp or mark used for stamping or marking
a weight, a measure or an instrument;

(c) knowingly sells, disposes of or exposes for sale a weight, a
measure or an instrument with a forged stamp or mark on
the weight, measure or instrument;

(d) with intent to defraud, alters a weight, a measure or an
instrument stamped or marked in accordance with this Act;
or

(e) does an act which amounts to fraud in the use for trade,
industry, health, safety or environment, of a weight, a measure
or an instrument

commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not
less than five hundred penalty units and not more than two thousand
penalty units or to a term of imprisonment of not less than two years
and not more than four years or to both.
Obstruction of inspector

69. A person who
(a) fails, neglects or refuses to produce for examination by an

inspector when lawfully required to do so, a certificate, a
weight, a measure, or an instrument in the possession or
custody, or on the premises of that person; or

(b) willfully obstructs an inspector in the performance of a
function under this Act,

38

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not
less than two hundred and fifty penalty units and not more than one
thousand penalty units or to a term of imprisonment of not less than
two years and not more than four years or to both.

Offences by an inspector
70. An inspector who

(a) stamps, marks or certifies a weight, a measure or an instrument
without duly verifying it by comparison with the proper
Working Standard; or

(b) repairs, alters or adjusts a weight, measure or an instrument

commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not

penalty units or to a term of imprisonment of not less than two years
and not more than four years or to both.

Seizure and forfeiture of weights, measures and instruments
71. (1) Where an inspector has reasonable cause to believe that an

offence under this Act has been committed in respect of the weight,
measure or instrument, the inspector shall seize the weight, measure or
instrument.

(2) Where the owner of the weight, measure or instrument cannot
be found within thirty days after the seizure, the weight, measure or
instrument shall be forfeited to the Republic.

(3) Subject to subsection (2), a weight, measure or an instrument
in respect of which an offence is committed under this Act may be

(4) A weight, measure or an instrument which is forfeited to the

Offences by body of persons
72. (1) Where an offence is committed by a body of persons,

(a) in the case of a body corporate, other than a partnership,
every director and officer of that body corporate shall be
deemed to have committed that offence; and

Ghana Standards Authority Bill, 2021

(b) in the case of a firm, every partner of that firm shall be

under subsection (1), if that person proves that the act in respect of which

title: Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund Amendment Bill, 2021
text:
The Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund was established pursuant to section 2
of the Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund Act, 2014 (Act 877) with a mandate to
mobilise, manage, coordinate and provide financial resources for investment in a
diversified portfolio of infrastructure projects in the country for national development.

Since 2017, Government has provided no financial support to the Fund.
Regardless of this, the Fund has since 2017 been able to invest three hundred million
United States dollars (US$300,000,000) in a portfolio of fourteen infrastructure projects
in seven different sectors covering airports, sea ports, energy, Information
Communication Technology and hospitality institutions across the country.

More importantly, the Fund has managed to bring in ten times that amount in co­
financings from other sources, resulting in a projected total of three billion United States
dollars (US$3,000,000,000) investments into Ghanaian infrastructure projects.. The
results further show that for each United States dollar (US$1) given to the Fund by
Government, the Fund has succeeded in attracting ten United States dollars (US$10) to
‘be used for projects of the Fund.

The Fund is currently poised to provide investments in the power sector,
refinancing to Independent Power Providers under the Energy Sector Recovery
Programme, collaborate in financing for the hospital initiative of the President, Agenda
111, the Accra-Tema Motorway Project, Affordable Housing, renewable energy,
additional toll roads and provide solutions to help address the shortages in university
accommodation.

MEMORANDUM
The object of the Bill is to amend the Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund Act,

2014 (Act 877) to provide for additional sources of funds and extend the period of

exemption from taxes.

The Fund is a permanent capital investment vehicle initially capitalised at two
hundred and fifty million United States dollars (US$250,000,000). The Fund
subsequently received seventy-five million United States dollars (US$75,000,000) from
the. Annual Budget Funding Amount under the Petroleum Revenue Management Act,
2011 (Act 815). The last Annual Budget Funding Amount of six point nine million United
States dollars (US$6.9million) was received from Government on SO01 January, 2017.
Vlence the total Government support received for the Fund is three hundred and twenty-
five million United States dollars (US$325m).

GHANA INFRASTRUCTURE INVESTMENT FUND (AMENDMENT/
BILL, 2021

1

The Fund was exempted from all taxes for a period of five years after
commencement of operations to enable the Fund use the savings of the Fund to support
investment programmes and projects.

The Fund commenced operations in February 2015 following the appointment of
the first Board of Directors, thus the tax exemption period ended in February 2020.
Government is extending the period of tax exemption in line with the period of tax
exemption granted to other Development Finance Institutions as the mandate of the
Fund is structured along the same lines as other Development Finance Institutions. This
will enable the Fund to continue to re-invest the savings of the Fund to enhance the
portfolio of infra-structure projects and further mobilise private sector funding to support
the development of more infra-structure projects in the country in accordance with the
mandate of the Fund.

The Earmarked Funds Capping and Realignment Act 2017, (Act 947) rearranged
the sources of revenue for the Fund by realigning some of the sources. This resulted in
the Fund not receiving any funding from Government since 2017. In view of the
additional investments that the Fund has lined up in the pipeline of projects of the Fund,
Government is restoring to the Fund, the revenue from the Annual Budget Funding

• Amount that was initially earmarked for the Fund as a source of revenue, prior to the
passage of Act 947, to support the Fund to carry out the mandate of the Fund within the
local and international environment.

The extension of the exemptions and the provision of additional sources of
revenue will make the Fund more competitive in carrying out the mandate of the Fund
and also better equipped to complete the social part of the mandate of the Fund In the
local and international environment.

The exemption is estimated to be one hundred and sixty-eight million Cedis while
the additional revenue sources will amount to approximately three hundred and sixty-one
million Cedis for the Fund in 2021.

Clause 1 amends section 5 of the Act to provide for sources of moneys for the
Fund. The sources of moneys for the Fund include an amount of money not exceeding
twenty-five per cent of the Annual Budget Funding Amount, repayment inflows of
moneys on-lent by the Ministry of Finance to Ministries, Departments and Agencies of
Government or State-owned enterprises for capital project or infrastructure development,
grants, donations, gifts and other voluntary contributions to the Fund, internally
generated funds, moneys that accrue to the Fund from investment made by the Fund, 

2

moneys borrowed or raised from local and international capital market or from affiliates
of the Fund and any other moneys approved by Parliament for payment into the Fund.

Clause 2 amends section 19 of the Act to provide for the Fund to be exempted
from the payment of any form of tax for the first ten years of the operations of the Fund.

Clause 3 is a consequential amendment which seeks to repeal section 9 of the
Earmarked Funds Capping and Realignment Act, 2017 (Act 947).

title: Exemptions Bill, 2022
text:
EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

MEMORANDUM

The object of the Bill is to provide for an exemptions regime including
variation or limitation of the scope; set clear eligibility criteria; provide
for the administration of exemptions and provide for the monitoring,
evaluation and enforcement of exemptions.

Tax Exemptions in Ghana are embedded in statutory legislation and
exemptions approved by resolutions by the Parhament of Ghana. These
include Income Tax exemptions, tax holidays, rebates, and concessions,
Import exemptions, Value Added Tax reliefs, and Excise Tax.

The rationale for granting these exemptions include attracting foreign
direct investment, alleviating the tax burden on the vulnerable in society,
encouraging business start-ups, attracting investment into specified sectors
or locations and supporting the development agenda of Government.

In the last ten years, tax exemptions namely Import Duty, Import
Value Added Tax, Import National Health Insurance Levy, Import Ghana
Education Trust Fund, Export-Import Levy, Special Import Levy and
Domestic Value Added Tax in the economy have grown even though
there has been a remarkable improvement to curtail the growth.

The total amount of exemptions granted in 2020 was one point
seventy-one billion Ghana Cedis, compared to two point forty-three billion
Ghana Cedis, two point twenty-five billion Ghana Cedis and three point
eight billion Ghana Cedis in 2019, 2018 and 2017 respectively. The total
amount of exemptions granted between 2012 to 2016 and 2017 to 2020
was four point fifty-six billion Ghana Cedis and nine point forty-seven
billion Ghana Cedis respectively.

These figures do not include exemptions from the payment of
corporate and individual income taxes, concessions on tax rates, petroleum
tax reliefs and customs tax exemptions enjoyed by diplomatic missions.

Exemptions distort fair competition among businesses in the same
industry where private projects are granted exemptions to improve their
profitability or viability, which are not available to other players of the
same industry. Additionally, where exemptions are granted on items that
are available locally, unfair competition is created for local manufacturers
of those goods.

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

The current challenges of the exemptions regime are sustained by
the existence of pre-determined tax exemptions in various legislation for
future projects the financials of which cannot be determined. The situation
is aggravated by an entrenched policy mindset on the part of both
Government entities and private suppliers that, by default, businesses that
supply goods, services and projects to the public sector should be exempted
from payments of customs and some domestic taxes.

Unfortunately, even where tax exemptions are necessary, they
invariably create opportunities for abuse and irregularities. Together with
the abuses, exemptions deny the country the much needed revenue, the
consequence being low revenue reporting, which translates into a generally
low overall tax effort represented by a tax to Gross Domestic Product
ratio of about thirteen per cent as at the end of 2020.

Exemptions when granted without the prior knowledge of the
Minister for Finance, disrupt budgeted revenue estimates and invariably
lead to an increase in tax expenditure and higher than planned deficits.

These, amongst others, are the challenges that the Bill seeks to address.
Monitoring plays a crucial part in ensuring that exemptions and

concessions are utilised by beneficiaries for the intended purposes. The
Bill thus provides for additional reporting requirements and mechanisms
to ensure the efficient and effective use of exemptions.

It has also been observed that some exemptions continue to exist on
our Statute book though they have become obsolete. The Bill seeks to
provide sunset clauses and a formal framework for reviewing these
exemptions.

The Addis Ababa Action Agenda which was endorsed by the United
Nations General Assembly in its Third International Conference on
Financing for Development (Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 13-16 July 2015),
includes a comprehensive set of measures aimed at addressing the
challenges of financing the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals. Inherent
in these measures is a commitment to “consider not requesting tax
exemptions on goods and services delivered as govemment-to-govemment
aid, beginning with renouncing repayments of value-added taxes and
import levies.” (Clause 58 of United Nations Resolution A/RES/69/
313 of July 27, 2015).

ii

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

The commitment is based on ithe recognition that tax exemptions
create significant difficulties for developing countries and run counter to
the objective of strengthening domestic resource mobilisation. In line
with this, the Committee of Experts on International Cooperation in
Tax Matters in 2020 provided some guidelines with regards to exemptions.
The Bill incorporates some of the measures enshrined in the United
Nations Resolution and the Guidelines issued by the Committee of
Experts.

The projected exemptions for the year2022 are expected to be lowered
by about five hundred million Ghana Cedis when the Bill is passed by
Parliament.

Clause 1 states the object of the Bill.

Clause 2 states the application of the Bill and resolves the conflict
between the Bill and other exemptions-related legislation by providing
that the Bill will prevail in case of any conflict or inconsistency with other
exemptions-related legislation.

Clause 3 defines exemption for the purposes of the Bill.

Clauses 4 and 5 provide for general responsibilities and the
responsibility of the Minister responsible for Finance.

Clause 6 deals with negotiation and approval of exemption and
prohibits persons from negotiating or entering into an agreement to grant
an exemption except with the prior written approval of the Minister.

Clause 7 provides the procedure for granting exemptions to
Ministries, Departments and Agencies.

Clauses 8 to 12 provide for exemptions to the President of the Republic
and other privileged persons.

Clause 13 provides for exemptions to free zone enterprises and seeks
to address the existence of licensed free zone enterprises that are not
export-oriented.

Clause 14 provides for general tax incentives available to all businesses
in particular industries or programmes.

iii

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

Clauses 15 and 16 set the requirements for the negotiation of special
tax incentives by strategic investors.

Clause Y1 deals with exemptions for executed treaties, agreements or
Conventions and clause 18 deals with exemptions for technical cooperation
programmes.

Clauses 19 and 20 provide for exemptions for programmes and
projects funded by grants and for concessional facility projects.

Clause 21 seeks to restrict exemptions granted to private suppliers or
contractors of goods, works and services to Government and State entities.

Clause 22 provides for exemptions in transactions by security agencies.

Clause 23 deals with administrative fees and other charges and clause
24 deals with transnational levies.

Clause 25 deals with the monitoring and reporting of exemptions.
The Minister is mandated to establish a schedule to review an exemption
so that each exemption is reviewed at least once every five years, clause
26.

Clause 27 deals with the transfer of ownership of an exempt item by
the holder of an exemption and clause 28 deals with local content.

Clause 29 provides for offences and penalties while clauses 30 and 31
provide for Regulations and interpretation respectively.

Clause 32 provides for a consequential amendment to the Ghana
Investment Promotion Centre Act, 2013 (Act 865).

Repeals, savings and transitional provisions are dealt with in clause
33.

KEN OFORI-ATTA
Minister responsible for Finance
