EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

BILL
ENTITLED

EXEMPTIONS ACT, 2022
AN ACT to regulate the application of tax exemptions and other

exemptions and to provide for related matters.

PASSED by Parliament and assented to by the President:

Preliminary Provisions

Object of this Act
1. The object of this Act is to

(a) provide for an exemptions regime including variation or
limitation of the scope, where necessary;

(b) set dear eligibility criteria;
(c) provide for the administration of exemptions; and
(d) provide for monitoring, evaluation and enforcement of

exemptions.

Application
2. (1) This Act applies to all exemptions.

3

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(2) This Act shall be read together with any other enactment
relevant to taxation, levies, fees and charges and public financial
management.

(3) Where there is a conflict or inconsistency between the
provisions of this Act and any other enactment related to exemptions,
the provisions of this Act shall prevail.

Definition of exemption
3. (1) For the purposes of this Act, an exemption is a deviation from

(a) a tax, levy, fee or charge provided for under an enactment,
or

(b) the timing of the payment of a tax, levy, fee or charge
which results in a reduction in the effective liability of the payer.

(2) Despite subsection (1), the power of the Commissioner-General
to remit assessed tax or extend the date on which a tax is payable shall
continue to apply.

General Provisions

General responsibility
4. (1) A person shall not enable another person to enjoy an exemption

unless that exemption has been lawfully granted under this Act.
(2) A person who seeks to benefit from an exemption shall satisfy

the requirements under this Act.
Responsibility of the Minister

5. (1) The power to
(a) submit a request for an exemption to Cabinet or Parhament,

or
(b) seek executive approval for an exemption

is vested in the Minister.
(2) The Minister shall, on receipt of a request for an exemption,

(a) vet the request for the exemption; and
(b) ensure that the exemption is consistent with the economic

management priorities of Government and the general
policy of the Government on exemptions.

(3) The Minister shall issue guidelines on
(a) the modalities for the vetting and granting of exemptions;

and

4

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(b) the procedure for an application for an exemption by an
individual.

(4) The Minister shall, subject to Cabinet or Executive approval,
seek the approval of Parliament by resolution for a request for
exemption in accordance with article 174 of the Constitution.

(5) The Minister shall
(a) monitor the use of an exemption as an economic management

tool; and
(b) report on the impact of an exemption in the annual national

budget presented to Parliament.
(6) The Minister shall advise Cabinet on matters relating to

exemptions.
(7) The Minister shall ensure that Ministries, Departments and

Agencies and other relevant stakeholders are sensitised on any new law
or requirement instituted to

(a) improve the effectiveness of the exemptions regime; or
(b) ensure compliance with this Act.

Negotiation and approval of exemption
6. (1) A person shall not negotiate or enter into an agreement to grant

an exemption except with the prior written approval of the Minister.
(2) An agreement reached between parties to grant an exemption is

of no effect and is not enforceable against the State unless subsection (1)
has been complied with.

(3) Where an exemption is contained in a contract to be placed
before Parliament for approval, the contract shall be accompanied with

(a) a detailed assessment of the value of the anticipated
exemptions contained in the contract;

(b) the list of items and taxes to which the exemptions are
applicable;

(c) a limit on the total value of the exemptions to be granted
under that contract;

(d) a time limit on the exemption to ensure that the exemption
does not exceed the duration of the contract; and

(e) the implications of the exemption on programmed revenue.
(4) A contract that contains an exemption shall not be submitted to

Parliament unless subsections (1) and (3) have been complied with.

5

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(5) An exemption vetted by the Minister and placed before
Parliament for approval may be varied by Parliament and the Minister
shall notify the person concerned and give effect to the variation.

Ministries, Departments and Agencies

Procedure for granting exemptions to Ministries, Departments and
Agencies

7. (1) An application for an exemption by a Ministry, Department or
Agency shall be made to the Minister.

(2) The Minister
(a) shall assess the application; and
(b) may make a recommendation to Cabinet for consideration.

(3) The recommendation referred to in subsection (2) shall state
clearly the basis for the recommendation.

(4) Where the Minister makes a recommendation to Cabinet on an
application for an exemption by a Ministry, Department or Agency and
Cabinet approves the recommendation, Cabinet shall direct the Minister
to submit the application to Parliament for the necessary approval.

(5) Where Cabinet does not approve of the recommendation, the
Minister shall inform the Ministry, Department or Agency of the
decision of Cabinet within fourteen days on receipt of the decision.

(6) Where the Minister does not make a recommendation to
Cabinet for an exemption, the Minister shall inform the Ministry,
Department or Agency of the decision within fourteen days on receipt
of the application.

Privileged Persons
The President

8. (1) Goods procured for the use of the President are exempt from
tax.

(2) Where an enactment provides for an exemption for the
President, the exemption shall be for the use of the President in the
capacity as President.

(3) A person who makes an application for an exemption in the
name of the President which is not for the use of the President commits 

6

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not less than
one thousand penalty units and not more than two thousand five
hundred penalty units or to a term of imprisonment of not less than six
months and not more than five years or to both.

(4) Where an application for an exemption made under subsection
(4) results in a loss of revenue, the person who makes the application is
liable to pay three hundred per cent of the applicable taxes.

Diplomats and diplomatic missions
9. (1) A diplomat shall be granted an exemption where a similar

exemption is granted to a Ghanaian diplomat in the country of that
diplomat.

(2) Goods and vehicles imported by or for the official use of a
body of the United Nations, the African Union, the Economic Community
of West African States, the Commonwealth, a diplomatic mission or a
consulate are exempt from the payment of customs duties and customs
taxes.

(3) On the first arrival in Ghana of an employee of the United
Nations, the African Union, the Economic Community of West African
States, the Commonwealth, a diplomatic mission or a consulate, the
household or personal effects of that employee, if that employee is not
engaged in any other business or profession in Ghana, are exempt from
the payment of customs duties and customs taxes.

(4) Goods and vehicles imported by or for the use of a permanent
member of the United Nations, the African Union, the Economic
Community of West African States, the Commonwealth, a diplomatic
mission or a consulate are exempt from the payment of customs duties
and customs taxes.

(5) For the purposes of this section, the Minister responsible for
Foreign Affairs shall submit to the Minister responsible for Finance on
an annual basis, a list of the diplomats and diplomatic missions that
qualify for exemption.

(6) A diplomat or a diplomatic mission shall enjoy an exemption
based on the list submitted under subsection (5).

(7) The Minister shall issue guidelines on the modalities for the
grant of exemptions to diplomats and diplomatic missions.

7

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

Persons with disability
10- (1) The following disability-related items are exempt from the

payment of customs duties and customs taxes:
(a) books, publications and documents specially designed for

the use of persons with disability on the recommendation
of the Minister responsible for Social Welfare;

(b) other items specially designed for the education, scientific
or cultural advancement of persons with disability, imported
by institutions or organisations recommended by the
Minister responsible for Social Welfare and approved by the
Minister;

(c) vehicles specially designed, adapted and modified for use
by persons with disability certified by the relevant licensing
authority and approved by the Minister; and

(d) specially designed items imported by persons with disability
for their educational, scientific or cultural advancement.

(2) A vehicle imported under paragraph (c) of subsection (1) shall
not be re-exported.

(3) A person who contravenes subsection (2) commits an offence
and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not less than one
hundred penalty units and not more than two hundred and fifty penalty
units or to a term of imprisonment of not less than six months and not
more than twelve months or to both.

Religious organisations
11. (1) The following worship-related imports are exempt from the

payment of customs duties and customs taxes:
(a) altar bread;
(b) communion wafer;
(c) altar wine;
(d) Catholic rosary;
(e) altar frontal;
(f) altar linen and vestments excluding choir robes and pulpit

gowns;
(g) Zamzam\
(h) Tasbi; and

8

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(i) other similar religious items used exclusively for worship
recommended by the Minister responsible for Religious
Affairs and approved by the Minister.

(2) For the purposes of subsection (1),
uTasbf' means an Islamic rosary; and
“Zamzam" means holy water imported from Mecca.

Donor and charity organisations
12. (1) An item for

(a) educational purposes,
(b) health purposes, and
(c) worthwhile causes

imported by a development partner, a charity organisation, a
philanthropist or any other not-for-profit organisation as a gift for
charitable purposes is, subject to subsection (2), exempt from customs
duties and customs taxes where the application is supported by a
recommendation by the relevant sector Minister and approved by the
Minister

(2) An application for the exemption referred to in subsection (1)
shall not be processed unless the application

(a) is made by the official head of the identifiable group that
benefits from the gift; and

(b) spells out in detail the specific items and the quantity of each
item expected in the donation.

(3) An application for the exemption referred to in subsection (1)
shall be accompanied with

(a) the background information of the donor or charity
organisation where the donor or charity organisation is new;
or

(b) a report of the activities of the donor or charity organisation
in the beneficiary social, educational or health institution
in the past twenty-four months, where the donor or charity
organisation is already in existence.

Private Businesses
Free zone enterprises

13. (1) A free zone enterprise that imports items into a free zone or
single factory zone is exempt from customs duties and customs taxes.

9

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(2) An import and an export in transit to or from a free zone are
exempt from customs duties and customs taxes, transit duties, excise duties,
tonnage taxes and other direct and indirect taxes, charges and levies.

(3) A company that is licensed as a free zone enterprise in
accordance with the Free Zone Act, 1995 (Act 504) but that does not
export

(a) a minimum of seventy per cent of the output of the
company, or

(b) the relevant percentage as specified in the licence of the Free
Zone Enterprise

shall pay three hundred per cent of all taxes due.
(4) The Ghana Revenue Authority shall recover the taxes due from

a free zone enterprise that fails to comply with subsection (3).
(5) A free zone enterprise shall submit an annual report to the

Ministry for each year of operations to ensure continuing eligibility.
(6) The annual report referred to in subsection (5) includes

(a) the number of employees;
(b) employee taxes;
(c) annual turnover;
(d) the percentage of goods exported with full export

documentation and destination; and
(e) exemptions enjoyed during the period.

General tax incentives
14. (1) The Minister may, on the recommendation of the relevant

sector Minister and with the approval of Cabinet, by legislative
instrument, make Regulations to grant an industry-specific or
programme-specific tax concession for an industry or investment
programme.

(2) Where the tax concession is on customs duties and customs
taxes, the list of the items to which the concession applies and the exact
concessional rate for each item shall be provided in the Regulations made
under this Act.

(3) Where the State seeks to take up a reciprocal carried interest in
a business that accesses general tax incentives, the particulars of the
carried interest shall be specified in the Regulations made under this Act.

10

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

Special tax incentives for strategic investments
15. (1) The State may, in addition to granting a general tax incentive

to a sector in accordance with an enactment, grant a specially-negotiated
tax exemption for investment where the State takes a commensurate
equity stake in the investment project.

(2) An entity that cedes an equity stake to the State in return for a
tax incentive shall have an unqualified right to buy back the equity stake
of the State at the prevailing market price.

Procedure for granting special tax incentives
16. (1) Cabinet shall, for the purpose of granting special tax

incentives and promoting major investments, determine the priority
areas of economic investments.

(2) The Ghana Investment Promotion Centre shall, within thirty
days after the determination of the priority areas referred to in
subsection (1), publish the priority areas

(a) in the Gazette;
(b) on the website of the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre;

and
(c) in a daily newspaper of nationwide circulation.

(3) An investor that seeks to invest in a priority sector may apply
to the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre stating clearly the cost details
of the investment and the exemptions required.

(4) The Ghana Investment Promotion Centre shall, upon receipt
of an application in subsection (3) and in consultation with the relevant
Ministry, Department or Agency,

(a) make a determination whether the investment is within the
priority areas of economic investment; and

(b) communicate the decision of the Ghana Investment
Promotion Centre to the applicant within thirty days after
the receipt of the application.

(5) Where the Centre determines that the investment project for
which the tax exemptions are being requested is in the priority area of
economic investment, the Chief Executive Officer of the Centre shall,
within five days of making the decision, forward the application to the
Minister.

11

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(6) The Minister shall, on receipt of the request from the Centre,
enter into negotiations with the prospective investor to arrive at the

(a) cost details of the investment;
(b) exact scope and details of the exemptions to be granted; and
(c) commensurate equity stake that the State may take in the

investment in return for the revenue forgone in granting the
exemptions.

(7) The Minister shall, on a successful conclusion of the negotiations
in subsection (6), take immediate steps to procure the necessary approvals
from Cabinet and Parliament for the investment incentives agreement to
be signed between the Ministry and the prospective investor.

Development Partner Projects
Executed treaties, agreements or Conventions

17. (1) An exemption from the payment of customs duties and
customs taxes may be granted under an executed treaty, agreement or
convention after ratification by Parliament.

(2) Each exemption under subsection (1) shall be considered on a
case by case basis.

(3) The Minister shall secure approval from Cabinet and
Parliament for the exemption referred to in subsection (1) before the
exemption takes effect.

(4) Where an item to which an executed treaty, agreement or
Convention applies is produced in or can be found in Ghana, a contractor
under the executed treaty, agreement or Convention shall procure the item
from the local market and the Minister shall not grant an exemption in
respect of the executed treaty, agreement or Convention.

(5) Despite subsection (4), where the item produced or found in
Ghana is not suitable for the execution of a contract, an application shall
be made to the Minister for approval.

Technical cooperation programmes
18. (1) Goods imported for the use of an International Agency for

purposes of a technical cooperation programme or project, shall be granted
the exemption required by the agreement governing the particular
programme or project.

12

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(2) Household goods imported for the use of personnel engaged
by an International Agency under a Technical Assistance Scheme may be
exempt from payment of customs duties and customs taxes on first
arrival in Ghana of that personnel.

(3) The Minister shall secure approval from Cabinet and Parliament
for the agreement referred to in subsection (1) before the exemption takes
effect.

(4) Where Ghana subscribes to or is a member of an international
multilateral institution and the financial commitment of the subscription
or membership has been approved by the Minister and Parliament in
accordance with the Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 961),
the approval of an exemption required by the membership or subscription
shall be in accordance with clause (3) of article 174 of the Constitution.

(5) Where Ghana subscribes to or is a member of an international
multilateral institution that comes with no financial commitment, the
exemption required by the membership or subscription shall be reviewed
by the Minister subject to the approval of Parliament in accordance with
clause (2) of article 174 of the Constitution.

Programmes and projects funded by grants
19.(1)  A programme or a project fully funded by a grant may be granted

an exemption from the payment of customs duties and customs taxes in
the agreement governing the particular programme or project.

. (2) Each exemption under subsection (1) shall be considered on a
case by case basis.

(3) The Minister shall secure approval from Cabinet' and
Parliament for the exemption referred to in subsection (1) before the
exemption takes effect.

(4) Where an item to be used for the programme or project is
produced in or can be found in Ghana, the contractor shall procure the
item from the local market and the Minister shall not grant an exemption
in respect of the programme or project.

(5) Despite subsection (4), where the item produced in Ghana is
not suitable for the execution of a contract, an application shall be made
to the Minister for approval.

13

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

Concessional facility projects
20. (1) The Minister shall not grant an exemption for a project funded

by a concessional facility unless the concessional facility agreement
requires the exemption.

(2) Each exemption under subsection (1) shall be considered on a
case by case basis.

(3) The Minister shall secure approval from Cabinet and Parliament
for the exemption referred to in subsection (1) before the exemption takes
effect.

(4) Where an item to be used for the project funded by the
concessional facility is produced in or can be found in Ghana, a
contractor under the project funded by the concessional facility shall
procure the item from the local market and the Minister shall not grant
an exemption in respect of the project funded by the concessional facility.

(5) Despite subsection (4), where the item produced in Ghana is
not suitable for the execution of a contract, an application for exemption
shall be made to the Minister for approval.

Commercial Government projects
21. (1) Goods, works or services imported or procured by Government

or a State entity from a private supplier or contractor are subject to the
payment of all customs duties and customs taxes and domestic taxes.

(2) A private supplier or contractor who supplies goods, works or
services to a State entity shall not be relieved of the obligation of that
private supplier or contractor to charge value added tax or any other tax
on a taxable supply.

(3) A person who acts on behalf of Government or a State entity
who signs a contract that

(a) exempts a private supplier or contractor from the payment
of customs duties and customs taxes or the payment of
domestic taxes, or

(b) relieves a private supplier or contractor from the obligation
of that private supplier or contractor to charge value added
tax on a taxable supply

14

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine
equivalent to the value of the unpaid customs duties and customs taxes,
uncharged value added tax and other unpaid domestic taxes or to a term
of imprisonment of not less than six months or to both.

(4) Without limiting the sanction applied in accordance with
subsection (3), a supplier or contractor that is unlawfully exempted from
the payment of customs duties and customs taxes, or domestic taxes or
that is unlawfully relieved of the obligation to charge value added tax on
a taxable supply, shall pay to the State in full the unpaid customs duties,
value added tax and other domestic taxes.

(5) A private supplier or contractor that pays to Government or a
State entity unpaid customs duties and customs taxes, unpaid value added
tax and unpaid domestic taxes shall not have a right to recover the amount
paid or any part of the amount paid from Government, the State entity
or the individual that procured the supply.

Security Transactions, User Charges and Fees and Transnational Levies
Security transactions

22. (1) A security agency shall, for the purpose  consideredofthisAct.be
a “State entity” and the provisions on exemptions in the procurement of
goods, works or services apply.

(2) Despite subsection (1), the Minister may exempt from customs
duties and customs taxes and other fees and charges

(a) arms, ammunitions, uniforms, accoutrements and equipment
including vehicles and musical instruments certified by the
Minister responsible for Defence or the Minister responsible
for the Interior and approved by the Minister to be imported
by the security agencies for the use of the security agencies
or in cooperation with other States for

(i) defending the territorial integrity of the State; or
(ii) participating in international peace keeping;

(b) parts, components or sub-assemblies of an item specified in
paragraph (a) to be imported for incorporation in or fitting
into that item;

(c) parts, components or sub-assemblies of an item, specified
in paragraph (a) for the repair, refurbishment or maintenance
of that item;

15

ofthisAct.be

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(d) goods imported for training or testing of an item specified
in paragraph (a)}

(e) articles, arms, ammunition, uniforms, accoutrements and
equipment including vehicles donated for the use of the
security agencies by

(i) a foreign Government, or
(ii) an international organisation or under a Technical

Cooperation Agreement; and
(f) goods, excluding vehicles, that are imported by an officer of

the security agencies returning to the country to resume
residence after participating in international peacekeeping
or an exchange programme.

(3) For purposes of this section, “goods” mean goods
(a) acquired by an officer of the security agencies for personal

use or household use,
(b) owned, possessed and used by an officer of the security

agencies abroad for at least six months before the return of
that officer to the country, and

(c) accompanying an officer of the security agencies at the time
of return of that officer to the country

but does not include goods imported by that officer for sale or otherwise
disposed of within twelve months from the date of importation.

Administrative fees and other charges
23. (1) An administrative fee or other charge charged by a service

provider for the provision of a service shall be paid for by a person that
uses the service.

(2) A person shall not use a service for which an administrative
fee or other charge is chargeable and be exempted from the payment of
the associated administrative fee and other charge.

Transnational levies
24. A person shall not be exempted from a levy imposed as an obligation

to a regional organisation in the nature of the African Union Levy or the
Economic Community of West African States Levy unless the exemption
is sanctioned by the relevant regional organisation -

16

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

Miscellaneous Provisions
Monitoring and reporting of exemptions

25. (1) A person that enjoys an exemption shall submit to the
Commissioner-General a statement of exemptions utilised in a year of
assessment

(a) at the end of each quarter; and
(b) when the person files a tax return for the year.

(2) The statement of exemptions utilised referred to in subsection
(1) shall indicate

(a) the total value of exemptions utilised;
(b) the tax types of the exemptions utilised;
(c) the legal basis for the exemptions utilised; and
(d) the aggregate amount of the total exemptions value utilised

to date and the remainder to be used up in future.
(3) The Commissioner-General shall submit to the Minister an

annual report on
(a) the categories of exemptions granted; and
(b) the total amount of exemptions utilised by taxpayers.

(4) The Minister shall, as part of the presentation of the annual
budget statement to Parliament, submit an annual report to Parliament
on

(a) all exemptions granted;
(b) the revenue forgone;
(c) explanations on how the exemptions granted are consistent

with the economic management priorities of the Government;
and

(d) any other matter that affects the exemptions regime.
Review of exemption

26. (1) An exemption created on or after the coming into force of
this Act expires at the end of the fifth year after the year in which the
exemption was created, unless the exemption is renewed before the
expiration date of the exemption.

(2) The Minister shall establish a schedule to review an exemption
so that each exemption is reviewed at least once every five years.

17

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(3) The schedule to review an exemption referred to in subsection
(2) may group exemptions into

(a) the persons that will benefit from the exemption;
(b) the objective of the exemption; or
(c) the policy rationale for the exemption.

(4) The review of each exemption includes
(a) the date the exemption was created and the statutory or

legal citation;
(b) the purpose, intent and goal of the exemption and whether

the exemption is an effective means of accomplishing the
purpose, intent and goal of the exemption;

(c) the fiscal impact of the exemption, including past fiscal
impacts and expected future fiscal impacts;

(d) the economic impact of the exemption including revenue
loss compared to economic gain and jobs created, retained
or lost as a result of the exemption;

(e) the return on the investment made by the exemption and
the extent to which the exemption is a cost effective use of
resources; and

(f) similar tax expenditures, if any, offered by other States and
the impact of the exemption on national and regional
economic competitiveness.

(5) The schedule to review an exemption referred to in subsection
(2) may provide for a public hearing on the exemption being reviewed.

Transfer of ownership of exempt item by holder of an exemption
27. Where a holder of an exemption seeks to transfer ownership of

an item exempted under this Act, the holder of the exempt item shall
seek approval from the Ghana Revenue Authority in accordance with
section 75 of the Customs Act, 2015 (Act 891).

Local Content
28. (1) Where an item to be used for a contract is produced in or can

be found in Ghana, the contractor shall procure the item from the local
market and the Minister shall not grant an exemption in respect of the
item.

18

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(2) Despite subsection (1), where the item produced in Ghana is
not suitable for the execution of a contract, an application shall be made
to the Minister for approval.

(3) This section applies to skills and technical know-how with the
necessary modifications.
Offences and penalties

29. (1) A person acting on behalf of the Government who
(a) makes an unauthorised commitment for the grant of an

exemption,
(b) provides false information to influence a decision for the

grant of an exemption,
(yin relation to the management or administration of an

exemption, willfully makes or signs a false documentation,
false return or false entry into records,

(d) fails to report knowledge or information in respect of an
exemption-related fraud committed by a person against the
State to the appropriate authority or law enforcement
authority, or

(e) by wilful act or omission, fails to take action on an exemption-
related fraud reported to that person

commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not
less than one hundred penalty units and not more than two thousand five
hundred penalty units or to a term of imprisonment of not less than six
months and not more than five years or to both.

(2) A payer of tax, levy, fee or charge who provides false information
to influence a decision relating to an exemption, commits an offence and
is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not less than one hundred
penalty units and not more than three hundred per cent of the value of
the exemption granted or to a term of imprisonment of not less than six
months and not more than five years or to both.

(3) Except as otherwise provided in this Act, a person who fails
to comply with a provision of this Act commits an offence and where a
specific penalty is not provided, is liable on summary conviction to a fine
of not less than one hundred penalty units and not more than three
hundred per cent of the value of the exemption granted or to a term of
imprisonment of not less than six months and not more than three years
or to both.

19

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

Regulations
30. The Minister may, by legislative instrument, make Regulations

(a) to provide for a list of items to which a tax concession on/
customs duties and customs taxes apply and the exact
concessional rate for each item;

(b) to specify the particulars of carried interest where the State
seeks to take up a reciprocal carried interest in a business
that accesses general tax incentives; and

(c) generally for the effective and efficient implementation of
this Act.

Interpretation
31. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,

“charitable purposes” means the non-commercial transfer of
items donated for the use of an identifiable group in need;

“Commissioner-General” means the person appointed under
section 13 of the Ghana Revenue Authority Act, 2009
(Act 791);

“concessional facility” means a loan that has a grant element of
thirty-five per cent and above;

“customs duties and customs taxes” includes import duty,
excise duty, import value added tax, import National Health
Insurance Levy, import Ghana Education Trust Fund,
Special Import Levy; COVID-19 Health Recovery Levy and
other charges collectible on imported or exported goods;

“development partners" includes International Monetary Fund,
World Bank, other bilateral partners or institutions, other
multilateral institutions, and aid coordinating groups;

“fee or charge” includes rates or any monies charged or levied
under any enactment;

“goods” means objects of every kind and description such as
raw materials, products, equipment and objects in solid,
liquid or gaseous form and electricity as well as services
incidental to the supply of the goods if the value of those
incidental services does not exceed the value of the goods,
and may be in the nature of movable tangible property,
thermal and electrical energy, heating, gas refrigeration, air
conditioning and water, excluding money;

20

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

“grant” means transfers made in cash, goods or services for
which no repayment is required;

“Harmonised Commodity Description and Coding System”
means the Harmonised System referred to in the Customs
Act, 2015 (Act 891);

“identifiable group” includes a community, a religious body, a
health facility, a training centre, an educational institution,
a registered association or a relevant government entity;

“import” means to bring or cause goods to be brought into the
country;

“levy” includes any imposition payable under an enactment;
“manufacture” means to make, produce or cause to be made or

produced, goods;
“Minister” means the Minister responsible for Finance;
“Ministry” means the Ministry responsible for Finance;
“persons with disability” means individuals with a physical,

mental, or sensory impairment, including a visual, hearing,
or speech functional disability which gives rise to physical,
cultural or social barriers that substantially limits one or more
of the major life activities of those individuals;

“private supplier or contractor” means an entity, person or
institution that is not publicly-owned or employed under
the Public Services in Ghana;

“privileged persons” means the President, diplomats, diplomatic
missions, persons with disability or any other person or
entity recognised under this Act;

“security agency” includes
(a) the Ghana Armed Forces;
(b) the Internal Intelligence Agency;
(c) the External Intelligence Agency;
(d) the Police Service;
(e) the Prisons Service;
(J) the Ghana National Fire Service;
(g) the Immigration Service; and

21

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(h) the Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue
Authority;

“services” means the furnishing of labour, time or effort not
involving the delivery of a specific end product other than
reports, which are merely incidental to the required
performance and may be in the nature of consulting and
professional and technical services excluding employment
agreements or collective bargaining agreements;

“State entity” includes a Ministry, Department or Agency, a local
government authority, a state enterprise or public corporation;

“vehicle” means a conveyance for the transport by land of goods
or persons;

“works” include work associated with the construction,
reconstruction, demolition, repair or renovation of a building,
structure or surface and may be in the nature of site
preparation, excavation, erection including erection of a
mast for telecommunication business, assembly, installation
of a plant, fixing of equipment and laying out of materials,
decoration and finishing, and any incidental activity under
a procurement contract; and

“worthwhile causes” means
(a) a charitable organisation which meets the

requirements of section 97 of the Income Tax Act,
2015 (Act 896); and

(b) any other worthwhile cause approved by the
Minister.

Consequential amendment
32. The Ghana Investment Promotion Centre Act, 2013 (Act 865) is

amended by the substitution for section 26 of section 16 of this Act.

Repeals, savings and transitional provisions
33. (1) A provision in any legislation other than

(a) the Value Added Tax Act, 2013 (Act 870),
(b) the Income Tax Act, 2015 (Act 896,
(c) the Excise Duty Act, 2014 (Act 878), and
(d) a treaty, agreement or Convention

that provides for the grant of an exemption is repealed.

22

EXEMPTIONS BILL, 2022

(2) Despite subsection (1),
(a) an exemption-related agreement signed between the

Government and a person on the basis of a provision
repealed by this Act, or

(b) an exemption-related resolution of Parliament passed on
the basis of a provision repealed by this Act

shall continue to be valid for the term of the agreement or resolution.
(3) The items in the Third Schedule of the Customs Act, 2015

(Act 891), that are set out in the Schedule are repealed.
(4) Despite subsection (1), existing provisions in the Customs Act,

2015 (Act 891) and the Schedules to Act 891, not specifically repealed by
this Act, shall continue to apply until the Customs Act, 2015 (Act 891) is
revised.

MEMORANDUM

The purpose of the Bill is to establish the Ghana Industrial Property
Office for the protection and use of patents, trademarks, industrial designs,
geographical indications and plant varieties.

Ghana is a signatory to a number of Intellectual Property
Conventions and Treaties as well as a member of the World Intellectual
Property Organisation (WIPO) and the African Regional Intellectual
Property Organisation (ARIPO). To meet the challenges of the 21“
Century, Ghana must be able to generate and apply knowledge and develop
new products and processes in relation to intellectual property. In today’s
knowledge-based economy, innovation will be a key driving force in
creating wealth and economic growth for Ghanaians. In this regard, the
Intellectual Property System plays a role in facilitating the effective
exploitation of innovative knowledge thus enhancing Ghana’s climate
of innovation to the benefit of the Ghanaian economy and society.

In recent years, intellectual property has taken a much more
significant role in the economy where the effective use of knowledge is a
decisive determinant of business success. Innovators are making
intellectual property protection decisions in the context of an increasingly
global market place. Indeed, intellectual property rights are increasingly
becoming, the “currency” that businesses use to secure competitive
advantage in the global marketplace.

Considering that intellectual property includes industrial property
and copyright and related rights, Ghana has already established a
Copyright Office which caters for the needs of authors, musicians and
producers, among others. However, a dedicated office to promote the
use of industrial property rights geared towards industrial development,
economic growth and competitiveness of industries has been touted for
years but is yet to be established. The establishment of an Intellectual
Property Office will inure to the benefit of the business community when
focus and attention is given to issues that affect the rights of innovators
in industry. This will address the needs and concerns articulated by users
and right holders of industrial property law, such as inventors, brand
owners, industrial and textile designers, among others.

GHANA INDUSTRIAL PROPERTY OFFICE BILL, 2023

Given the enhanced value of intellectual property rights to innovators
operating in a knowledge-based global economy, intellectual property
offices around the world have experienced significant increases in demand
for intellectual property protection in recent years. Most intellectual
property offices around the globe are modernising in order to be able to
deliver service to all their clients. As a result of this, intellectual property
offices are transforming from the old mindset of a legalistic regime to a
business-oriented one based on quality service delivery. The intellectual
property offices are currently designing services around the needs of
clients. There is therefore a constant challenge to modernise intellectual
property offices as the needs of their clients are evolving rapidly.

Intellectual property protection is overlooked by many Ghanaians
as a critical instrument that provides the foundation for investment and
growth opportunities. Businesses often fail to recognise or value intellectual
property as a strategic asset. It is therefore imperative that Ghana
modernises and strengthens the intellectual property system. The process
of modernisation and strengthening will affect systems including
intellectual property legislation, its associated workflow and office
practices.

As part of the process for the modernisation and strengthening of
Ghana’s Intellectual Property System, the Government of Ghana,
through the Ministry of Trade and Industry with technical support from
the Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property (IPI) and funding from
the Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), launched the
Ghana Intellectual Property Policy and Strategy. This was done under
the Trade Sector Support Programme which requires that the Ghana
Industrial Property Office be established to enhance the effective use of
industrial property for innovation and national development.

The establishment of the Ghana Industrial Property Office seeks to
ensure that the national environment for the use and protection of patents,
trademarks, industrial designs, geographical indications and plant
varieties incorporates the provisions for giving effect to Ghana’s
obligations under the Hague Agreement for the International Deposit of
Industrial Designs. This serves the needs of industry by adopting
provisions under the Agreement on the Trade Related Aspects of 

ii

GHANA INDUSTRIAL PROPERTY OFFICE BILL, 2023

Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) and other treaty obligations that
Ghana is a signatory to that are progressive and modem and that
strengthen the design protection system for industry and businesses.

The Ghana Industrial Property Office seeks to design a modem,
balanced system of intellectual property rights that improves the business
environment, encourages innovation, know-how and technology transfer,
facilitates productivity improvements, investment, competitiveness and
exports and contributes to social and economic development. This will
ensure that an efficient automated industrial property management
system and an electronic copyright register is put in place.

Clauses 1 to 11 of the Bill deal with the Ghana Industrial Property
Office. Clause 1 of the Bill establishes the Ghana Industrial Property Office
as a body corporate. The object of the Office in clause 2 is to protect and
promote intellectual property rights in the country.

Clause 3 provides for the functions of the Office which include the
implementation of the relevant industrial property laws, provision to
the public of industrial property information for technological and
economic development, representing the Government on matters related
to industrial property and promoting the development of intellectual
property rights in the country. Others include making recommendations
to the Government on matters related to industrial property, promoting
and facilitating the training of intellectual property human capital in the
country and promoting the commercialisation of intellectual property
rights.

Clause 4 provides for the governing body of the Office which is a
Board consisting of eleven members. It is the responsibility of the Board
to ensure the efficient and effective performance of the functions of the
Office. The duties and. liabilities of members of the Board are provided
for in clause 5. A member of the Board has the same fiduciary relationship
with the Office and the same duty to act with loyalty and in good faith as
a Director of a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2019
(Act 992). •

GHANA INDUSTRIAL PROPERTY OFFICE BILL, 2023

Clauses 6 to 10 provide for standard provisions on the tenure of office
of members of the Board, meetings of the Board, disclosure of interest
of members of the Board, establishment of committees of the Board
and allowances payable to members of the Board and members of a
committee of the Board. Clause 11 provides for ministerial directives.

Administrative and Financial Provisions are dealt with in clauses 12
to 20. Clause 12 provides for the appointment of a Director-General for
the Office in accordance with article 195 of the Constitution. The
Director-General is responsible for the day-to-day administration and
operations of the Office and is answerable to the Board in the performance
of the functions as specified under clause 13.

The appointment of other staff for the efficient and effective
performance of the functions of the Office is provided for in clause 14.
The appointment is to be done by the President in accordance with article
195 of the Constitution.

Clause 15 makes provision for the funds of the Office. The funds
include moneys approved by Parliament, fees and charges that accrue to
the Office in the performance of its functions, donations and grants, and
interests on investments made by the Office. The Board may open bank
accounts with the approval of the Controller and Accountant-General
where the Board considers necessary, clause 16.

The Office is permitted to obtain loans and credit facilities that the
Office requires for the implementation of its functions, clause 17. The Bill
further provides in clause 18 for the management of the finances of the
Office. Subject to the Ministries, Departments and Agencies (Retention
of Funds) Act, 2007 (Act 735) and the Earmarked Funds Capping and
Realignment Act, 2017 (Act 947), the Office is authorised to retain twenty
per cent of all moneys realised in the performance of the functions of the
Office.

The standard provisions on accounts and audit and annual report
and other reports are provided for in clauses 19 and 20.

The final group of clauses, which are catered for under clauses 21 to
26, deal with miscellaneous provisions.

iv

GHANA INDUSTRIAL PROPERTY OFFICE BILL, 2023

Clause 21 provides for the protection of an authorised officer from
personal liability for any act done diligently in the performance of a
function or the execution of a duty under the Bill. The requirement of
an authorised officer who receives information in the performance of a
function under the Bill to keep the information confidential is provided
for in clause 22. Clause 23 makes provision for the common seal of the
Office to be kept by the Director-General.

Clause 24 enumerates the matters for which Regulations are required.
Clause 25 deals with interpretation of terms and expressions used in the
Bill and clause 26 provides for transitional provisions.

GODFRED YEBOAH DAME

Attorney-General and Minister for Justice

Date: 4th January, 2023.

v

GHANA INDUSTRIAL PROPERTY OFFICE BILL, 2023

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

BILL
ENTITLED

GHANA INDUSTRIAL PROPERTY OFFICE ACT, 2023

AN ACT to establish the Ghana Industrial Property Office for the
protection and use of patents, trademarks, industrial designs,
geographical indications and plant varieties and to provide for related
matters.

PASSED by Parliament and assented to by the President:

Ghana Industrial Property Office

Establishment of the Ghana Industrial Property Office
1. (1) There is established by this Act, the Ghana Industrial Property

Office as a body corporate.
(2) The Office may, for the performance of the functions, acquire

and hold property, dispose of property and enter into a contract or any
other related transaction.

(3) Where there is a hindrance to the acquisition of land, the land
may be acquired for the Office under the Land Act, 2020 (Act 1036) and
the cost shall be borne by the Office.

2

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

Object of the Office
2. The object of the Office is to protect and promote intellectual property

rights in the country.
Functions of the Office

3. To achieve the object under section 2, the Office shall
(a) ensure the implementation of relevant industrial property

laws;
(b) provide to the public information on industrial property

for technological and economic development;
(c) represent the Government on matters related to industrial

property;
(d) promote the development of intellectual property rights in

the country;
(e) make recommendations to the Government on matters

related to industrial property;
(f) promote and facilitate the training of intellectual property

human capital in the country;
(g) provide advice, training and assistance in relation to

intellectual property to ministries, departments and agencies
who administer intellectual property;

(h) promote the commercialisation of intellectual property
rights;

(i) manage technical cooperation and exchange in the area of
industrial property with foreign organisations;

(j) register and regulate industrial property rights;
(k) administer industrial property laws; and
(I) perform any other function that is incidental to the object

of die Office.
Governing body of the Office

4. (1) The governing body of the Office is a Board consisting of
(a) a chairperson with not less than fifteen years’ experience in

industrial property law and practice;
(b) the Chief Directors of the following Ministries:

(i) the Ministry responsible for Justice; and
(ii) the Ministry responsible for Trade and Industry;

3

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

(c) one representative of the following Ministries not below
the rank of a Director with not less than ten years’ expertise
in industrial property law and practice, nominated by the
respective Minister:

(i) the Ministry responsible for Environment, Science,
Technology and Innovation;

(ii) the Ministry responsible for Food and Agriculture;
(iii) the Ministry responsible for Health; and
(iv) the Ministry responsible for Education;

(d) one representative of the Council for Scientific and Industrial
Research not below the rank of a Deputy Director nominated
by the Director-General;

(e) the Director-General of the Office; and
(f) two representatives from the private sector one of whom is

a woman nominated by the President.
(2) The President shall appoint the chairperson and other members

of the Board in accordance with article 70 of the Constitution.
(3) The Board shall ensure the efficient and effective performance

of the functions of the Office.
Duties and liabilities of members of the Board

5. (1) A member of the Board has the same fiduciary relationship with
the Office and the same duty to act with loyalty and in good faith as a
Director of a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2019
(Act 992).

(2) Without limiting subsection (1), a member of the Board shall
not

(a) engage in a conduct or an activity that may undermine the
integrity of the Office; or

(b) make improper use of any information obtained as a result
of the performance of the duties of the Office or by virtue
of the position of the member as a member of the Board.

(3) A member of the Board who contravenes this section ceases to
be a member of the Board.

Tenure of office of members of the Board
6. (1) A member of the Board shall hold office for a period of four

years and is eligible for re-appointment, for another term only.
(2) Subregulation (1) does not apply to the Director-General.

4

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

(3) A member of the Board may, at any time, resign from office, in
writing, addressed to the President through the Minister.

(4) A member of the Board, other than the Director-General, who
is absent from three consecutive meetings of the Board without sufficient
cause ceases to be a member of the Board.

(5) The President may, by letter addressed to a member, revoke the
appointment of that member.

(6) Where a member of the Board is, for a sufficient reason, unable
to act as a member, the Minister shall determine whether the inability
would result in the declaration of a vacancy for the unexpired term.

(7) Where there is a vacancy
(a) under subsection (3), (4) or (5) or subsection (3) of section 5

or subsection (2) of section 8;
(b) as a result of a declaration under subsection (6); or
(c) by reason of the death of a member,

the Minister shall notify the President of the vacancy and the President
shall, in accordance with this Act, appoint a person to fill the vacancy for
the unexpired term.

Meetings of the Board
7. (1) The Board shall meet at least once every three months for the

conduct of business at a time and place determined by the chairperson.
(2) The chairperson shall, at the request in writing of not less than

one-third of the membership of the Board, convene an extraordinary
meeting of the Board at a time and place determined by the chairperson.

(3) The quorum at a meeting of the Board is seven members of the
Board.

(4) The chairperson shall preside at meetings of the Board and in
the absence of the chairperson, a member of the Board elected by the
members present from among their number, shall preside.

(5) Matters before the Board shall be decided by a majority of the
members present and voting, and in the event of an equality of votes, the
person presiding shall have a casting vote.

(6) The Board may co-opt a person to attend a meeting of the Board
but that person shall not vote.

5

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

(7) The proceedings of the Board are not invalidated by reason of
a vacancy among the members or a d efe ct in the app o intment or qualification
of a member.

(8) Subject to this section, the Board may determine the procedure
for the meetings of the Board.

Disclosure of interest
8. (1) A member of the Board who has an interest in a matter for

consideration by the Board
(a) shall disclose, in writing, the nature of the interest and the

disclosure shall form part of the record of the consideration
of the matter; and

(b) is disqualified from being present at or participating in the
deliberation on or determination of the Board in respect
of that matter.

(2) A member ceases to be a member of the Board if that member
has an interest in a matter before the Board and

(a) fails to disclose that interest; or
(b) is present at, or participates in, the deliberation on the

matter.
(3) Without limiting any further cause of action that may be instituted

against a member, the Board shall recover any benefit derived by the
member who contravenes subsection (1) in addition to the revocation of
the appointment of that member.

Establishment of committees
9. (1) The Board may establish committees consisting of members

of the Board or non-members or both, to perform a function of the
Board.

(2) A committee composed of members and non-members of the
Board shall be chaired by a member of the Board.

(3) Section 8 applies to a member of a committee of the Board.

Allowances
10. Members of the Board and members of a committee of the Board

shall be paid the allowances approved by the Minister in consultation
with the Minister responsible for Finance.

6

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

Ministerial directives
11. The Minister may issue directives, in writing, on matters of policy

to the Board and the Board shall comply.

Administrative and Financial Provisions
Appointment of Director-General

12. (1) The President shall, in accordance with article 195 of the
Constitution, appoint a Director-General for the Office..

(2) The Director-General shall hold office on die terms and conditions
specified in the letter of appointment.

(3) The Director-General shall be a professional with not less than
fifteen years’ experience in the field of intellectual property with
considerable knowledge and experience in intellectual property law.

Functions of Director-General
13. (1) The Director-General is

(a) responsible for the day-to-day administration and operations
of the Office; and

(b) answerable to the Board for the performance of the functions
of the Office.

(2) The Director-General shall perform other functions determined
by the Board.

Appointment of other staff
14. (1) The President shall, in accordance with article 195 of the

Constitution, appoint for the Office other staff that are necessary for the
efficient and effective performance of the functions of the Office.

(2) The President may, in accordance with clause (2) of article 195
of the Constitution, delegate the power of appointment in subsection (1)
in writing to the Board.

(3) Other public officers may be transferred or seconded to the
Office or may otherwise be requested to give assistance to the Office.

(4) The Office may engage the services of experts and consultants
as the Office considers necessary on the recommendation of the Board.

7

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

Funds of the Office
15. The funds of the Office include

(a) moneys approved by Parliament;
(b) fees and charges that accrue to the Office in the performance

of the functions of the Office;
(c) donations and grants; and
(d) interests from investments.

Bank accounts
16. The Board may, with the approval of the Controller and Accountant-

General, open bank accounts that the Board considers necessary.

Loans and investments
17. (1) Subject to article 181 of the Constitution and the Public

Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921), the Office may obtain loans
and credit facilities that the Office requires for the implementation of its
functions.

(2) The Office may with the approval of the Minister responsible
for Finance borrow, by way of overdraft or otherwise, sums that the
Office may require to meet its current obligations or perform its functions
under this Act.

(3) The Office may make prudent investments in an instrument
other than a Government instrument that it considers necessary.

Management of the finances of the Office
18. (1) The Board shall manage and control the finances of the Office

and determine matters that arise out of the financial administration of
the Office in accordance with the Public Financial Management Act,
2016 (Act 921).

(2) Subject to the Ministries, Departments and Agencies (Retention
of Funds) Act, 2007 (Act 735) and the Earmarked Funds Capping and
Realignment Act, 2017 (Act 947), the Office is authorised to retain twenty
per cent of all moneys realised in the performance of the functions of the
Office.

(3) The preparation and submission of estimates and the reporting
and accounting of estimates are subject to the Public Financial Management
Act, 2016 (Act 921).

8

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

(4) The provisions of Article 187 of the Constitution which relate
to the Auditor-General shall apply to the moneys retained under the Act.

(5) Despite any other provision in any enactment to the contrary,
internally generated funds

(a) can only be utilised if the activities on which the expenditure
will be incurred have been programmed and approved in
the expenditure budget of the Office, and

(b) shall not be used for the payment of salaries, staff benefits
and other allowances except where the allowances are directly
related to the provision of services that will lead to increased
revenue.

Accounts and audit
19. (1) The Board shall ensure that the Office keeps books, records,

returns and other documents relevant to the accounts in the form
approved by the Auditor-General.

(2) The Board shall submit the accounts of the Office to the
Auditor-General for audit at the end of the financial year.

(3) The Auditor-General shall, within six months after the end of
the immediately preceding financial year, audit the accounts and
forward a copy each of the audit report to the Minister and the Board.

(4) The financial year of the Office is the same as the financial
year of the Government.
Annual reports and other reports

20. (1) The Board shall, within thirty days after receipt of the audit
report, submit an annual report to the Minister covering the activities
and operations of tide Office for the year to which the annual report relates.

(2) The annual report shall include the report of the Auditor-General.
(3) The Minister shall, within thirty days after the receipt of the

annual report, submit the report to Parliament with a statement that the
Minister considers necessary.

(4) The Board shall submit to the Minister any other report which
the Minister may require in writing.

Miscellaneous Provisions
Protection from liability

21. An authorised officer is not personally liable for any act done
diligently in the performance of a function or the execution of a duty
under this Act.

9

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

Confidentiality
22. (1) An authorised officer who receives information in the

performance of a function under this Act shall not communicate the
information to an unauthorised person.

(2) An authorised officer who contravenes subsection (1) commits
an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not less than
five hundred penalty units and not more than one thousand penalty units
or to a term of imprisonment of not less than two years and not more
than four years or to both.
Common seal of the Office

23. (1) The Director-General shall keep the common seal of the Office
and apply the seal to documents determined by the Office.

(2) The application of the common seal of the Office shall be
authenticated by the signature of the Director-General.
Regulations

24. (1) The Minister may, on the advice of the Board, by legislative
instrument, make Regulations generally for the effective implementation
of this Act.

(2) Without limiting the generality of subsection (1), the Regulations
may provide for

(a) the national framework governing industrial property rights
and promoting the development of industrial property;

(b) the procedures for the grant of industrial property rights;
(c) the conditions of service for the Office; and
(d) matters for the purpose of carrying out the principles and

• provisions of this Act.
Interpretation

25. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,
“authorised officer” means a member of staff of the Ghana

Industrial Property Office;
“Board” means the governing body of the Office established

under section 4;
“geographical indication” means an indication which identifies

goods as originating in the territory of a country, or a region
or locality in that territory, where a given quality, reputation
or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable
to its geographical origin;

10

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

“industrial design” means the ornamental aspects of an article
in industry or handicraft;

“industrial property” means a patent for inventions, trademarks,
industrial designs, geographical indications and plant varieties;

“intellectual property” means creations of the mind and may
be in the nature of inventions, literary and artistic works,
symbols, names and images used in commerce;

“Minister” means the Minister responsible for Justice;
“Office” means the Ghana Industrial Property Office established

under section 1;
“patent” means the title granted to protect an invention;
“plant varieties” means plant groupings within a single botanical

taxon of the lowest known rank which groupings irrespective
of whether the conditions for the grant of a plant breeder
right are fully met, can be

(a) defined by the expression of the characteristics
resulting from a given genotype or combination of
genotypes;

(b) distinguished from any other plant groupings by the
expression of at least one of the characteristics that
result from a given genotype or combination of
genotypes; and

(c) considered as units with regard to their suitability
for being propagated unchanged; and

“trademark” means a sign or combination of signs capable of
distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from
the goods and services of another undertaking.

Transitional provisions
26. (1) The rights, assets and liabilities accrued in respect of the properties

vested in the Registrar General’s Department established under the Civil
Service (Structure) Regulations, 1961 (L.I. 139) in relation to industrial
property in existence immediately before the commencement of this Act
are transferred to the Ghana Industrial Property Office established under
this Act and accordingly proceedings relating to matters on industrial
property taken by or against the Industrial Property Section of the Registrar-
General’s Department may be continued by or against the Ghana Industrial
Property Office.

11

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

(2) Persons employed in the Industrial Property Section of the
Registrar-General’s Department are transferred to the Ghana Industrial
Property Office established under this Act.

(3) A transfer to the Ghana Industrial Property Office shall for
the purposes of pension and other retirement benefits constitute a
continuous service in the Legal Service.

(4) The terms and conditions of service of a person transferred to
the Ghana Industrial Property Office under subsection (2) shall not be
less favourable than those applicable to that person immediately before
the commencement of this Act.

12

Ghana Industrial Property Office Bill, 2023

title: Ghana Boundary Commission Bill, 2023
text:
PARUAWeSt UNDARY COMMISSION BILL, 2023
Li B R ■

—**“ MEMORANDUM

The object of the Bill is to establish the Ghana Boundary Commission
to determine and demarcate the land boundaries of Ghana and delimit
the maritime boundaries of Ghana in accordance with accepted principles
of international law and to protect and secure the interest of the Republic.

The Ghana Boundary Commission Act, 2010 (Act 795) was passed
by Parliament and assented to by the President on 22nd April, 2010.
Act 795 in its current form does not adequately reflect best practice in
international and internal boundary architecture. Act 795 does not include
some contemporary functions of the Commission as compared to
international best practice. The current functions of the Commission are
woefully inadequate and do not cover key areas for an integrated response
to boundary disputes. There are also major omissions in the constitution
of the governing body of the Commission. Key Ministers such as the
Ministers responsible for the Interior and National Security are absent.

Furthermore, the Act does not also provide for the creation of the
office of the Commissioner General of the Ghana Boundary Commission
in line with similar institutions in the country. In addition, the Act fails
to provide for the establishment of Departments of the Commission and
regional offices for the efficient and effective implementation of the
functions of the Commission. Also, detailed financial provisions are not
provided for in Act 795 which is hampering the implementation of the
functions of the Commission.

The lines of reportage between the Commission, Ministries,
Departments and Agencies necessitate a holistic review to ensure clear
channels of reportage. The required changes to Act 795 necessitate a repeal
of the Act and the enactment of a new comprehensive piece of legislation
to adequately respond to emerging national and international boundary
challenges and cater for the strategic direction in handling boundary
disputes.

In this regard, the Bill seeks to provide for the expansion of the
governing Board and the functions of the Commission based on
international best practice and considering Ghana’s national security

GHANA BOUNDARY COMMISSION BILL, 2023

architecture. The Bill expands the existing role of the Commission to
include the appropriate measures to deal with any boundary dispute that
affects the territorial sovereignty of Ghana or that may arise within the
country with a view to settling the disputes, promote trans-border
cooperation and border community development, and formulate policies
and implement programmes on international boundaries, specifically land
and maritime boundaries.

The Bill also provides clear guidelines on the channels of reportage.
In this regard, two technical committees namely, the Land Boundary
Technical Committee and the Maritime Boundary Technical Committee
are to be established. These committees have the Commissioner-General
as the chairperson with membership drawn from the relevant State agencies
and other stakeholders.

Administratively, the Bill seeks to provide for the establishment of
the office of the Commissioner-General. The Bill also provides for the
creation of five Departments, each to be headed by a Director and the
establishment of satellite regional offices of the Commission where
required. In addition, the Bill provides for the appointment of other staff
of the Commission and the establishment of an Internal Audit Unit in
accordance with the Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921).
Provision has also been made for funding of the activities and programmes
of the Commission.

Ultimately, the Bill seeks to repeal the Ghana Boundary Commission
Act, 2010 (Act 795) to establish the required national structures to address
emerging boundary challenges and to take cognisance of other significant
matters not catered for in Act 795.

Clause 1 establishes the Ghana Boundary Commission as a body
corporate. The objects of the Commission as specified in clause 2 include
undertaking negotiations to determine and demarcate the land boundaries
of Ghana and delimiting the maritime boundaries of Ghana in
accordance with accepted principles of international law in collaboration

ii

GHANA BOUNDARY COMMISSION BILL, 2023

with the Lands Commission, protecting and securing the interest of the
Republic in determining and demarcating land boundaries and delimiting
maritime boundaries of Ghana and adopting international best practice
in the demarcation of land boundaries and delimiting of maritime
boundaries of Ghana, among others.

Clause 3 provides for the functions of the Commission. These include
negotiating with a neighbouring country concerning a land boundary,
maritime boundary or air boundary between Ghana and that country; in
collaboration with relevant security agencies, ensure the security of the
boundaries of Ghana to safeguard the territorial sovereignty of Ghana
at all times; in collaboration with the Lands Commission, undertaking
the physical demarcation and survey of land boundaries and the
delimitation of maritime boundaries and whenever determined by the
Board, placing of buoys or other maritime markers along some or all of
the courses of the maritime boundaries of Ghana. Other functions of
the Commission include advising Government on the most appropriate
strategy for the negotiation of a land boundary or maritime boundary;
advising Government on international Conventions in relation to the
borders of Ghana and the signing and ratification of treaties related to
land and maritime boundaries; addressing issues related to the use of
natural resources that straddle land boundaries and maritime boundaries;
and formulating policies and implementing programmes on international
boundaries specifically land and maritime boundaries.

In clause 4, the Commission is empowered for purposes of physical
demarcation of a land boundary, to appoint official or licensed surveyors
or any other officer with their agents, servants and workmen to enter
land to demarcate or survey the land. This is to be undertaken in
accordance with the Lands Commission Act, 2008 (Act 767) and the Land
Act, 2020 (Act 1036). An officer or surveyor demarcating or surveying
boundaries may cause a notice to be served on any person owning,
occupying or otherwise interested in the abutting land or the land to be
surveyed, and on any person employed on or connected with the
management or cultivation of the land, requiring the person to attend or

iii

GHANA BOUNDARY COMMISSION BILL, 2023

be represented by an agent for deliberations on the demarcation at the
time and place stated in the notice. It is a criminal offence for a person to
willfully or unlawfully destroy, remove or alter a boundary post, to fail to
comply with an order in a notice served on that person, or willfully
obstruct, hinder or resist an authorised officer of the Commission in the
course of official duty of demarcating a boundary.

Clause 5 empowers an authorised officer to use firearms, in the
discharge of duties under the Bill or any other enactment.

The governance of the Commission is provided for in clauses 6 to 17.
The governing body of the Commission is a Board consisting of the
Minister responsible for Lands and Natural Resources as the chairperson
and the Ministers responsible for National Security, Interior, Defence,
Foreign Affairs and Energy. The other members are the Attorney-General
and Minister for Justice, representatives of Ministries responsible for
Finance, Local Government and Transport, the National House of Chiefs,
the Ghana Institution of Geoscientists, academia with expertise in
international security matters nominated by the Minister and the
Commissioner-General. The President is to, in accordance with article
70 of the Constitution, appoint the chairperson and other members of
the Board. The Board is to ensure the effective and efficient performance
of the functions of the Commission.

Standard provisions on duties and liabilities of a member of the
Board, tenure of office of members of the Board, meetings of the Board
and disclosure of interest are provided for in clauses 7, 8, 9 and 10
respectively.

The establishment of committees is provided for in clause 11. The
Board may establish committees consisting of members of the Board or
non-members or both to perform a function of the Board. In addition,
the Bill establishes the Land Boundary Technical Committee and the
Maritime Boundary Technical Committee. The provisions of clause 10
on disclosure of interest apply to members of a committee of the Board.

iv

GHANA BOUNDARY COMMISSION BILL, 2023

The membership of the Land Boundary Technical Committee
provided for under clause 12 include the Commissioner-General as the
chairperson and the Director of Surveys of the Lands Commission.
Representatives of the Ministries responsible for Lands and Natural
Resources, Justice, Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration, and National
Security are also members of the Committee. The Customs Division of
the Ghana Revenue Authority, the Immigration Service and the Ghana
Armed Forces are also represented. Two other persons nominated by the
Commission are also members of the Committee. The Land Boundary
Technical Committee is to meet at a time and place determined by the
chairperson.

Clause 13 provides for the functions of the Land Boundary Technical
Committee. The Land Boundary Technical Committee is to deal with
land boundary disputes with the view to settling the disputes, define land
boundaries with neighbouring countries and internal boundaries within
Ghana in accordance with the demarcation instrument or document,
proffer solutions to land boundary disputes and promote the development
and effective management of land boundaries. The Committee is also to
make recommendations to the Board on land boundary matters.

Clause 14 provides for the Maritime Boundary Technical Committee.
The membership of the Maritime Boundary Technical Committee
includes the Commissioner-General as the chairperson, representatives
of the Ghana Armed Forces, the Office of the Attorney-General and
Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration,
Petroleum Commission, the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation,
the Ghana Maritime Authority and the Ministry responsible for National
Security. The Director of the Survey and Mapping Division is also a
member of the Maritime Boundary Technical Committee. The
Commission is also to nominate two other persons as members of the
Commission. The time and place for the meetings of the Maritime
Boundary Technical Committee are to be determined by the chairperson
of the Committee.

GHANA BOUNDARY COMMISSION BILL, 2023

The functions of the Maritime Boundary Technical Committee are
provided for in clause 15. The Maritime Boundary Technical Committee
is responsible for dealing with matters affecting the maritime borders of
Ghana, participating in the delimitation of international maritime
boundaries in accordance with the delimitation instrument or documents
for that purpose, and proffering solutions to international maritime
boundary disputes. The Maritime Boundary Technical Committee is also
to promote trans-border cooperation and border area development and
make recommendations to the Board on international maritime boundary
matters.

Allowances for members of the Board and members of a committee
of the Board are provided for in clause 16. They are to be paid allowances
approved by the Minister in consultation with the Minister responsible
for Finance. The chairperson may give directives to the Board on matters
of policy and the Board is to comply, clause 17.

Clauses 18 to 25 provide for administrative matters. Departments of
the Commission are provided for in clause 18. The Commission is to
have a Boundaries Operations Department, Research Department, Survey
and Delimitation Department, Policy, Plans and Programmes
Department and an Administration Department. Nevertheless, the Board
may on the recommendation of the Commissioner-General realign the
Departments for the effective and efficient performance of the functions
of the Commission. A Department of the Commission is to be headed
by a Director.

Clause 19 enjoins the President to, in accordance with article 195 of
the Constitution, appoint a Commissioner-General for the Commission.
The Commissioner-General is to hold office on the terms and conditions
specified in the letter of appointment. The Commissioner-General is
responsible for the day-to-day administration of the affairs of the
Commission and is answerable to the Board in the performance of the
functions under the Bill, clause 20. The Commissioner-General may
however delegate a function to an officer of the Commission but is not
relieved of the ultimate responsibility for the performance of the delegated
function.

GHANA BOUNDARY COMMISSION BILL, 2023

Clause 21 enjoins the President to, in accordance with article 195 of
the Constitution, appoint a Deputy Commissioner-General. The Deputy
Commissioner-General is to hold office on the terms and conditions as
specified in the letter of appointment. The Deputy Commissioner-General
is to assist the Commissioner-General in the performance of the functions
of the Commissioner-General and to perform any other function as
assigned by the Commissioner-General.

The appointment of a Solicitor-Secretary is provided for in clause
22. The President is to in accordance with article 195 of the Constitution
appoint a Solicitor-Secretary for the Commission. The Solicitor-Secretary
is the secretary to the Board and the committees of the Board and is in
charge of the Legal Section of the Commission. The Solicitor-Secretary
is also responsible to the Commissioner-General in the performance of
functions.

Appointment of other staff by the President that are necessary for
the effective and efficient performance of the functions of the Commission
is provided for in clause 23. The appointments are to be done in accordance
with article 195 of the Constitution. In addition, the Commission may,
for the effective and efficient performance of the functions of the
Commission, engage the services of consultants and experts on the
recommendation of the Commissioner-General.

The Commission is to have an Internal Audit Unit in accordance
with section 83 of the Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921),
clause 24.

The Board may, on the recommendation of the Commissioner-
General, establish satellite regional offices of the Commission, clause 25.
A satellite regional office of the Commission is to perform functions of
the Commission in the region as the Board may direct.

Financial provisions are spelt out in clauses 26 to 30. The funds of the
Commission include moneys approved by Parliament, donations, grants,
gifts and internally generated funds, clause 26. Clause 27 provides for the

moneys for the Commission to be paid into a bank account opened with

Standard provisions on accounts and audit, and annual report and

Disclosure of information is dealt with in clause 32. An employee of

A person who contravenes this clause commits an offence and is liable on

Collaboration with other bodies is provided for in clause 33. The
