BILL
ENTITLED

GHANA BOUNDARY COMMISSION ACT, 2023

AN ACT to establish the Ghana Boundary Commission to determine
and demarcate the land boundaries of Ghana and delimit the
maritime boundaries of Ghana in accordance with accepted
principles of international law, to protect and secure the interest of
the Republic in determining and demarcating land boundaries and
delimiting maritime boundaries of Ghana and to provide for
related matters.

PASSED by Parliament and assented to by the President:

The Ghana Boundary Commission
Establishment of the Ghana Boundary Commission

1. (1) There is established by this Act, the Ghana Boundary Commission
as a body corporate.

(2) For the performance of the functions of the Commission, the
Commission may acquire and hold property, dispose of property and
enter into a contract or any other related transaction.

3

Ghana Boundary Commission Bill, 2023

(3) Where there is a hindrance to the acquisition of land, the land
may be acquired for the Commission under the Land Act, 2020 (Act 1036)
and the cost shall be borne by the Commission.
Objects of the Commission

2. The objects of the Commission are to
(a) in collaboration with the Lands Commission, undertake

negotiations to determine and demarcate land boundaries
of Ghana and delimit the maritime boundaries of Ghana
in accordance with accepted principles of international law;

(b) protect and secure the interest of the Republic in determining
and demarcating land boundaries and delimiting maritime
boundaries of Ghana;

(c) adopt international best practice in the demarcation of land
boundaries and delimiting of maritime boundaries of
Ghana;

(d) promote an effective and efficient management of the
boundary demarcation and delimitation processes; and

(e) ensure consideration of the interest of Ghanaians affected
by the placement of boundaries.

Functions of the Commission
3. To achieve the objects under section 2, the Commission shall

(a) negotiate with a neighbouring country concerning a land
boundary, maritime boundary or air boundary between
Ghana and that country;

(b) in collaboration with relevant security agencies, ensure the
security of the boundaries of Ghana to safeguard the
territorial sovereignty of Ghana at all times;

(c) in collaboration with the Lands Commission, undertake
the physical demarcation and survey of land boundaries
and the delimitation of maritime boundaries;

(d) whenever determined by the Board, place buoys or other
maritime markers along some or all of the courses of the
maritime boundaries of Ghana;

(e) advise Government on the most appropriate strategy for
the negotiation of a land boundary or maritime boundary;

(f) through negotiation, determine cross-boundary matters
among communities;

4

Ghana Boundary Commission Bill, 2023

(g) encourage negotiated settlement of border disputes in
preference to litigation;

(h) intervene, determine or deal with a boundary dispute among
regions, districts or communities within Ghana with the
view to settling the dispute;

(i) promote trans-border cooperation and local community
development;

(j) advise Government on international Conventions in
relation to the borders of Ghana, and the signing and
ratification of treaties related to land and maritime boundaries;

(k) address issues related to the use of natural resources that
straddle land boundaries and maritime boundaries;

(I) formulate policies and implement programmes on intemational
boundaries including land boundaries and maritime
boundaries;

(m) coordinate with the relevant international body on
maritime demarcation across the international sea bed; and

(n) perform any other function ancillary to the objects of the
Commission.

Powers of the Commission and an Authorised Officer
Powers of the Commission

4. (1) In accordance with the Lands Commission Act, 2008 (Act 767)
and the Land Act, 2020 (Act 1036), the Commission may, for the
purpose of physical demarcation of a land boundary, appoint an official
surveyor, a licensed surveyor or any other officer with the agents,
servants and workmen of the official surveyor, licensed surveyor or other
officer to enter land to demarcate or survey the land.

(2) An officer or surveyor demarcating or surveying boundaries
may cause a notice to be served

(a) on any person owning, occupying or otherwise interested
in the abutting land or the land to be surveyed, and

(b) on any person employed on or connected with the
management or cultivation of the land,

requiring the person to attend or be represented by an agent for
deliberations on the demarcation or survey at the time and place stated
in the notice.

5

Ghana Boundary Commission Bill, 2023

(3) An officer or surveyor may
(a) issue a notice calling on any person who is able to give

information on the boundaries of land in whose possession
or power any document related to the boundaries is alleged
to be, to meet the officer or surveyor and give information
or produce the document on the date and at a place
specified in the notice;

(b) place a boundary post in the manner prescribed in the
Technical Guidelines for Surveying and Mapping in Ghana
in the line of demarcation; and

(c) for the delimitation of a maritime boundary or demarcation
of a freshwater boundary,

(i) conduct hydrographic surveys in accordance with
international standards; and

(ii) create and manage a database of the hydrographic
surveys carried out on the maritime boundaries of
Ghana.

(4) A person who
(a) willfully or unlawfully destroys, removes or alters a boundary

post,
(b) fails to comply with an order in a notice served on that

person, or
(c) willfully obstructs, hinders or resists an authorised officer

of the Commission in the course of official duty to demarcate a
boundary,

commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not
less than two hundred penalty units and not more than five hundred penalty
units or to a term of imprisonment of not less than six months and not
more than three years or to both.

Power to use firearms
5. An authorised officer may, in the discharge of duties under this Act

or any other enactment, use firearms.

of

(a) the Minister responsible for Lands and Natural Resources
as the chairperson;

(b) the Ministers responsible for the following:
(i) National Security;
(ii) Interior;
(iii) Defence;
(iv) Foreign Affairs; and
(v) Energy;

(c) the Attorney-General and Minister responsible for Justice;
(d) one representative of the following:

(i) the Ministry responsible for Finance not below the
rank of a Director nominated by the Minister
responsible for Finance;

(ii) the Ministry responsible for Local Government not
below the rank of a Director nominated by the
Minister responsible for Local Government;

(iii) the Ministry responsible for Transport not below the
rank of a Director nominated by the Minister
responsible for Transport;

(iv) the National House of Chiefs nominated by the
National House of Chiefs;

(v) the Ghana Institution of Geoscientists nominated
by the Ghana Institution of Geoscientists; and

(vi) academia with expertise in international security
matters nominated by the Minister; and

(e) the Commissioner-General.
(2) The President shall, in accordance with article 70 of the

Constitution, appoint the chairperson and other members of the Board.
(3) The Board shall ensure the efficient and effective performance

°f the functions of the Commission.

Duties and liabilities of a member of the Board
7. (1) A member of the Board has the same fiduciary relationship with

the Commission and the same duty to act with loyalty and in good faith
as a director of a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2019
(Act 992).

(2) Without limiting subsection (1), a member of the Board has a
duty to

(a) act honestly and in the best interest of the Commission in
the performance of the functions of that member;

(b) exercise the degree of care and diligence in the performance
of the functions of that member that a person in that
position would reasonably be expected to exercise in the
circumstance;

(c) avoid making use of information acquired by virtue of the
position of that member so as to benefit that member or to
the detriment of the Commission.

(3) A member of the Board who contravenes subsection (1) or (2)
commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not
less than one hundred penalty units and not more than two hundred and
fifty penalty units.
Tenure of office of members of the Board

8. (1) A member of the Board shall hold office for a term of four years
and is eligible for re-appointment for another term only.

(2) Subsection (1) does not apply to the Ministers of State specified
under paragraph (b) of subsection (1) of section 6, the Attorney-General
and Minister responsible for Justice and the Commissioner-General.

(3) A member of the Board may at any time resign from office in
writing addressed to the President through the chairperson of the Board.

(4) A member of the Board who is absent from three consecutive
meetings of the Board without sufficient cause ceases to be a member of
the Board.

(5) The President may, by a letter addressed to a member, revoke the
appointment of that member.

(6) Where a member of the Board is, for a sufficient reason, unable
to act as a member, the Minister shall determine whether the inability
would result in the declaration of a vacancy.

9. (1) The members of the Board shall meet at least once every three

months for the conduct of business at a time and in a place determined

title: Energy Commission Amendment Bill, 2023
text:
ENERGY COMMISSION (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2023

MEMORANDUM
The object of the Bill is to amend the Energy Commission Act, 1997

(Act 541) to revise upwards the correlative penalties for offences
committed under the Act, to provide for the imposition of administrative
penalties and to empower the Minister responsible for Energy, on the
advice of the Commission, to make Regulations on the unlawful
connection to an equipment, an installation or a facility for the supply,
transmission, distribution or sale of electricity or natural gas, and for the
importation, assembly, manufacture, sale, installation and operation of
equipment and accessories for the transmission, wholesale supply,
distribution or sale of electricity or natural gas, and other related matters.

The Energy Commission Act, 1997 (Act 541) was enacted to establish
the Energy Commission with a mandate to regulate and manage the
development and utilisation of energy resources and grant licences for
the transmission, wholesale supply, distribution and sale of electricity
and natural gas among other related functions.

In 2016 the Act was amended to provide for the promotion of local
content and local participation in the Electricity Supply Industry in
Ghana.

The Commission has for the past twenty-five years played its role as
an effective technical regulator of the electricity and natural gas sectors.
During that period, the Commission has observed several infractions of
the provisions of the Act. The penalties stipulated for the various offences
under section 54 of Act 541 are not deterrent enough to guarantee
compliance with the respective provisions of the Act. In particular, the
failure to obtain a licence to carry out specific activities; the unlawful
destruction or damage of equipment, an installation of a facility for the
supply, transmission, distribution or sale of electricity or natural gas; or
the failure to comply with a standard of performance prescribed by the
Commission attracts a penalty which does not necessarily correlate to
the gravity of the offence. Furthermore, the absence of an upper threshold
does not provide a yardstick to determine the range of penalties that may
be imposed for the different categories of offences.

ENERGY COMMISSION (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2023

The increasing trend of malpractices dealing with unlawful
connections on the part of some consumers and non-consumers in the
electricity supply industry, has sometimes led to overload of the power
distribution systems and consequently resulted in bad voltage quality from
the suppliers. Other issues emanating from connection malpractices have
been the recurrent fire outbreaks oi Jamage to electrical appliances of
other consumers and invariably the loss of revenue to Government and
the utilities that provide power.

The unlawful means of connecting to an electric current source
without the knowledge of licensed distribution utilities have adverse effects
such as contributing to high commercial losses to the licensed utilities
and consequently impacting on the bills of other consumers. Additionally,
this results in unfair competition among businesses, since those who do
not indulge in unlawful connections end up with a higher overhead
expenditure or cost as compared to those who indulge in unlawful
connections.

Act 541 does not address these problems and the Bill seeks to plug
the loopholes by creating an offence and correlative penalty.

The inablity of the Commission to impose adminstrative penalties
is also a basis for the amendment of Act 541. The imposition of
administrative penalties under Act 541 will provide a mechanism for the
Commission to ensure regulatory compliance.

In sync with the creation of the new offence of unlawful connections,
the Bill further provides for the enactment of Regulations in respect of
unlawful connections of electricity and natural gas. The Bill further
empowers the Minister, on the advice of the Commission, to make
Regulations to prohibit the manufacture, importation, assembly, sale and
installation of equipment and accessories except by persons licensed or
registered by the Commission.

Clause 1 of the Bill amends section 41 of the Energy Commission
Act, 1997 (Act 541) to include as part of the sources of funds in the Energy 

ii

ENERGY COMMISSION (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2023

Fund, funds realised by the Commission from the imposition of
administrative penalties.

Clause 2 of the Bill amends in part, subsection (1) of section 54 of
the Energy Commission Act, 1997 (Act 541) to include a new offence of
unlawful connection to an equipment, an installation or a facility for the
supply, transmission, distribution or sale of electricity or natural gas.
The clause further amends subsection (1) of section 54 to revise upwards
the penalty units and the term of imprisonment for an offence committed
under the section.

Clause 3 amends the Act by the introduction of a new section 54A,
on administrative penalties.

Clause 4 amends section 56 of Act 541 to empower the Minister to
make Regulations in respect of unlawful connection to an equipment, an
installation or a facility for the supply, transmission, distribution or sale
of electricity or natural gas and for the importation, assembly,
manufacture, sale, installation and operation of equipment and accessories
for the transmission, wholesale supply, distribution or sale of electricity
or natural gas.

Clause 4 further amends section 56 by the repeal of subsection (2)
which is spent in the light of the repeal of the Statutory Instruments Act
1959 (No. 52) by section 52 of the Interpretation Act, 2009 (Act 792).

Clause 5 amends section 57 on interpretation to define “unlawful
connection”.

Hon. Dr. Matthew Opoku Prempeh
Minister responsible for Energy

(3) Where an offence under this Act or the Regulations,

title: National Service Authority Bill, 2024
text:
NATIONAL SERVICE AUTHORITY BILL, 2024

MEMORANDUM

The object of the Bill is to establish the National Service Authority to mobilise and post persons
qualified to undertake national service in areas of national priority for national development,
inculcate the values of civic responsibility, discipline, patriotism, national cohesion and
voluntarism in persons qualified to undertake national service and promote employability,
entrepreneurship, technology and innovation among persons qualified to undertake national
service.

In Ghana, the origin of the National Service Scheme is traced to the Builders Brigade
established under the Builders Brigade Act, 1957 (Act 37). The Brigade provided the youth
with an opportunity to render patriotic service in the execution of development projects,
especially in the rural areas. The Brigade was initially opened to Ghanaian males up to forty-
five years but was later expanded to accommodate females and renamed the Workers’
Brigade. The participants, primarily illiterates, were engaged in the agricultural sector, flood
control, construction, craftsmanship and road rehabilitation. Subsequently, in 1969, the
National Service Corp was introduced under the National Service Corp Act, 1970 (Act 329)
to replace the Workers’ Brigade.

Act 329 was succeeded by the National Redemption Council Decree, 1973 (N.R.C.D. 208),
which established the Ghana National Service Scheme. In an attempt to strengthen the
Scheme to deliver effectively and attend to national call, N.R.C.D. 208 was repealed by the
passage of the Ghana National Service Scheme Act, 1980 (Act 426).

The Ghana National Service Scheme Act, 1980 (Act 426) established the National Service
Scheme with the core mandate of mobilising and deploying Ghanaian citizens of eighteen.
years and above for national priority development programmes through a mandatory national
service programme.

The Scheme has been in existence for almost five decades and it has become imperative
that a new legislation is passed to address the challenges facing the Scheme and align Act

426 with the changes that have occurred with time.

Over the years, Cabinet decisions, Presidential fiats and Ministerial directives have led to the
implementation of changes in the operation of the Scheme without an amendment to Act 426
to reflect the changes. The criteria for persons who qualify to undertake national service, 

i

which is provided for under Act 426 as a citizen of eighteen years and above, has been

revised to a citizen who completes tertiary education. Under Act 426, the duration for national

service is two years. In practice, the duration for national service is one year. The six months

military training required under Act 426 has also been scrapped. In effect, the current practice

of national service is at variance with what is provided for Act 426.

Another major challenge of the Scheme is the lack of a corporate status. The Scheme also

lacks clarity in the objective and scope due to the fact that Act 426 does not provide the

objects of the Scheme. This gap has exposed the implementation of the Scheme to ambiguity.

The Scheme has also encountered administrative challenges that constrain the operations of
the Scheme and require reform. These challenges include the lack of adequate funds to
manage the various activities of the Scheme, inadequate administrative and logistical

infrastructure to meet the ever-increasing number of national service personnel posted across

the sixteen regions of the country and weak collaboration between the Scheme and partners

of the Scheme including tertiary institutions and public and private sector institutions.

The need for a change in status and a shift in policy and implementation of the Scheme in

order to secure sustainable ways of living up to the mandate of the Scheme has also been

underscored by various studies. The National Service Scheme has not lived up to its target

as a pathway for graduate employment. The Scheme merely acts as a receptacle for
Ghanaian graduates to be posted for the mandatory period of national service. When the

period of national service ends, the host institutions are unable to retain the national service

personnel, leaving the national service personnel to join the unemployed graduate population.

Currently, there is no mechanism to track the number of graduates who secure jobs, whether

formal or informal, after their national service. A report released by the Institute of Statistical

Social and Economic Research (ISSER), in 2017, indicated that only ten per cent of graduates

in Ghana are employed within one year after completing their mandatory national service and

it may take up to ten years for the remaining ninety per cent to secure permanent employment.

For the 2023 national service year, the Scheme posted about one hundred and seventy-five

thousand (175,000) national service personnel into the Ghanaian economy. If the report of

the Institute of Statistical Social and Economic Research is given due recognition, then only

about seventeen thousand five hundred (17,500) graduates who have completed national
service would be employed by the end of 2023. The issue of graduate unemployment is a 

z

cause for concern because developmental economists have established a strong correlation

between youth unemployment and the emergence of civil strife.

The Service also lacks a strategic link with other state agencies that deal with pro-youth

policies and programmes, and provide entrepreneurial support initiatives, including the

National Youth Authority, the National Entrepreneurship and Innovation Programme and the

Ghana Enterprises Agency.

The Bill seeks to establish an Authority as a body corporate with the requisite legal capacity

to develop and implement policies and programmes for national service. The Bill also provides

for_collaboration -between relevant-institutions-to create a safety "net- for graduates* who

successfully complete their mandatory national service.

The Bill repeals the Ghana National Service Scheme Act, 1980 (Act 426) and introduces
several innovations to the law on national service. Under the Bill, qualification for national
service includes citizenship and the completion of a course of study at a tertiary education
institution, whether in the country or abroad. A national service person is also required to be
not more than forty years at the time of completion of the relevant course of study.

Further, a tertiary education institution is to forward to the Board, not later than three months
before the end of each academic year, a list of final year students and the respective courses
of study of the students.

Under the Ghana National Service Scheme Act, 1980 (Act 426), national service personnel
are required to render a mandatory service of two years, including a minimum military training
period of six months. The Bill recognises the inherent challenges associated with a
compulsory military training requirement of six months and has therefore introduced a training
period of six weeks in areas including military drills-; emergency response health-aid and
safety measures for national service personnel. Furthermore, the Bill introduces a one-year
national service period to accord with the current practice.

The Authority is also tasked with the duty to monitor and supervise institutions which take on
national service personnel to ensure that the right conditions of work are provided for the
personnel, including persons with disability. This is necessary to ensure compliance with the
labour laws of the country and to protect the youth from exploitation.

The fast-growing number of graduates being churned out by the increasing number of tertiary
institutions across the nation and the attendant impact on the administration of the Scheme
under Act 426 have necessitated the passage of the Bill to provide for regional and district 

3

offices which will be responsible for carrying out the functions of the Authority at the regional
and district levels as directed by the Board and operational directorates and departments that
are necessary for the effective performance of the functions of the Authority.

The Bill considers the need to equip the youth, particularly national service personnel, with
skills relevant to the job market, both as employees and entrepreneurs.

Clauses 1 to 3 provide for the establishment of the National Service Authority.

Clause 1 establishes the Authority as a body corporate.

The objects of the Authority, as specified in clause 2, are to mobilise and post persons
qualified to undertake national service in areas of national priority for national development,
inculcate the values of civic responsibility, discipline, patriotism, national cohesion and
voluntarism in persons qualified to undertake national service and promote employability,
entrepreneurship, technology and innovation among persons qualified to undertake national
service.

The functions of the Authority are provided for in clause 3. The Authority is required to develop
and implement policies and programmes for national service, organise sensitisation and
awareness programmes on national service, post a person qualified to undertake national
service to a user agency or to a programme in a field determined by the Board and provide
persons qualified to undertake national service with an early opportunity to participate in
nation building and development.

Other functions of the Authority include facilitating the process for persons qualified to
undertake national service to enter the job market through work in the public or private sector
after completion of national service, in collaboration with relevant institutions, organising
training in areas including military drills, emergency response, health-aid and safety measures
to inculcate the values of civic responsibility, discipline, patriotism, national cohesion and
voluntarism in persons qualified to undertake national service and ensuring that a user agency
provides a conducive condition of work at the user agency for a person posted to undertake
national service, including a person with disability.

Furthermore, the Authority has the mandate to provide an opportunity for entrepreneurship
and innovation among persons qualified to undertake national service, develop a code of
ethics to regulate the conduct of national service personnel and user agencies during the
period of national service and monitor compliance with the code of ethics and collaborate with
relevant institutions to develop a platform to host a database of national service personnel
and persons who have completed national service, for purposes of facilitating job
opportunities. The Authority is also required to provide an opportunity for persons qualified to 

4

undertake national service to gain the practical experience required for employment and for
career planning and develop programmes to mobilise resources to sustain the operations of
the Authority.

The governance of the Authority is provided for in clauses 4 to 13. Clause 4 provides for the
governing body of the Authority, which is a Board consisting of the chairperson nominated by
the President, the Director-General of the Authority, one representative each from the
Ministries responsible for Education, Employment and Labour Relations, Finance, Food and
Agriculture, Interior, Defence, Health and Local Government and Rural Development, not
below the rank of a Director, nominated by their respective Ministers.

Other members of the Board are the President of the National Service Personnel Association, 
one representative from the Association of Ghana Industries, nominated by the President of
the Association of Ghana Industries and one other person nominated by the President, who
is a woman.

Clause 5 enumerates the functions of the Board. The Board is responsible for ensuring the
effective and efficient performance of the functions of the Authority.

The Board is also mandated to approve policies, programmes and proposals of the Authority
and approve programmes for the advancement of the quality of life of persons qualified to
undertake national service.

The duties and liabilities of members of the Board are spelt out in clause 6. Under the clause,
a member of the Board is under the same fiduciary relationship with the Authority as a director
of a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2019 (Act 992).

Standard provisions on tenure of office of members of the Board, meetings of the Board,
disclosure of interest and establishment of committees, allowances and policy directives are
provided in clauses 7,8,9,10,11 and 12 respectively.

Clauses 13 to 21 provide for the administration of the Authority.

Clause 13 empowers the Board, on the recommendation of the Director-General, to establish
directorates and departments of the Authority that are necessary for the effective and efficient
performance of the functions of the Authority.

The appointment and functions of the Director-General of the Authority are specifically dealt
with in clauses 14 and 15. Under clause 14, the President is to appoint a Director-General for
the Authority in accordance with article 195 of the Constitution. The Director-General is 

s

responsible for the day-to-day administration of the affairs of the Authority and is answerable
to the Board in the performance of functions under the Bill, clause 15.

Clause 16 provides for the appointment of two Deputy Directors-General by the President in
accordance with article 195 of the Constitution.

The Deputy Directors-General are appointed to be responsible for finance and administration,
and programmes and operations, clause 17. In addition, a Deputy Director-General is to
perform any other functions assigned by the Director-General.

Clause 18 provides for the Head of the Legal Department of the Authority as the Secretary to
the Board. The Secretary is required to arrange the business of the Board, record and keep
minutes of the meetings of the Board and perform any other function that the Board may direct
in writing.

Other staff of the Authority required for the effective and efficient performance of the functions
of the Authority are to be appointed by the President in accordance with article 195 of the
Constitution, clause 19.

Clause 20 provides for the Authority to establish regional and district offices of the Authority
for the performance of the functions of the Authority as directed by the Board.
Under clause 21, a regional or district office is to have a Director who is mandated to exercise
oversight responsibility for a regional or district office and perform other functions determined
by the Board.

Clause 22 provides for an Internal Audit Unit in accordance with section 83 of the Public
Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921).

Financial provisions are covered under clauses 23 to 27 of the Bill.

Clause 23 provides for the funds of the Authority. The funds of the Authority are moneys
approved by Parliament, administrative penalties, donations, gifts and grants, internally
generated funds, including fees payable to the Authority for a service rendered by the
Authority and moneys derived from projects or initiatives undertaken by the Authority with the
approval of the Board.

Clauses 24 and 25 provide for the bank account and expenses of the Authority respectively.

Standard provisions on accounts and audit and annual report and other reports are provided
for in clauses 26 and 27 respectively.

6

Clauses 28 to 35 provide for matters in respect of national service.

A person is qualified to undertake national service if that person is a citizen, has completed a
course of study at a tertiary education institution and is below forty years of age at the time of
the course study, clause 28.

Clause 29 makes it mandatory for a tertiary education institution to forward to the Board, not
later than three months before the end of each academic year, a list of final year students and
the respective courses of study of the students.

Clause 30 empowers a user agency to apply to the Authority for the posting of national service
personnel to the user agency.

Under clause 31, a person who qualifies to undertake national service and has completed a
course of study in a tertiary education institution in a foreign country is required to apply to
the Authority to undertake national service. The clause further requires a person who is
unable to complete national service immediately after completion of a course of study in a
tertiary education institution to apply to the Authority to undertake national service the
following year or to defer national service for a period of not more than five years after the
person qualifies to undertake national service.

Clause 32 empowers the Board to direct a person qualified to undertake national service to
be engaged for the purpose of national service in a field determined by the Board.

The duration for national service is specified in clause 33. Under the clause, the duration for
national service is one year, consisting of field service and, as determined each year by the
Minister, having regard to the availability of funds and the priority of Government, training for
a minimum of six weeks in areas including military drills, emergency response, health-aid and
safety measures. However, the clause empowers a person to apply for an extension of
national service for a further period of one year for purposes of coaching and mentorship.

The Authority may exempt a person qualified to undertake national service from undertaking
national service, clause 34. The Authority may exempt a person who is qualified to undertake
national service where that person was in full-time employment before embarking on a course
of study at a tertiary education institution and on any other ground determined by the Authority
in accordance with Government policy in respect of exemptions from national service.

Clauses 35 and 36 provide for terms and conditions of engagement of a person qualified to
undertake national service and a Certificate of National Service respectively.

7

Clause 37 empowers a person who fails to complete national service to apply to the Authority
to re-take national service. Under the clause, a person fails to undertake national service
where that person is absent from post for a period of three consecutive months.

Under clause 38, an employer is prohibited from employing a person who is qualified to
undertake national service but has not undertaken or completed the period of national service,
unless the person is exempted under clause 34. To this end, an employer is required to
ascertain from a prospective employee whether or not the employee has completed national
service. The clause further prohibits the Registrar of Companies from registering a company,
partnership or business name of a person who is qualified to undertake national service but
has not undertaken or completed the period of national service, unless the person is
exempted under clause 34.

Miscellaneous provisions are covered by clauses 39 to 43. Clause 39 mandates a private
user agency, a non-subvented agency and a state-owned enterprise that applies for national
service personnel to pay to the Authority, an amount that is not less than twenty per cent of
the prevailing allowance for national service personnel in respect of each person that
undertakes national service at the private user agency, the non-subvented agency or state-
owned enterprise.

Clause 40 deals with the mode of an application to the Authority under the Bill. Under the
clause, an application to the Authority is to be made in a form determined by the Authority or
electronically on the website of the Authority.

Clause 41 provides for appeals. Under the clause, a person who is dissatisfied with a decision
of the Authority is entitled to appeal against the decision to the Board. A person who is
dissatisfied with the decision of the Board is further entitled to appeal against the decision to
the Minister.

Clause 42 empowers the Minister, in consultation with the Board, to make Regulations to
provide for matters including the areas of activity for the purpose of national service and the
conditions under which a person qualified to undertake national service may be engaged or
exempted from national service.

Under clause 43, the Authority may issue administrative guidelines to give full effect to the
provisions of the Bill.

The interpretation of words and expressions used in the Bill is dealt with in clause 43.

8

Clause 44 provides for repeals and savings whilst clause 45 deals with transitional matters.

NATIONAL SERVICE AUTHORITY ACT, 2024

AN ACT to establish the National Service Authority to mobilise and post persons qualified to
undertake national service in areas of national priority for national development; inculcate the
values of civic responsibility, discipline, patriotism, national cohesion and voluntarism in
persons qualified to undertake national service; and promote employability, entrepreneurship,
technology and innovation among persons qualified to undertake national service and provide
for related matters.

PASSED by Parliament and assented to by the President:

National Service Authority

Establishment of the Authority
1. (1) There is established by this Act, the National Service Authority as a body
corporate.

(2) The Authority may, in the performance of the functions of the Authority, acquire
and hold property, dispose of property and enter into a contract or any other related
transaction.

(3) Where there is a hindrance to the acquisition of land, the land may be acquired
for the Authority under the Land Act, 2020 (Act 1036) and the cost shall be borne by the
Authority.

Objects of the Authority
2. The objects of the Authority are to

(a) mobilise and post persons qualified to undertake national service in
areas of national priority for national development;

12

(b) inculcate the values of civic responsibility, discipline, patriotism, national
cohesion and voluntarism^ in persons qualified under section 28 to
undertake national service; and

(c) promote employability, entrepreneurship, technology and innovation
among persons qualified to undertake national service.

Functions of the Authority
3. To achieve the objects of the Authority, the Authority shall

(a)—develop and implemenrpolicies~arid^programmes fof national service;

(b) organise sensitisation and awareness programmes on national service;

(c) post a person qualified to undertake national service to a user agency
or to a programme in a field determined by the Board;

(d) provide persons qualified to undertake national service with an early
opportunity to participate in nation building and development;

(e) facilitate the process for persons qualified to undertake national service
to enter the job market through work in the public or private sector after
completion of national service;

(f) in collaboration with relevant institutions, organise training in areas
including military drills, emergency response, health-aid and safety

measures;

(g) ensure that a user agency provides a conducive condition of work at the
user agency for a person posted to undertake national service, including
a person with disability;

(h) provide an opportunity for persons qualified to undertake national
service to gain the practical experience required for employment
and for career planning;

13

(i) provide an opportunity for entrepreneurship and innovation among
persons qualified to undertake national service;

(j) develop a code of ethics to regulate the conduct of national service
personnel and user agencies during the period of national service and
monitor compliance with the code of ethics;

(k) collaborate with relevant institutions to develop a platform to host a
database of

(i) national service personnel; and

(ii) persons who have completed national service, for purposes of
facilitating job opportunities;

(I) develop programmes to mobilise resources to sustain the operations of
the Authority; and

(m) perform any other function ancillary to the objects of the Authority.

Governance of the Authority

(a) the chairperson nominated by the President;

(b) one representative each of

(i) the Ministry responsible for Education not below the rank of a
Director, nominated by the Minister responsible for Education;

(ii) the Ministry responsible for Employment and Labour Relations
not below the rank of a Director, nominated by the Minister
responsible for Employment and Labour Relations;

(iii) the Ministry responsible for Finance not below the rank of a
Director, nominated by the Minister responsible for Finance;

(iv) the Ministry responsible for Food and Agriculture not below the
rank of a Director, nominated by the Minister responsible for
Food and Agriculture;

(v) the Ministry responsible for the Youth not below the rank of a
Director, nominated by the Minister responsible for the Youth;

(vi) the Ministry responsible for Defence not below the rank of a
Director, nominated by the Minister responsible for Defence;

42. The Minister shall, within twelve months after the coming into force of this Act and in
consultation with the Board, by legislative instrument, make Regulations to provide for

(a) the areas of activity for the purpose of national service;

(b) the conditions under which a person qualified to undertake national
service may be engaged or exempted from national service;

(c) the projects and initiatives to be executed by the Authority for purposes
of mobilising resources for the Authority;

(d) the terms and conditions of service of the staff of the Authority; and

(e) any other matter necessary for the effective and efficient implementation
of this Act.

Administrative guidelines
43. The Authority may issue administrative guidelines to give full effect to the provisions
of this Act.

Interpretation
44. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,

“Authority" means the National Service Authority established under section 1;

30

“district” includes the area of authority of a District Assembly, a Municipal Assembly
and a Metropolitan Assembly;

"employer’’ includes the Government;

“field service" means the part of national service that is undertaken at the place to
which a person is assigned by the Authority;

“medical practitioner” means a person registered to practise medicine under Part Two
of the Health Professions Regulatory Bodies Act, 2013 (Act 857);

“Minister” means the Minister responsible for Education;

“national service" means-the requisite-duties that a person -who-is qualified-under­
section 28 is mandated to undertake;

“non-subvented agency” means a public institution that does not receive public funds;

“post" means to assign a prospective national service personnel to a field service;

"programme" means a series of activities undertaken by the Authority for the purpose
of improving the conditions of national service personnel, the operations of the
Authority or achieving the objects of the Authority;

"relevant institutions” mean public institutions or private institutions that collaborate
with the Authority in the operations of the Authority;

“state-owned enterprise means an entity, whether incorporated or not under the
Companies Act, 2019 (Act 992), whose shares are wholly owned by
Government;

"tertiary education institution" includes a university, a university college, a technical

university, a post-secondary diploma awarding institution, a tertiary technical
and a vocational training institution specified in the Third Schedule to the

Education Regulatory Bodies Act, 2020 (Act 1023) and a post-secondary

professional training institution;

“user agency” includes an institution which a person qualified to undertake national
service is posted to by the Authority to undertake national service; and

31

“user agency fee” means the fee imposed on a private user agency, a non-subvented
agency or a state-owned enterprise under section 38.

Repeal and savings
43. (1) The Ghana National Service Scheme Act, 1980 (Act 426) is repealed.

(2) Despite the repeal of the Ghana National Service Scheme Act, 1980 (Act 426),
any by-laws, national service postings, exemptions from national service, notices, orders,
directions, appointments or any other act lawfully made or done under the repealed
enactment and in force immediately before the coming into force of this Act shall continue to
have effect as if made or done under this Act until revoked, reviewed, cancelled or terminated.

(3) This Act shall not affect

(a) an offence committed,

(b) criminal proceedings commenced, or

(c) penalties imposed

under the repealed enactment before the coming into force of this Act.

Transitional provisions
44. (1) The Board of the Ghana National Service Scheme in existence immediately
before the coming into force of this Act shall, until the Board of the Authority established under
this Act is constituted, perform functions of the Board provided under this Act.

(2) The assets, rights, obligations and liabilities of the Ghana National Service
Scheme in existence immediately before the coming into force of this Act are transferred to
the Authority established under this Act.

(3) The district and regional offices of the Ghana National Service Scheme existing
immediately before the coming into force of this Act, shall be deemed to have been
established under this Act and shall continue to function in accordance with the provisions of
this Act.

(4) A person in the employment of the Ghana National Service Scheme
immediately before the coming into force of this Act, shall on the coming into force of this Act,
be deemed to have been duly employed by the Authority established under this Act on the
terms and conditions which are not less favourable in aggregate to the terms and conditions
attached to the post held by the person before the coming into force of this Act.

32

(5) Any moneys held in a bank account of the Ghana National Service Scheme
before the coming into force of this Act shall, within one month after the coming into force of
this Act, be paid into the bank account opened under section 24.

title: Value Added Tax Amendment Bill, 2022
text:
VALUE ADDED TAX (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2022

MEMORANDUM

The object of the Bill is to amend the Value Added Tax Act, 2013 (Act 870) to
broaden the scope for the taxation of electronic commerce, provide for the electronic
issuance of a tax invoice, an up-front payment of Value Added Tax by an unregistered
importer and the zero-rating of the supply of locally assembled vehicles.

The digital economy presents a potentially untapped source of revenue for
Ghana as the country continues to witness an increase in e-commerce activity and a
decrease in profits from traditional industries as a result of COVID-19. Ghana has seen
a drop in traditional tax revenues as digital multinationals trade remotely with no
physical presence. These digital multinationals create value and make significant profit
through the supply of online services to consumers in Ghana. There is therefore the
need to amend our tax laws to include provisions for taxing non-resident persons who
supply digital and telecommunication services.

The local assembling of vehicles under the Ghana Automotive Development
Programme commenced in 2020 with the Volkswagen Group. Currently, there are over
seven companies operating under the Programme and producing salon cars, SUVs and
pick-ups. Government, as part of measures to ensure that the vehicles are sold at
competitive prices, has decided to zero-rate the sale of these vehicles for a period of
eighteen months.

Compliance with the Value Added Tax has traditionally been a challenge due to
the largely informal nature of transactions in the economy. Quite a number of importers
who are registrable for Value Added Tax are currently not in the database of the Ghana
Revenue Authority. To assure revenue, an up-front payment of twelve and a half per
cent on the cost, insurance and freight value of a taxable good imported by a person
who has not registered for Value Added Tax will be imposed at the ports of entry. An
importer will however be permitted to recover the up-front payment when the importer
registers and files a Value Added Tax return.

Accordingly, the Bill seeks to amend the Value Added Tax Act, 2013 (Act 870) to
broaden the scope for the taxation of electronic commerce, provide for the electronic
issuance of a tax invoice, an up-front payment of Value Added Tax by an unregistered
importer and the zero-rating of the supply of locally assembled vehicles.

It is envisaged that cumulatively, the amendments to the Value Added Tax Act,

AN ACT to amend the Value Added Tax Act, 2013 (Act 870) to provide for the up-front

PASSED by Parliament and assented to by the President:

Section 15A inserted

1. The Value Added Tax Act, 2013 (Act 870) referred to in this Act as the “principal
enactment" is amended by the insertion after section 15, of

"Up-front payment by unregistered importer

15A. (1) A person who

(a) imports taxable goods; and

(b) is not registered for the tax

is, in addition to the penalty provided in section 15, liable to make an upfront

(2) A person may recover an upfront payment made under subsection

Section 16 of Act 870 amended

2. The principal enactment is amended by the substitution for section 16, of

“Unregistered, non-resident persons who provide telecommunication
services or electronic commerce

16. (1) An unregistered, non-resident person who provides

shall register if that person makes a taxable supply.

4

(2) A non-resident person who contravenes a provision of this Act and

(3) For the purposes of subsection (1),

(a) “digital service” includes

(i) social networking;

(ii) online gaming;

(iii) cloud services;

(vi) online advertisement services;

(b) “electronic commerce" includes a business transaction,

to

transmission, emission or reception; and

(iii) political, cultural, artistic, sporting, scientific or

Section 41 of Act 870 amended

3. The principal enactment is amended by the substitution for section 41, of

“Issue of tax invoice or sales receipt

41. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this Act, a taxable person shall, on
making a taxable supply of goods or services, issue to the recipient, a tax invoice
in the form and with the details that are prescribed by the Commissioner-General.

title: University of Engineering and Agriculture Sciences Bill , 2025
text:
UNIVERSITY OF ENGINEERING AND AGRICULTURAL SCIENCES BILL, 2025

MEMORANDUM

The purpose of the Bill is to establish the University of Engineering and
Agricultural Sciences. The Bill also seeks to provide for the governance
arrangements and management of the University.

Higher education offers further training and improvement in the status of human
capital in any society. In Ghana, the right to higher education is, subject to the
availability of resources, a constitutional requirement that Government has to satisfy.
It is the duty of Government, therefore, to invest in the establishment of universities
in order that higher education is, to the greater extent possible, made available to all
citizens.

University education has since independence remained largely accessible to a
very small segment of the Ghanaian society. The introduction of the free senior high
school education would soon impact on university education. There is therefore the
need to establish more places of higher education in the country in order to
accommodate the increasing number of graduates from the senior high schools.

Government every year allocates huge resources to the public universities for
the performance of their functions. Recognisably, public universities are semi-
autonomous educational institutions. However, since the public universities depend
hugely on public finance there is the need for greater accountability in the utilisation
of resources allocated to the public universities. Transparency, accountability and
efficiency depend on a well-structured governance architecture and legal framework
that will ensure consistency and commonality in the administration of public
universities whilst recognising the peculiarities in the objects of the various
institutions.

The Bill, thus, seeks to provide for the establishment of the University of
Engineering and Agricultural Sciences and also spell out the governance structure,
finance, administration and regulation of the activities of the University in a
structured, harmonious and coordinated manner.

1

Clauses 1 to 4 provide for the establishment of the University of Engineering
and Agricultural Sciences. The University is established as a body corporate under
clause t

The aims of the University in clause 2 are to provide higher education in
engineering, agriculture, agro-entrepreneurship, emerging digital discipline and the
built environment as well as create, through research, applied engineering and
agricultural technologies for the advancement of agro-entrepreneurship and the built
environment. Other aims include the establishment of connections within the
engineering and agriculture sectors to train graduates for specific professions or
advanced research in the field of operation, and train and provide engineers and
agriculturalists with relevant competence in supporting sustainable improvement in
agro-entrepreneurship and the built environment.

Clause 3 provides for the establishment of campuses of the University. The
main campus of the University is to be located in Bunso in the Eastern Region.
Additionally, the University is required to establish a campus at Kenyasi in the
Ashanti Region and Acherensua in the Ahafo Region. The University is empowered
to, in consultation with the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission, establish a
campus in any other place that the Council determines.

Clause 4 deals with the award of degrees, diplomas and certificates by the
University. The University is empowered under the clause to award its own degrees,
diplomas and certificates as well as confer honorary degrees. In the same vein, the
University is also entitled to withdraw a degree, a diploma or a certificate that the
University has awarded if the University has evidence that proves, among others,
that the degree, diploma or certificate was obtained through fraud or academic
malpractice.

Clauses 5 to 12 make provision for the governance of the University. Clause 5
provides for the Council. The Council is the governing body of the University and
consists of eighteen persons including a chairperson nominated by the President, the
Vice-Chancellor of the University and three persons nominated by the President, at
least one of whom is a woman. Institutions such as the Ministry responsible for
Agriculture, the Ghana Institution of Surveyors, the Ghana Tertiary Education
Commission, the Engineering Council, the Conference of Heads of Assisted
Secondary Schools, the Association of Ghana Industries and representatives of the
University community are represented on the Council. The chairperson and other
members of the Council are to be appointed by the President in accordance with
article 70 of the Constitution.

2

The functions of the Council are spelt out in clause 6. The functions include
ensuring the achievement of the aims of the University, determining the strategic
direction of the University, monitoring and evaluating the implementation of policies
of the University and promoting income-generating activities as part of the
programmes of the University. The Council is also required to control the finances of
the University, determine the allocation and effective and efficient use of funds, make
professorial level appointments, on the recommendation of the Appointments
Committee of the Academic Board and collaborate with accredited Universities in the
country or abroad with similar objects as may be determined by the Ghana Tertiary
Education Commission.

Clause 7 grants the Council general powers to do or provide for any matter in
relation to the University that the Council considers necessary or expedient.

The standard provisions on the tenure of office of members of the Council,
meetings of the Council and disclosure of interest are provided for in clauses 8, 9
and 10 respectively.

Clause 11 mandates the Council to establish committees and assign to the
committees, functions that the Council considers appropriate. A committee that
consists of members and non-members of the Council is to be chaired by a member
of the Council.

Clause 12 provides for allowances. The Minister, in consultation with the
Minister responsible for Finance, is to determine the allowances to be paid to
members of the Council and members of committees of the Council.

The administration of the University is dealt with in clauses 13 to 25. The
Principal Officers of the University are the Chancellor, the chairperson of the Council
and the Vice-Chancellor, clause 13. A Principal Officer of the University is to, before
assuming office, take and subscribe to the Official Oaths.

Clause 14 deals with the Chancellor of the University. The Council is required to
appoint the Chancellor for the University. The Chancellor is the titular head of the
University and takes precedence over the other officers of the University. Where the
integrity and welfare of the University are threatened by any matter, the Chancellor is
empowered to, in consultation with the Council, intervene.

Clause 15 provides for vacancy in the office of the Chancellor. The office of the
Chancellor becomes vacant on the resignation, incapacitation, death, removal from 

3

office or expiry of the term of office of the Chancellor. The clause further provides
that the grounds and procedures for the removal of the Chancellor from office must
be in accordance with the Statutes of the University.

Provision is made under clause 16 for the appointment and duties of the Vice-
Chancellor. The Vice-Chancellor is the academic and administrative head of the
University and chief disciplinary officer of the University. Under the clause, the Vice-
Chancellor is responsible to the Council for the maintenance of order, discipline and
ensuring the effective and efficient administration of the University.

Clause 17 deals with the office of the Pro Vice-Chancellor. The University is to
have a Pro Vice-Chancellor who is appointed by the Council in accordance with the
Statutes of the University. The Pro Vice-Chancellor is to attend a meeting of the
Council but is not entitled to vote at the meeting.

Clause 18 establishes the Academic Board which is answerable to the Council.

The membership of the Academic Board is provided for in clause 19. These
include the Vice-Chancellor, the Pro Vice-Chancellor, Deans and Vice-Deans,
Professors and Associate Professors, the Librarian and the Registrar of the
University.

The functions of the Academic Board are provided for in clause 20. The
functions of the Academic Board include the formulation and implementation of the
academic policies of the University, the regulation of programmes of instruction and
study, subject to accreditation by the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission and the
regulation of the conduct of examinations and the conferment of honorary degrees
and award of degrees, diplomas and certificates.

Clause 21 mandates the Academic Board to establish standing and ad hoc
committees for purposes of carrying out functions specified in the Statutes of the
University.

The Council is required to appoint a Registrar for the University in accordance
with the Statutes of the University, clause 22. The Registrar is to hold office for a
renewable term of four years on the terms and conditions specified in the letter of
appointment in accordance with the Statutes of the University. The Registrar is
responsible to the Vice-Chancellor for the day-to-day administration of the affairs of
the University.

4

Ill IBS

M

W
II
M

The University is to have a Director of Finance under clause 23. The Director of
Finance is to be appointed in accordance with the Statutes of the University and is
responsible to the Vice-Chancellor in the performance of functions.

The Council is further mandated under clause 24 to appoint other staff that may
be necessary for the effective and efficient performance of the functions of the
University.

The Council may make arrangements that the Council considers appropriate for
the internal organisation of the University under clause 25. The internal
arrangements may include the award of professorships and promotion of lecturers,
and the appointment and promotion of academic staff and administrative staff.

Financial matters of the University are dealt with in clauses 26 to 31. Clause 26
enumerates the sources of funds of the University. These include moneys approved
by Parliament, internally generated funds, loans and grants, research grants,
endowments, donations and gifts and moneys from any other source approved by
the Council. The Council may invest the funds of the University that are not required
or needed for immediate use as the Council considers appropriate.

The Council is also empowered under clause 27 to borrow money on behalf of
the University and, for this purpose, use the property of the University as security.
This is subject to article 181 of the Constitution and section 76 of the Public Financial
Management Act, 2016 (Act 921).

The Bill makes provision in clause 28 for an Internal Audit Unit to be established
in accordance with the Public Financial Management Act, 2016 (Act 921).

The standard provisions on accounts and audit and annual report and other
reports are dealt with in clauses 29 and 30 respectively.

Clause 31 exempts the University from the payment of taxes, duties and other
charges that the Minister responsible for Finance may, in writing, determine with the
prior approval of Parliament in accordance with the Exemptions Act, 2022 (Act 1083).

Clauses 32 to 42 deal with miscellaneous matters. Clause 32 requires the
Council of the University to enact Statutes. The Statutes are to provide for the
regulation of the appointments and termination of appointments of staff of the
University, determine the persons who form the academic staff of the University,
determine the persons who are authorised to sign contracts, cheques and other 

5

documents on behalf of the University and the procedure in relation to transactions
entered into by the University.

Clause 33 requires the University to have a Convocation with the membership
specified in the Statutes of the University. The Convocation is to receive and discuss
a report from the Vice-Chancellor on the state of the University and future plans for
the University. The Convocation is also permitted to express an opinion on any
matter that affects the University as well as refer the matter to the Council or the
Academic Board.

A student who is admitted to the University is required to take and subscribe to
the Matriculation Oath and sign the Matriculation Register, clause 34. A student who
fails to sign the Matriculation Register is to be prevented by the University from
graduating from the University.

The University is mandated under clause 35 to hold a Congregation composed
of persons specified in the Statutes of the University for the purpose of conferring
honorary degrees and awarding degrees, diplomas and certificates.

Clause 36 provides for the Students' Representative Council with the
responsibility to represent students duly admitted and registered to study at the
University.

Clause 37 deals with matters on intellectual property. The intellectual property
rights in a creative work, research or any other intellectual enterprise, funded or
otherwise undertaken with the resources of the University, vests in the University.

Clause 38 emphasises the academic freedom of the University. The University,
in the performance of the functions of the University, has the right and responsibility
to preserve and promote the traditional principles of academic freedom in the
conduct of the internal and external affairs of the University.

Clause 39 prohibits discrimination in the University. Under the clause, the
University or an officer of the University is prohibited from discriminating against a
person on the basis of the race, ethnic origin, political opinion, colour, gender,
occupation, religion or creed, disability, social or economic status of that person.

Clause 40 is on dispute settlement. For the purposes of settling disputes, the Bill
establishes the University of Engineering and Agricultural Sciences Appeals Board to
hear and determine matters affecting the staff of the University including a breach of 

6

a contract of employment by the University and the promotion of persons duly
employed by the University.

Finally, clauses 41 and 42 make provision for the interpretation of words and
phrases used in the Bill and transitional arrangements, respectively.

HARUNAIDDRISU, M.P.

UNIVERSITY OF ENGINEERING AND AGRICULTURAL SCIENCES ACT, 2025

AN ACT to establish the University of Engineering and Agricultural Sciences and to provide
for related matters.

PASSED by Parliament and assented to by the President:

University of Engineering and Agricultural Sciences

Establishment of the University of Engineering and Agricultural Sciences
1. (1) There is established by this Act, the University of Engineering and Agricultural

Sciences as a body corporate.
(2) For the performance of the functions of the University, the University may

acquire and hold property, dispose of property and enter into a contract or any other related
transaction.

(3) Where there is a hindrance to the acquisition of land, the land may be
acquired for the University under the Land Act, 2020 (Act 1036) and the cost shall be borne
by the University.

Aims of the University
2. (1) The aims of the University are to

(a) provide higher education in engineering, agriculture, agro-entrepreneurship,
emerging digital disciplines and the built environment;

(b) create, through research, applied engineering and agricultural technologies for
the advancement of agro-entrepreneurship and the built environment;

(c) establish strong connections within the engineering and agriculture sectors to
train graduates for specific professions or advanced research in the field of
operation;

10

(d) train and provide engineers and agriculturalists with relevant competence in
supporting sustainable improvement in agro-entrepreneurship and the built
environment; and

(e) develop strong linkages between the University, industry and the community
to ensure the holistic training of engineering and agriculture professionals.

(2) For the purpose of achieving the aims of the University under subsection (1),
the University shall

(a) determine the programmes to be taught at the University, placing emphasis on
courses of special relevance to the needs of the community for national
development;

(b) promote the use of relevant and practical tools including information and
communication technology for teaching, research, administration and
dissemination of knowledge;

(c) institute curricula within the context of learner-centred and problem-based
learning techniques that are practical and relevant to engineering - and
agriculture education and training;

(d) promote the use of teaching and problem-solving methods that ensure critical
and independent thinking;

(e) undertake research in courses that are within the mandate of the University,
but with special emphasis on

(i) matters that relate to engineering and agriculture training within and
outside the country; and

(ii) subjects that relate to engineering and agriculture training within and
outside the country;

(f) disseminate the results of research undertaken through the publication of
books, journals, papers and any other suitable means;

(g) provide extension and consultancy services in engineering and agriculture
training and related disciplines in higher education;

(h) promote problem-based training by the use of analytical and creative tools
through research and training; and

(i) make higher education equally accessible to all on the basis of capacity by
every appropriate means.

(3) In furtherance of paragraph (i) of subsection (2), the University shall ensure
that the proportion of fee-paying students at any time does not exceed the percentage
approved by the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission in consultation with the Minister.

11

Campuses of the University
3. (1) The main campus of the University shall be situated in Bunso in the Eastern

Region.
(2) The University shall establish a campus of the University at

(a) Kenyasi in the Ashanti Region; and
(b) Acherensua in the Ahafo Region.

(3) The University may, subject to approval from the Ghana Tertiary Education
Commission, establish a campus in any other place that the Council may determine.

Award of degrees, diplomas and certificates
4. (1) The University shall, in accordance with subsection (8) of section 14,

(a) award degrees, diplomas and certificates; and
(b) confer honorary degrees.

(2) The University may withdraw a degree, a diploma or a certificate that the University
has awarded if the University has evidence that proves that

(a) the degree, diploma or certificate was obtained through fraud or academic
malpractice; or

(b) the process of acquiring the degree, diploma or certificate was tainted by an
act that, in the opinion of the University, undermines the integrity of the award.

Governance of the University

University Council
5. (1) The governing body of the University is a Council consisting of

(a) a chairperson, nominated by the President;
(b) the Vice-Chancellor;
(c) three other persons nominated by the President, at least one of whom is a

woman;
(d) one representative each of

(I) the Ministry responsible for Agriculture not below the rank of a Director
nominated by the Minister responsible for Agriculture;

(II) the Ghana Institution of Surveyors nominated by the Ghana Institution
of Surveyors;

12

(iii) the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission nominated by the Ghana
Tertiary Education Commission;

(iv) the Engineering Council nominated by the Engineering Council;
(v) the Students' Representative Council nominated by the Students'

Representative Council;
(vi) the Conference of Heads of Assisted Secondary Schools nominated

by the Conference of Heads of Assisted Secondary Schools;
(vii) junior and senior staff associations nominated by the junior and senior

staff associations;
(ix) the alumni of the University nominated by the alumni of the University;

and
(x) the Association of Ghana Industries nominated by the Association of

Ghana Industries; and
fej three members of the Convocation representing the professorial, non-

professorial and non-teaching staff nominated by Convocation.
(2) The President shall appoint the chairperson and other members of the

Council in accordance with article 70 of the Constitution.
(3) The President shall, in making the appointments under paragraphs (a) and (c)

of subsection (1), have regard to
(a) academic and professional qualifications;
(b) leadership qualities;
(c) expertise in finance and management; and
(d) knowledge and relevant experience in engineering and agricultural sciences.

(4) The chairperson of the Council shall, in the absence of the Chancellor,
preside at the Congregation and any other meeting or ceremony of the University.

Functions of the Council
6. The Council shall

(a) ensure the achievement of the aims of the University;
(b) determine the strategic direction of the University;
(c) monitor and evaluate the implementation of the policies of the University;
(d) promote income-generating activities as part of the programmes of the

University;
